div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
One of the first sensational trials at the Old

Bailey in which Mr. Montagu Williams was en- gaged was designated the great police perjury case of 1863. On the evidence of some constables a quartette of fine young loafers were tried for an attempted burglary at a house in the Regent's-park, but were acquitted. Some friends, on their behalf, then brought a counter-action against their ac- cusers. Sergeant Ballantine defended the police, with Mr. Williams as his junior, and Sergeant Shee was retained for the prosecution. In spite of the magnificent oratory of Ballantine and the active co- operation of his rising junior, the trial resulted in a verdict against their clients the police, who were sentenced to long periods of penal servitude.

Among the Church livings which will shortly fall to Lord Herschell's disposal is that of. Nuneaton, Warwickshire, the annual value of which is about £BOO. Canon Bellairs, the present incumbent, is one of the best-hated men in the town, his broad views not being at all in accord with those of the Tory manufacturers and tradesmen who comprise the "aristocracy "of the place. Early this year an attempt was made by Mr. F. A. Newdigate, M.P., and Bishop Perowne to induce the worty canon to resign in order that the appointment of a successor might fall to the lot of Lord Halsbury, who was ready to pop a friend of Mr. Newdigate into the vacancy, but Mr. Bellairs preferred to remain in possession until the end of the year, and the design was thus thwarted.

Archdeacon Hessey, who died on Christmas Eve, had a vein of quiet humour in him. Some years ago, when the late Archdeacon Sinclair was Vicar of Kensington, there was a gathering at the vicarage after some function in the parish church. " Who preached ?" asked Dr. Hessey, of the clergyman sitting next him. " The Archdeacon," replied his neighbour, "and a very good sermon it was too." " Was it now?" continued Dr. Hessey ; " I wonder -whether I know it. What was the subject ?" "It was from such and such a text," was the reply, " and the subject was Eve's emotions at the birth of Cain.' " " Oh, yes, I know it," remarked Dr. Hessey, " It's a very good sermon. I've heard it more than once, and wondered what the Archdeacon as a bachelor, could possibly know about the sub- ject."

Mr. Horace W. C. Newle, one of the moat success- ful of the younger generation of playwrights, is now only :25 years of age, being born in Wiltshire in 1870. He was educated at Hertford and Christ's Hospital. He was destined for the navy, though he has been engaged in literary pursuits ever since he was 17, being a regular contributor to the defunct Ariel. He won " The Players' " lever de rideau competition with a one act drama entitled "Leon- ore," and has already sold a play to Mr. W. S. Pen- ley, which will shortly be produced in the pro- vinces. He has also written a blank verse tragedy, and a four act drama " Oiga," which is to be pro- duced in the new year, and Mr. Grein has a play of which he thinks most favourably. An operetta Las also emanated from his pen, as well as a play for Miss Violet Vanbrugh.

Colonel Hutton, the Queen's newest A.D.O , is a tall, well-built, soldierly-looking man of four-and- forty, with a bronzed aquiline face and dark mous- tache and hair. During the last half of his live- and-twenty years of service—the colonel joined his "crack" regiment, the 60th Rifles, in 1867—he has seen a good deal of fighting. The Zulu war, the Boer fiasco, the Egyptian campaign, the Nile expe- dition—in all of these he played a part, received clasps and medals, and was frequently mentioned in dispatches. His energy and skill have been specially devoted to the organisation of the mounted infan- try, not only in his foreign campaigns, but at Aldershot since his home appointment in 1887. The colonel, who has a town house in Bolton-st., is a particularly pleasant and agreeable companion, and in the discharge of his social duties is admirably as- sisted by his wife, a daughter of the late General Sir A. J. Lawrence.

The Speaker of the House of Commons has lately presented to the parish church of Sand, Bedford- shire, a memorial window in memory of Mrs. Peel, and it is now to be seen above the altars, making the fourth of the stained glass windows that adorn the interior of the sacred edifice. There is another monument in the same church connected with the Peel family, viz., a marble status, by Theed, set up to the memory of Captain Sir William Peel, son of Sir Robert Peel, who was at the head of the naval brigade, during the Crimean War, and died in India while engaged on active service during the Mutiny. Otherwise the church, though ancient, contains little of interest. Sandy has developed wmider- fully of late years, and from being a mere village, surrounded by gardens for the growth of onions and cucumbers, has become an important place with over two thousand inhabitants. It is healthy, central, and not unpicturesque with its fir-clad hills. The Speaker lives just outside the village in a house built by himself in 1877.

Mr. Albert Toft, the young sculptor who has just been entrusted with the commission for the bronze statue of the late Henry Richards, president of the Peace Society, which will be erected in his native place, has probably had:one of the hardest struggles for art that men ever endured, though he is now a successful sculptor, and no one of his age has done mere in the way of portrait busts. He was born at West Bromwich just 30 years ago, and was educated in Birminghatn,where his father was chief modeller in the firm of Messrs. Elkington and Co., which firm he left to join he Wedgwoods. This brought the family to the Potteries, with which town the name bas been associated since the seventeenth century, and it was there that young Tort began ohs train- ing as a pottery modeller, at the same time attend- ing evening art classes, sometimes remaining at his studies all night. His industry was rewarded by gaining a scholarship at South Kensington for three years, during which time he worked almost entirely from tie nude, and gained many honours.

Dr. Churchill JulinF, Anglican Bishop of Christ- church, New Zealand, is about to visit England on private and diocesan business. His superfine digni- fied brother prelates is this country will not go into ecstasies over this news, for Dr. Julius is the most unconventional of Anglican prelates. It will be re- membered that about a year ago he was hauled up in a chair at the end of a rope to a height of two or three hundred feet in order to lay the topmost brick of his cathedral spire. Before that he had distin- guished himself 'by refusing an episcopal carriage and pair, and snubbing the would-be presenters with the intimation that theordinary public means ot conveyance were good enough tor him. From 1884 to 1890 he was Archdeacon of the Ballarat goldfield, and there it was his habit to knock about at all hours, administering personal chastisement to wife-beaters, and bring them to the lock-up with- out troubling the police in the matter. In Ballarat, too, lie both preaciied and collected for the dockers on strike in London. He is the son of the late Dr. Julius, of Richmond, Surrey, and graduated at Wor cester College, Oxford, in 1869. Before emigrating to the Antipodes he was successively curate of St Giles, Norwich ; vicar of Shapwick, Somerset ; and -Vicar of Holy Trinity, Islington.

Those who are familiar at Brighton or Monte Carlo with the somewhat striking personality of Lady Euston may not remember that she once figured as the victim in a cause celebre in which Montagu Williams was engaged—the second trial of Froggatt, the fradulent solicitor. A good many years ago her ladyship, who was then Mrs. Kate Smith, and who will some day, in all probability, be Duchess of Grafton, was one of the most attrac- tive ladies in her own set at the Westend. Her charms won the affections of young Mr.Fitzroy,now Lord Euston, who married her. Froggatt WWI one of Mrs. Fitzroy's trustees, and when he was impri- soned for complicity in the turf frauds, in which , one or two well-known London detectives_ were also concerned, the dividends on Mrs. Fitzroy, .5 sub. stantial settlement came to an untimely end. On inquiry it was found that every pennr of the cap- ital had been sold out by Froggatt, who on his dis- charge from prison was re-arrested and tried for the fraud at the Old Bailey, a trial in which Lady Euston, the whole of whose fortune had disap- peared, gave evidence, which lasted some days, and in which the skill and eloquence of Montagu Williams were displayed. The result was a further term of penal servitude for Froggatt, who in vain made a piteous appeal to the judge, and who never lived to regain his liberty.

The to great pests of county courts are travell- ing drapers or tallymen and extortionate money- lenders. Mr. G. Pitt-Lewis tells us of plans adopted by judges to get rid of these nuisances. The tally- man is in the habit of getting workmen's wives to buy some useless piece of nery at more than a reasonable price, and then a the husbands for the

money. A wife has an implied authority to make contracts for her husband, but a late county court judge used to argue that the tallyman's contract was of a special kind—a promise to pay by instal- ments. "I do not," he said, " find that the wile had authority to make any special bargain. Mr. Tallyman is nonsuited." And this decision held goad and was never appealed against. Other county court judges have adopted, Mr. Pitt-Lewis tells us,- equally short (and excellent) ways with extortion-4, ate money-lenders. The judge would argue that if la man borrowed money at an extortionate rate of ,of interest, he must have been very hard pressed, and must have known that ha was unable to pay. He wanted proof that the man who had borrowed on such terms had ever had the means of paying the interest ; and so exacting was the amount of proof, needed to do this that the usurioas petty money lender would transfer his " practice " to a more com-1 plaisant judge. If judges were to adopt these plans, Mr. Pitt-Lewis thinks that special legislation would; I not be necessary, but unfortunately county court: judges sympathise in most cases with the tallyma and the money-lender.

div.head: WHEN EDISON WAS YOUNG. AN ENTERTAINING YARN.
div.p: WHEN EDISON WAS YOUNG. AN ENTERTAINING YARN.

"I was an operator in the Memphis office when Thomas A. Edison applied to the manager for a position," said Mr. A. G. Rock-feller, a member of the Reminiscence Club, St. Louis. "He came walk- ing into the office one morning, looking like a verit- able hayseed. He wore a hickory shirt, a pair of butternut pants tucked into the tops of boots a size too large and guiltless of blacking. Where's the boss ?" was the query, as he glanced round the office. No one replied at once, and he repeated the ques- tion. The manager asked him what he could do for him, and Edison proceeded to strike him for a job. Business was rushing, and the office was two men short, so almost any kind of a lightning-slinger was welcome. He was assigned to a desk, and a fusilade of winks went the rounds of the office, for the 'jay' was put on the St. Louis wire, the hardest in the office. At the end of the line was an operotor who was chain lightening, and knew it. Edison had hardly got seated before St. Louis called. The new corner responded, and St. Louis started in on a long report, and he pumped it in like a house afire. Edison threw his leg over the arm of the chair, leisurely transferred a wad of spruce gum from his pocket to his mouth, picked up a pen, examined it critically, and started in, about 200 words behind. He didn't stay there long, though. St. Louislet out another link of speed, and still another, and the instrument hummed like an old-sewing machine. Every man in the office left his desk, and gathered ' round the 'jay' to see what he was doing with that electric cyclone. Well, sir, he was right on the word, and was putting it down in the prettiest copperplate hand you ever saw, even crossing his t's, dotting his i's, and punctuating with as much I care as a man editing telegraph for ' printers. St. Louis got tired by and by, and began to slow down. Edison opened the key and said, Here, here ! This is no primer, class! Get a hustle on you! Well, sir, that broke St. Louis all up. He had been 'raw-hiding' Memphis for a long time, and we were terribly sore, and to have a man in our office that could walk all over him made no feel like a man whose horse had won the Derby. I saw the • wizard' not long ago. Ile doesn't wear a hickory shirt, nor put his pants in his boots, but he is very far fro:n being a dude yet."

div.head: WONDER IF TODDLES KNOWS NOW.
div.p: WONDER IF TODDLES KNOWS NOW.

When a boy I was always fond of eating and drink- ing—especially of eating. What boy isn't ? I had an appetite then, and a digeston also. One day a gentleman came to dine at our house. I shall never forget that man. He had dull eves and a purple com- plexion. He watched my styla of eating for about five minutes, and then said to my father. " Does your boy ever suffer from dyspepsia ?" "Never heard him complain of it," replied my father. "Do you ever suffer from dyspepsia, Toddles ?" (They called me Toddles, but it was not my real name.)

"No, pa," I answered. " What is dyspepsia. pa ?" My purple faced friend regarded me with a look of amazement and envy, and solemnly said, " You will find out—some day. The above incident a well-known Englishman tells about himself. Whether he has since found out what dyspepsia is, he doesn't say. Likely enough. His father's guest was well booked on the subject. That we may guarantee. That's how he got the purple skin and the dull eyes. And that's what made hipri fairly turn sour with envy when he saw the boy eating like a hungry dog, and with as little fear of the consequences. 21h , dear, dear ! if we elderly men and women could eat now as we could when our chins came just up to the top of the table ! But we can't, that's certain. Why not? Well, here's one good woman tells why she couldn't, and she was so much in earnest in the tale that she went before the Mayor of Leeds and had it put into form which carries weight and conviction with it. Thus we have it :

div.head: [COPY.]
div.p: [COPY.]
" I. Caroline Nixon (wife of Ezra Nixon, wholesale clog manufacturer), of 4, St. Agnes Mount, Stoney Hock Lane, and 85, Upper Accommodation-road, Leeds, do solemnly and sincerely declare as follows

" lip to November, 1885, I was always )itrong and hearty. At this time I fell into a low weak state. I was tired, languid, and low spirited. I had a bad taste in the mouth and expectorated a deal of phlegm. My appetite was poor, and after eating I had great pain at the chest and between the shoulders, and so bad was this that I was afraid to eat. I got no sleep at night, and for weeks would lie awake most of the night, and was worse tired in the morning than when I went to bed. I was quite worn out, and got so weak that I could scarcely get about the house. As it was, had to constantly lie down on the couch. Having a large family to look after, I was compelled to be 'up and doing, otherwise I should have been in bed. I had often heard people speak of Indigestion and Dyspepsia, but did not think it was so bad as I found it. In this miserable condition I continued week after week, only to find myself getting weaker and weaker. I saw a doctor in York Road, •who gave me medicine, but I got no better. Getting anxious, I went to a clever, experienced doctor, but after being under his treatment some time ' I gave up taking his medicine, for I got worse instead of better. Both doctors said I was suffer- ing from indigestion, but they were unable to do anything fer me. I now lost all faith in physic, and looked on my case as incurable, when one day a book was left at the house telling of a medi- cine called Mother Seig,?l's Curative Syrup, and I read of several cases resembling mine having been cured by it. I sent te Mr. Cole, Chemist, in Marsh Lane and got a bottle. After taking the Sytup three days I felt re- lief, my appetite returned and my food digested, and before I had taken one large bottle I was cured,and have siace kept in good health. After my recovery one of my daughters was taken bad with rheumatism, so I gave her some Seigel's Syrup and she soon got well. If any of my family ail anything a dose or two of the Syrup soon sets them right, and for the past four or five years we have needed no doctor owing to taking the medicine. I consider that Seigel's Syrup has saved my life, and I have recommended it to many, and if pub- lishing this statement others may come to be benefited, I give permission to the proprietors to use it as they think proper.

"And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true. By virtue of the provisions of the Statutory Declaration Act, 1835 (Will. IV.,c, 62). (Signed) CAROLINE NIXON. " Declared before me at Leeds in the") County of York by the said Caroline I Nixon, this 6th day of October, 1891. } " (Signed) ALP. COOKE, " 3fayor of Leeds."i

Mrs. Nixon says " I have often heard people speak of indigestion and dyspepsia, but did not think it was so bed as I found it." There's just where the trouble is. Healthy folks simply can't imagine what a concentrated horror, what a death-in-liie, this disease is. If they could they would take every precaution against it. Even Toddles would have eaten fewer tarts, puddings, and cakes. For indigestion and dyspepsia, lightly as we speak of it in our ignorance,actually destroys more human beings than war, pestilence, and famine combined, and the only trustworthy remedy, so far as we yet know, is the one mentioned and used by Mrs. Nixon.

div.head: 44,• THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 31, 1892
div.p: 44,• THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 31, 1892

vrete'reand bra body Nifo-fe ne—graspert my inten- tion, but when it dawned upon him, he struggled and tried to free himself. For a time we wrestled in deadly silence, he giving way inch by inch before my superior weight. Hugh, spare me !he cried at length as we neared the edge of the cliffs. But murder was in my heart as I answered, Have you spared me my love? You wanted to go away, so go.' And with the strength of a maniac I lifted and threw him. 'His hands caught the edge of the cliff, to which he clung with a despairing grip, and never, Oh Heaven ! shall I forget the look he gave me. I can see it now, it has never left me, and wherever I look, there are his horror-stricken eyes fixed on mine. For a moment he hung suspended, and then, with a cry for help, disappeared from my sight. 'lt was only now that I fully realised what I had done, when he was beyond my help. There could be no doubt that he was dead, death was the cer- tain fate of anyone falling from those awful cliffs. I was a murderer. I had taken the life of my brother whom my mother on her death-bed com- mitted to my care, and this was how I had fulfilled my trust. 'My feelings were indescribable. I was filled with remorse, and flung myself on the ground, clutching at the earth in agony. How long I lay there I know not, but when my reason returned, night had fallen. My first and only idea was flight, and that as rapidly as possible. Hugh Gwywdd must be buried with his brother. The murderer must take another name. Home and friends must know me no more, we would perish together. So I fled. '1 made my way to Holyhead, and it was sty intention to work my passage to America as a sailor. On reaching that town, I bought gorse coarse sailor clothes and as I allowed my beard to grow, I was soon so altered in appearance, that I might have passed my most intimate friend on the same footpath without fear of recognition. I boarded in a common lodging house, and became a companion of the lowest dregs of society. Of oourse I had changed my name, and I assiduously studied the manners and talk of sailors, that I might more easily pass for one. At last I got a berth, and after a stormy passage, landed in America. It is needless to describe my life during all these intervening years, suffice it to say it has been one long history of misery and wretchedness. And now, though I never intended to set foot in Wales again, here I am, come home to die, drawn by an impulse I could not resist. Your great kindness in nursing a forlorn stranger has conquered my resolution, otherwise no one would ever have known that this wreck who lies before you is Hugh Gwywdd of Bryn Llwyd.' So finished the history of this miserable sinning creature, and a few days later he left this world of care and sorrow and entered his eternal rest." Silence filled the room for some minutes after the Vicar had completed the story and then as there was still sufficient light I begged him to show me the grave and the scene of the tragedy. We walked out in the still, cool evening air to the little churchyard, the inmates of which are lulled to sleep by the never- ceasing murmur of the restless sea. He pointed to a grave, marked with a plain headstone, on which two initials were cut "H. G.," nothing more, for it was his dying wish that he should remain unknown even in the grave. We left the grave in silence and walked towards the cliffs; the big waves of the Irish Sea came rolling along until they encountered the rocks, when, bursting with a booming noise, the spray flew so high that it reached us where we stood. "It was here," my companion said, in a hushed voice, and we stood awhile in silence, picturing the whole scene as it had taken place. 'Both brothers are to be pitied, but how much preferable the fate of the one who died here,' I qaid. "God rest their souls," the Vicar said fervently as we turned our steps toward his house. We parted at the Vicarage gates, and the next day I left the village. In due course I arrived at home, and settled down to another year's work. Some time afterwards I heard that the kind old man was dead, so I may now use the per- mission he gave me to publish this sad story on his decease. And I trust it will interest my readers as much as it did me, when I heard it related in that little out-of-the-world village on the rock- bound coast of Anglesey.

CLYAIRE—" After all, society is a hollow thing ?" Cooley—" You don't seem able to get into it, though." "DID you and Dennis Anderson come to terms in your dispute ?" asked a business man of his coachman. Yes, sor ; and very uncompliment'ry terms they wor, sor." MRS. GRIMSHAW—" He was awfully unlucky to break his leg.' Mrs. Malaprop —" I don't see how you can say so. He recovered £l5O damages, and it cost only £2O to have it set."

"QUEER critters women is," said Uncle Jehiel. "When one of 'em starts in to git a man all the others tries to head her off, an' then, soon as she gits him, they all turn round and help her to man- age him." FOR a neat mixture of metaphors it is not easy to beat the opening sentence of a recent paragraph in a morning contemporary—" Many are the pit- falls which lie in the path of a man who sits down to make his will." AN old Scottish matron was one day sadly com- plaining of the depravity of modern times. She wound up her diatribe with the assertion that "Paradise was now changed into a pair o' dice, and matrimony into a matter o' money.'

BnowN—" You don't seem to have a very high opinion of your husband's ability ?" Mrs Malaprop—" No, he's a very ignorant man. Last night he spoke of persons acting in concert when he should have known that they only sing at such entertainments."

A Scomi boy was one morning at breakfast, when he bawled out, "Oh, mistress, there's a flea running in the milk, and its legs are touching the bottom." The mistress said, " What, Jock, de ye no' get eneuch o' milk ? " The boy replied, "0, yes, mistress, plenty for the porridge I get." AT a dinner party one day, Sir John H--, whose character was considered not to be altogether unexceptionable said he would give them a toast, and looking hard in the face of Mrs. M--, who was more celebrated for wit than beauty, gave "Honest men an' bonny lasses ' " With all my heart, Sir John," said Mrs. M--, " for it neither applies to you nor me." LITTLE BESSIE had been offended in some way. She went off into a corner of the room and turned her back on the company. "I'm mad," she exclaimed, sulkily. ''l wish I didn't have any , papa or mamma.' "That's wrong, dear," said her mother. "We are the best friends you have.' "Well," said Bessie, still sulking, "I don't mind havin' papa. He isn't here much. But I m gettin' awful tired of the rest of you." Two schoolboys one day, on the banks of the Yarrow, observed a bird's nest built on the arch of a bridge over a deep pool. They were most anxious to get at the eggs, but could think of no way of accomplishing their object. At last it was resolved that one should hold on by the edge of the bridge and the other creep down and hold by his neighbour's legs. When nearly accomplishing their object the uppermost boy got tired, and called out to his neighbour, " Hold, hold, till I spit on my hands," and with that both of them fell into the water and were nearly drowned.

tillOSTS.—Ttiere is a curious case related ot a man who was a well-known character, and a man of sense—where it was said he used to see a number of people in the room with him. Now, he him:Lit has described the whole of the phenomenon and all the adjuncts to it. He has said, after taki,g a cup of coffee or tea, or so on, they came into his room in great numbers; and as he got better, and less nervous, he has only seen the arms or legs of the persons, without seeing any other part of them. Now, this is all an irregblar action of the retina of the eye. A gentleman sitting in his library one day, reading or writing, on turning round his head. saw, sitting in a chair, a woman in a red cloak. And he said, How came you in here, good Woman? The woman said nothing. What is the meanim: of your being here, woman? No answer was made. 179 u have no right to be here ;go out of the room. Sh e took no notice of him. He got up and rang the bell for the servant. The servant came in. Turn this woman out. What woman, sir? Why, the woman in the red cloak. There's no woman, nor any red cloak, sir. Well, go and fetch the doctor for roe; tell him lam ill, and wish to speak with him. The man, however, was not to be frightened by this, because he knew it was a delusion of his sight. Now, I have had it so often that it has been a matter rather of amusement to me, than anything else. I have stood before a glass, and seen the upper pan of my head and eyes, and nose very distinctly; but I never saw that I had any month or jaw; and I have seen my shoulders very well, but all was blank between my nose and shoulders. Why, now I say, what can you make of this but that it is errors of action, or inactivity in parts of the retina I—A bernstkit's Leehwvsg-
THEIR CHRISTMAS BASKET.
BY ELIZABETH CAMPBELL.

The Brantwood Mansion was the handsomest house in the neighbourhood, and the outward appearance thereof, and the grounds surrounding it were the admiration of all beholders. These same beholders would have equally admired the interior of the house if they could have had the opportunity; but for the past five years visitors there were very rare, and those who did occasionally venture on a call did not care to prolong their visits, and seldom repeated them; for they said the atmosphere within was gloomy and uninviting, notwithstanding the splendour of grand furniture, handsome pictures, and frescoed ceilings. It was Christmas Eve, but the Brantwood Man- sion instead of blazing with light as a grand old place, the home of wealthy people, ought to do, on such a festal occasion, was dark and gloomy. Lights shone in only a single apartment—a sitting. room of Mrs. Brantwood's, where a bright coal fire burned in the highly polished grate, and a study. lamp on the centre-table gave f•"..:1 a subdued but steady light. A middle-aged couple were the only occupants of the room, and they sat, one on either side of the table, apparently absorbed in the books lying in front of them. They had sat so for nearly an hour and neither had turned a leaf of the books, and probably had not read a word on the pages open before them. For both were thinking of an only daughter—anti an only child, for she was all in the world to them—who was now far away in some distant land, perhaps, but they knew not where, and scarcely hoped in this world to look upon her face again. Ada Brantwood had been a spoiled and petted child on whom her father ang mother had lavished the whole treasure of their affections. At first they had been disappointed because the daughter had not been a son, for they had wanted an heir to perpetuate the family name, and to in- herit the family wealth, but they soon got over that disappointment; and as Ada grew to girlhood, and then toward womanhood, they began to dream of the grand marriage she would make, and deter- mined to find in her husband the son Heaven had denied them. They chose the husband, too, and for a little while it seemed as if Ada was willing to abide by their choice; but all at once she grew strangely indifferent to Oliver Villard ; and a few weeks after that she was missing one morning, and a note found stuck in the corner of her looking-glass told "dear papa and mamma" that she had gone away to get married to Herr Valentine Bergman, the German tutor of a young friend, whom she had met, and fallen in love with, at her friend's house. The note added that she hoped "dear papa and mamma wouldn't be very angry, and a letter would reach her at—" and then she gave her friend's address.

But alas! papa and munma were terribly angry, and very justly so too; it is true "mamma's" anger very soon dissolved in a rain of tears, but " papa's " lasted long enough to enable him to write a very hard and bitter letter to Ada, forbidding her to ever hope for his forgiveness, and applying such harsh and unjust terms to her husband that the young wife felt, in her turn, that she could never forgive her father. Often, oh I how often Mr. Brantwood had wept tears of regret—of remorse, over that letter sent to his only child in the first heat of anger! For when that anger had cooled, and it had not taken long, either, the news that he heard of his daughter was that she had gone with her young husband to a far distant land—a land that seemed to the bereaved parents the other end of the world—Australia. He sent messages of forgiveness after her; he adver- tised in all the papers, but he never from that hour heard one word of or from his pretty blue-eyed Ada. Once be heard that the vessel on which she was said to have sailed was lost; but that he dared not, and would not, believe; for he still prayed each night that closed the day for the return of his little girl. And he had studiously kept that dark rumour from his wife's ears, all unconscious that she, too, had heard it, and with like care for his feelings, endeavoured to keep him from learning it.

It was of all this, and much more—of memories of their girl's happy childhood, of the Christmas- tree, laden with gifts, on which her bright young eyes used to rest in childish rapture each successive Christmas morn, and then, as she grew older, of the gifts they used to give her, selecting them for weeks before the happy day, and always receiving such in turn from her—for she was the only one privileged to bring gifts to them. Suddenly Mrs. Brantwood heard a long, deep, sad sigh and it was echoed with pitiful promptitude from the other side of the table. Husband and wife looked up, and looked across into each other's earful eyes. "Ah, Henry," sobbed the wife, "no one will send us a Christmas-boy to-morrow."

It was the nearest of a reproach to any word she had spoken since their daughter went away. "Dearest, try to forgive me, for, oh I never can forgive myself!" sighed the unhappy father. And then a prolonged and very loud ring at the front door bell prevented a reply, and, indeed, caused both Mr. and Mrs. Brentwood to start nervously to their feet with simultaneous exclama- tions of surprise. "Who can that be, at this hour?" said Mrs. Brentwood. I never before heard the bell give out such a peal." " I can't imagine," answered Mr. Brentwood. "We are not expecting visitors; indeed,"—and this was added with a sigh—" nobody cares to visit us now.' And then the housemaid appeared at the door, bearing what seemed to be a very heavy basket— it was certainly a very large one—and panting and nearly breathless with the exertion of bring- ing it up stairs, she set it down on the floor, and gave her message in jerks, stopping frequently for breath. "If you please, ma'am, it was left at the door; leastways, there wasn't a soul there when I got the door opened; and cook and me carried it in, and she helped me part of the way up stairs; and this was pinned to the top, which we had to read it, ma'am, to see who it was meant for." And then she handed a written paper to Mrs. Brentwood. The lady hastily glanced over the lines on it, and read them aloud: " A Christmas-box for Mr. and Mrs. Brantwood. Please carry with great care; something very precious inside." 46 How strange," mused the lady. "What can it be? And who can have sent us anything so strange for a present However, we will open it, and see what it is. Lift off the covering, Mary."_

Mary proceeded to lift off a soft, thin, fleecy shawl of white Shetland wool, and then, stooping to see what came next, uttered a wild exclamation Of astonishment. "0, ma'am, a baby 1" And then, like a true woman, she fell on her knees beside the basket, and clasped her hands in a transport of delighted surprise. Mrs. Brantwood, noway behind her servant in

amazement, or pleasure either, knelt on the other side, and bent in rapture over the lovely, white dimpled darling. There never was a prettier baby In the world; and now, as the lady bent over it, a pair of heavenly blue eyes looked up at her, the rosebud mouth dimpled with smiles, and stretch- ing out two tiny hands, the baby cooed like a dove.

"0, you angel I" cried Mrs. Brantwood, half smothering it with kisses. And then taking the little creature with great care into her arms, she carried it over to Mr. Brentwood. "See, Henry, dear, a baby? Such an angel • and with the blue eyes, and hair like gold, too hat a gift from Heaven, whoever has sent it! Mr. Brantwood looked with milder, more mascu- line admiration on the lovely infant; but, in his way, he was glad to see it, too. "See! What is this' he said, bending over it,

and detaching a tiny slip of paper that w-a's pinned to the dress. Then holding it close to the lamp, he read: "Her name is Ada.' Mrs. Brantwood became very pale, and trembled so that she was glad to take the chair Mary hastened to bring to her. " Let me see that, Henry," she said, putting out her tremulous hand for the paper, and holding the still laughing and cooing baby closer to her breast. And then she, too, read the slip of paper. "Her name is Ada 1' faltered the trembling mother. "And her yellow hair and blue eyes—oh! father 1 father 1 I dare not hope it, but if it only might be 1" And then there was a rustling outside in the hall, and a still girlish figure rustled in, and kneeling at the feet of her parents, sobbed out: ler It is—it is—mother I—father !---it is your mighty, wicked girl! Forgive me for the sake of this little Ada 1" Happily, joy seldom kills, or else Ada's experi- ment in surprises might have had a far from bright termination. As it was, she caught her mother's half-fainting form in her w ins in time to save it from slipping to the floor. While Mr. Brentwood ' caught them all three—mother, daughter, and I grandchild—to his heart; and then the handsome young German husband came in for his share of j =acme. And in all the district there' wasi DA

happier Christmas Eve than that within the wars of Brantwood Mansion. Lights gleamed from every window; a yule-log Wowed in the old- fashioned dining-room fire-place; and, late though it was, a Christmas tree was prepared for the morn- ing. Gifts raiNed in on every side, and fairest and sweetest and best among them all was Mr. and Mrs. Brantwood's golden-haired, blue-eyed visitor in the CHRISTMAS BASKET.

div.head: AN EASTERN SIORY.
div.p: AN EASTERN SIORY.

Many of our readers will remember the story in the Arabian Nights' Entertainments, in which a good Mohammedan who went upon a journey lost his money by having deposited it in a put of ol.vcs, which he placed in the custody of a merchant till he should return. A story, somewhat similar, though a little more humorous, is told by Fuller in his amusing "Narrative of a Tour through some parts of the Turkish Empire," and which he mention he heard from a friend in Aleppo; he entitles it

- THE JEW OF HAMM. Once upon a time there lived in }Tomah a certain Turk called Mustapha, who having accumulated some wealth by carrying on a trade in goat's hair, determined to make a pilgrimage to Mecca. His family consisted of his wife and two slaves; and as the lady insisted on not being left behind, the good man resolved to sell off his stock of goat's hair, to take all his household with him, and to shut up his house till his return. The only difficulty that pre- sented itself was what to do with his money. He did not like to run the risk of being robbed of it in his journey through the Desert, he did not like to leave it in an empty house, and there were not any of his friends to whom he wished to trust the secret of his wealth. After much deliberation, he placed it in separate parcels at the bottom of five large earthen jars, which he then filled up with butter, and on his departure sent them to the house of one of his neighbours, a Jew named Mousa, to keep till his return, telling him that it was a stock which he had laid in for winter con- sumption. The Jew, however, from the weight of the jars and other circumstances, suspected that they contained something more valuable; and as soon as Mustapha was fairly on his way to Damascus to join the caravan, he ventured to open them; when finding his expectations realised, he took out the gold, and filled them up again with batter so carefully, that nobody could tell that they had been disturbed. The poor Turk, on his return from the pilgrimage, soon found out the trick his neighbour had practised upon him; but as the jars were exactly in the same apparent state as when he left them, and as there was no evidence as to their contents, it was plain that no legal process could give him any redress. He therefore set about to devise some other way of punishing the Jew, and of recovering, if possible, his property; and in the mean time he did not communicate his loss to any person but his wife, and enjoined on her the strictest secrecy.

After long consideration a plan suggested itself. In one of his visits to the neighbouring town of Horns, where he was in the habit of going to sell his goat's hair to the manufacturers of the mash- lakhs, for which that plo.ce is famous, he fell in with a troop of gypsies, who had with them an ape of extraordinary sagacity. He prevailed on them to sell him this animal; and, conveying it privately to his house at Haufah, shut it up in a room to which no one but himself had access. He then went to the bazaar, and bought one of the dark scanty robes and the small caps, with a speckled handkerchief tied close.y round It, which is the prescribed cos- tume of the Jews throughout the Turkish empire. This dress he took care invariably to put on when- ever he went to visit his ape; and as he always carried him his meals, and indeed never allowed any other person to see him, the animal in the course of a few weeks became extremely attached to him, jumping on his neck, and hugging and caressing him as soon as he entered the room. About this time, as he was walking along the streets one day he met a lad, the son of the Jew Mouse, and, having enticed him into his house by the promise of some figs, he shut him up a close prisoner in a detached department in his garden, at such a distance from the street and from the other houses in the town that the boy could not discover to any one the place of his confinement. The Jew, after several days' search, not being able to obtain any tidings of him, concluded that he had either been drowned, or had strayed out of the town, and fallen in the hands of some wandering Bedouins; and as he was his only child, fell into a state of the greatest despair; till at length he heard by accident, that just about the time that the boy was missing, he had been seen walking in company with Hadgi Mnstapha. The truth instantly flashed on his mind, and he recognised in the loss of his son some stratagem which the Turk had planned in revenge for the affair of the butter-jars. He immediately summoned him before the Cadi, accused him of having the boy in his possession, and insisted on his immediately restoring him. Mustapha at first strenuously denied the fact; but when one of the wit- nesses postively declared that he saw the boy go into his houce, and when the Cadi was about to pro- nounce his decree that he should bring him into court dead or alive, he exclaimed, "There is no God but Allah. and his power is infinite; he can work miracles when it seemeth good in his sight. It is true," continued he, addressing himself to the CAI. "that I saw the Jew Mousa's son passing by my house; and, for the sake of the old friendship sub- sisting between his father and myself, I invited him to come in and to eat some figs which I had just been gathering. The boy, however, repaid my hospitality with rudeness and abuse: nay, he even blasphemed the name of our holy prophet; but scarcely had the words passed his lips, when, to my surprise and horror, he was suddenly changed into a monkey. In that form I will produce him: and as a proof that what I tell you is true, you will see that he will immediately recognise his father."

At this instant a servant, who was waiting on the outside, let loose the ape into the divan, who, seeing that the Jew was the only perzon present in the dress to which he was accustomed, mistook him for his master, jumped upon hin., and clung round his neck with all the expressions of fondness which the child might have been supposed to exhibit on being restored to his parent. Nothing more was wanting to convince the audience of the truth of Mustaplia's story: "A miracle, a real miracle!" they cried out; " and the Jew was ordered to take the monkey, and retire from the court. A compromise was now his only resource; and, accordingly, as soon as it was dark, and he could go unobserved, he repaired to Mustapha's house, and offered, if he would liberate his son, to restore all the money which he had taken from the butter-jars. The Turk, having attained his object, consented to release his pr.soner ; but, In order to keep up his own credit, he stipulated that the child should be removed privately, and that the father with his whole family should immedi- ately quit the place. The popular belief in the miracle thus remained unshaken; and so great was the disrepute into which the Jews fell in consequence of this adventure, that they all de- parted one after the other, and none have ever since been known to reside in Hamah.

A TALE OF 1910.
t
THE CAPTURE OF LIVERPOOL.

"Strange, yes, strange indeed," said Jack Brakespear sitting in his club smokerootn one afternoon in mid- winter, and addressing his iriend Tom Ponsonby„ "Strange indeed, that fora hundred years or so the wield has never seen a really great naval war. Ws think we know everything, and yet we are ignorance incarnate as to what a naval engagement would result in, or the thousand and one problems it would solve." " You don't'forget," observed Ponsonby, "that affair at Liverpool and the fighting between the Italians and Austrians in the Adriatic many years before ?" "Oh no, but those affairs proved nothing; at least, they only upset some preconceived ideas and calcula- tions. Ironclad rams were at one time going to be all destructive in naval war. Well, at Lissa, we had the spectacle of an ironclad, deemed well-nigh invulnerable being run into and sunk by a wooden vessel. It was startling, but the only result vras to drive navalconstruc- t ors to pile on more and more armour." "That action at Liverpool," said Ponsenby, " surely, there's a lot to learn from that, though, indeed, as I was up country ' at the time, ten thousand miles away, and only got back to England the other day, I never really comprehended the ins and outs of that busi- ness!' _

As for that," replied Brakespear, " you probably know all there is to tell, so simple is the yarn. There's nothing to be learnt from it about the science of war, but it shows up twentieth century strategy as a fine art. As a feat of arms it was nothing to that feat of the Mus- covite a few years earlier, when one morning, or in a sight and morning 200,000 men were landed all the coast at Kilia, near the entrance from the .Black Sea into the Bosphorus. and before he had tasted his early cup of coffee the Padishah was in the hands of the Christian invaders, and isolated, in every way, from the whole world." '• Yes, yes.; but that's somewhat ancient history, as things go, said the travelled Torn Ponsonby. " It's that little business on the Mersey I want to hear about." .
--;;-.JUst so. Then here goes for a plain unvar- nished TALE OF THE IDES OF MARCH.

- - - It i a remarkable story, of course, how the great sea- port was captured. The war came very suddenly. It bad been spoken of and speculated upon fora long time: but it fell out at last like a bolt from the blue. All was quiet at home and abroad. Parliament had met at Westminster two months earlier, when the usual declar- ations were made in regard to the pacific relations sub- sisting between ourselves and all Foreign Powers. Three months before that again Ministers had declared the outlook at home and abroad to be most satisfactory, the Continent having settled dawn after its recent troubles and the fresh arrangements of the ,map of Europe. Russia had been thwarted as to her more ambitious de- signs, and, being torn by internal dissensions, was con- sidered as inoffensive to outsiders.

The Mediterranean had become an almost Franco- Russian lake. But just at that moment no sinister .designs were suspected in that quarter. This by way of prelude. I am only concerned here with one incident of the struggle. Europe woke up one morning and .found that the war monsoon had burst. Before a week had elapsed the British Minister was well on his way ,home from St. Petersburg. The first blow of the enemy was a well-planned one, and was meant to cripple the food supplies of the coun- try ail paralyse our oversea. commerce, The foreign trade of the Mersey was vast, and through its portals the larger part of England was kept in daily bread, to say nothing of the import of raw materials for manufac- turing purposes, and the shipment of cotton and hard- ware goods to all parts of the world. To paraphrase the expression of Blucher, What a port to loot! What a commerce to annihilate! But how wasit to be done? The navigation ofliverpool Bay was no easy matter for large warships, granted all the facilities of clear weather, good pilots, and carefully buoy ed channels, with light- ships and lighthouses, and excellent charts. In case of war such could not possibly be hoped for, and moreover the approaches to the port would be rendered difficult and perilous in every possible way. To force an enemy's teet into the Mersey after forty-eight hours' warning would be a hazardous undertaking at the best. Its at- tempt would most likely lead to disaster, and at the opening of hostilities, perhaps to be of a prolonged char- acter, and with a naval power like Great Britian, it would never do to throw away a squadron of ironclads on a mere gambling enterprise. So the enemy con- ceived, we may imagine, but the scheme was not aban- doned. Skill in strategy was resorted to. Russia numbered among her allies two principalities, scarcely distinguishable as to their independence, though governed by their own Sovereigns and Assemblies, and claiming separate recognition abroad, and on the high seas. Tharsalia, one of the petty States, which had been _ _ . . .

carved out of the Sultan's dominions, went to war against us on the alleged ground that a ship of hers had been fired on the previous autumn for supposed piracy on thEeCyprian coast, and that all negotiations for re- paration had ended in failure. It was a picked-up quarrel. At the moment scarcely a thought was given to the arraying of the sparrow hawk side by side with the eagle. It was regarded as an impudent move, a display of 'cheek,' as a desire to improve the shining bout, but nothing more. It was really a piece of Homeric astuteness. Tharsalia had no army to speak of, but she possessed two or three very fast power- ful ships of war built for her by Russia at one of her naval dockyards in the Black Sea. If not quite the most imposing or modern of floating Gibraltars, and if some- what diminutive and insignificant in bulk in accordance with current notions, these same vessels were not to be Sneezed at with their dynamite-shell-throwing gunS,their flying torpedoes, and aerial ballistre calculated to wipe out a city as every charge dropped from the skies. One of these warships, the St. Sophia, had entered the Mer- sey some time alter Christmas, and proceeded to the once favoured anchorage roadstead in the Sloyne, far removed from the ordinary river traffic. It was given one that the St. Sophia had come to the port for repairs and it was understood that those in charge of her were negotiating with the company owning the new graving docks, near Warrington, on the Ship Canal. Such was the story current. The officers and men made them- selves quite at home, went out when invited, and did a good trade with the shipping contractors, who were all in the highest spirits, and blessed the flag of the little unknown principality which they had seldom seen or heard of before. Bills were paid with remarkaole promptness. The gallant crew went about a good deal, and were for the most part carelessly taken as" hands" off a foreign yacht or some such craft. For all that was seen of the St. Sophia herself che mignt have been anchored a hundred miles out in the channel. She was a matter of curiosity for a day or so to the few persons who,from their windows at home, could observe her as she lay at her moorings, swinging on a short cable with every tide. Scarcely a vessel ever passed her, that part of the river being almost deserted, even by coasting schooners, since the removal of the Ship Canal entrance to Tranmere Bay, the development of the Liverpool decks northward, and the continued revolution and growth of the port by means of the hopper dredger. But this is digression. "Not at all," interrupted the interested Ponsonby. "It's a case of truth stranger than fiction." "Well, one morning in March, the war cloud burst, and in the twinkling of an eye Liverpool was cap- tured." "Nonsense! Impossible !" exclaimed Ponsonby. "There must have been treachery." The imperturbable Brakespear, taking no heed, re- sumed : "The St. Sophia played the part of the wooden horse in the Trojan City. She was packed with men, and had on board every imaginable engine of destruc- tion. Two days before, it appears, she had been joined by two small gunboats, yachts they looked like, and nothing more. I can assure you, was required to " hold up" the port, as the bush highwaymen say, if only for once the schemes of men did not gang agley. And they didn't. A more perfectly contrived plot was was never more successfully carried to a triumphant issue. 111 that darkest hour which precedes the dawn the St. Sophia and her satallites had weighed anchor,and moved down the river and taken up positions opposite the Prince's Stage. A party of marine engineers had, it afterwards transpired, been ashore on leave the night before. Between nine and ten o'clock on that cold and foggy morning, this shore party, moving with extraor- dinary deftness and possessed of the fullest local infor- mation, had entered and seized the Central Telegraph office in Victoria-st., and cut the wires, completely des- troying the instruments and connections. Posses- sion was at the same time taken of the telephones. The Lord Mayor, on his reaching the Town Hall, as he al- ways did punctually at ten o'clock,was asked the favour of an interview. He found himself the recipient of a mandate as terrific as any ever fulminated. He was given half-an-hour in which to sign a surrender of the city to the enemy, with a guarantee of a ransom of two millions sterling, in default of which the city was to be bombarded, and the port laid in ruins. " But, gentlemen, gentlemen," cried the horrified chief magistrate, " what do you mean, what can you mean ? Last night we were at peace with all the world. I wake Up to this horrified nightmare. Where is your declare-
tion of war? Bow do I know even who and what you are?"

—"Declarations of war," said the polite naval lieuten- ant of the St. Sophia, speaking the most fluent English, "are things of the past. Such a declaration was in early times a condition of the legality of a war. Inter- national law abandoned that position long ago, and strategy H. le Lor Haire, simply laughs at it. We are here to publish the fact of war, and to secure the first fruits of it. H. le Lor Maire is a man of the world,and has travelled, and he knows when I tell him our strength and the number of our guns, that we can accomplish what we say." In the most precise and convincing fashion the infer- matioh in question was conveyed to the worthy chief of the city, by this time very wide awake indeed, though he had been overworked entertaining Royalty for the two previous days. He looked around him almost in anguish, down at the floor, up at the ceiling, with a lon and fond studyof the electric bells; then his eyes caught sight of the telephone receiver, towards which he impul- sively made a step, as if to break through the polite and defenential, but, all the time impassible cordon of officers surrounding him. His object was seen. The naval lieutenant again spoke— 'All messages from H. i. Lor Moire must go through an interpreter. Your worship is permitted to summon any one, naval or military officer, who may live near at hand, and whose advice can be of use, and also a half- dozen of the leading bankers and merchants in the city prepared to hand over acceptable to the amount of the city ransom. And meantime," concluded the officer, slightly inclining his head, "the time is passing rapidly." This looked business-like indeed. The Lord Mayor groaned. He suggested despatching messengers to sum- mon a conclave of the first citizens of the town. The proposal was agreed to as regards the messengers, who were to belong to the landing party ; but the counsellors to be limited as above, and all to meet at the Town Hall without delay. Under protest, the Lord Mayor, a long- headed Northerner, signed the requisition of the leading commercial houses and the messengers got their instruc- tions and departed, leaving his lordship as he counted tile wear,* moments to trust, like Micawber, that some- thing would turn up. A tedious twenty minutes passed. Never was it imagined possible that the civic parlour could have looked and felt so repulsively cold, gloomy, and forbid- ding as it did that morning. Anything was better than dead silence, and the Lord Mayor talked and the incom- parable naval lieutenant replied. He made no secret of the strategy that had been employed. He and his men had been sailing in and out of the Mersey in various vessels for some years. The St. Sophia had sealed orders when she entered several weeks before, which orders were being carried out in every detail. Two hundred picked men, some of them dressed as bluejackets, others as British Volunteers,and a few as civilians had remained ashore over night ; of course they had not all landed at once ; some had been ashore, scattered about the city for days, picking up information and studying their respec- tioe stationS, all of them previously allotted. Each man knew that he carried his life in his hands, and all that, but what . did they care but to do their duty. And the officer in command quietly shrugged his shoulders as he proceeded to light a cigarette, casually observing,'" We can hold the place without open show of forte, for one , hour, at all events ; quite enough for us. In three hours more it is high water, and we cross the bar, but we shall not sail from Liverpool, M. le Lor Maim, unless wise counsels prevail, for Liverpool will no longer exist." Hardly had the lieutenant concluded his little speech, delivereil in the blandest of tones, when there entered Major Sharpies, an adjutant of Volunteers, and an officer who had seen much service in many barters of the world. Dazed was hardly the word for his expres- sion of countenance as to the newly-arrived major the Lord Mayor briefly but succinctly, considering. the cir- cumstances, unfolded the situation. The major, who was a quick•witted man, soon perceived that this was no mere game of bluff. In his official capacity he could say nothing without communicating with his superiors. As a private citizen and a soldier versed in the power of gunnery and explosives, as against a defenceless town taken by surprise, there could be no hesitation in giving his opinion. The St. Sophia in less than the time men- tioned above might do more for the port than the Mexi- can mule when it "kicked the stuffing out of time and space." It was a case of Liverpool delendez set failing the terms offered he would accept the latter, and see the Tharsalians clear of the coast. That was by this time the Lord Mayor's own opinion as one of the merchant princes of the city, the chairman of a bank, and per-( sonally and officially cognisant of the enormous in- terests hanging in the balance. The clocks. in the town had just tolled the half hour when three of the city magnates entered the Mayor's parlour:; they included the local manager of the Bank of England,who had implored all the way down Castle-street to be allowed to send just a short wire to his " governor" or to the Chancellor of the Exchequer. Denials couched in the most gentle language were the sole response. The officer in command or the landing party now observed that his duty was done, as there was ushered into the room, in quiet civilian costume, but wearing a single decoration, on his coat, and with his commission and a copy of his instructions in his hand., the captain of the St. Sophia, who, after a courteous introduction, stated that half an hour at furthest he must be in action or else preparing to steam out of the Mersey. He had, he, said, been given to understand that the chief magis- trate of the city had accepted their conditions,, and it alone remained for these to be honoured. He had a gentleman with him who would go through the securit- ies, which must be of the highest, and of an interna- tional, character—or, at least, negotiable on any Ex- change. Failing these they must have bullion. The ransom was paid. _ _

It was agreed that the Lord Mayor and his military adviser should accompany the captain of the St. Sophia on board his vessel, and make good the contract there, having first seen for themselves the real eature of the situation. The party left the Landing stage in the iron- clad's steam launch, towing a rider-gig in which to bring back the city's representatives. There was no hitch in concluding the negotiations for the release of the port and estuary, and the whole of Liverpool Bay. As the chief magistrate stepped off the deck of the vessel her captain smilingly remarked, in. French, that of course he would be pursued, but that he could out-steam any British battleship, and blow out of the water any cruiser. And as the gig's painter 'was cast off and she dropped up stream, the major was heard to observe, looking up at the ponderous turrets, and their murderous long range guns, " By Mars, the God of War: I'm not an easily moved man, and I dislike the business much, but all the same, I feel sure we've acted for the best." "And that," said Jack Brakespear, "is the end of the yarn." "Yes a thousand thanks for it. I recollect all about the sequel. There was a terrible rumpus. The scandal of the defenceless condition of the West Coast Was played for all it was worth by the Opposition and the War Minister and the First Lord of the Admirality were promptly thrown overboard.''_. • . . _ . . . . .

And," added Brakespear, " the pigeon holes in their departments were found stuffed with memorials and petitions from citizens, merchants, bankers, under- writers, and others, calling attention to the peril of Liverpool. One protest stated that within the space of eighteen months no less than eleven large and small foreign ships of war had entered and left the port, with- out welcome, without farewell, without inquiry. The fatuous indifference displayed in the whole matter re- called the saying of the old sage as to how little the nations realise by what fools and foolish systems they are governed. There was one Minister who quoted in his defence from a book just then published that there always was a guardship in the Mersey, usually a power- ful irodclad. Why, there had been no guardship of any kind in the estuary for over forty years, and that was a fact which could not fail to be appreciated by foreign Powers, though it was apparently, not known to the Ministers of the Crown at home."—Liverpool Daily Post
