div.head: ItfOTS IN IDAHO.
div.p: THE ItfOTS IN IDAHO.

ACQUITTAL OF AN ACCUSED WORKMAN. Borss, IDAHO, TIIESDAY.—The jury in the case of Leasure. who was tried yesteiday for murder and con- spiracy in connection with the Cceur d'Alene mining riots in July last, returned a verdict of not guilty. This is virtually equivalent to a declaration that the acts of the union miners were of a defensive and not of a rebellious character. Leasure was indicted jointly with 42 others on the charge of conspiracy and murder in exploding the Francisco mine.

div.head: , UNUSUAL HAUL OF SPRATS.
div.p: , UNUSUAL HAUL OF SPRATS.

A remarkable scene was witnessed by hundreds of spectators on Southsea beach on Monday afternoon. Some Portsmouth fishermen who were dragging the dcep water channel leading into the harbour at a poiat near Southsea Castle discovered a huge shoal of sprats and succeeded in making a splendid haul. So heavily laden was one of the nets that it burst within a few yards of the shore, but enough of its contents remained in the meshes to make a very remarkable take. One of the biggest nets was brought ashore with greater success. The spectators watched with interest the tiny fish leap- ing by thousands over the nets, but many GE these were recaptured by amateur fishermen with hand nets. Boat after boat was filled flush with the water, and when filially the net was dragged upon the beach and shaken out tens of thousands were gathered up in baskets. It was estimated that the biggest net contained a shipload, and is sprats have been selling at 4s. a bushel, the haul will make for the fisherman a very seasonable Christmas box. It is said that such a slice of luck has never been experienced in the memory of the most ancient fisher- man of the port.

div.head: --e-- A. FAMOUS SEA CAPTAIN.
div.p: --e-- A. FAMOUS SEA CAPTAIN.

Captain John Vine Hall, who commanded the Great Eastern, died early on Christmas Day, at his residence. Avenue-road, Hampstead, after a long illness, in his eightieth year. At the age of fourteen he began his long nautical life as midshipman on board the East Indian Company's ship Inglis. In a few years he became thiid officer of the Lord Amherst, another of the company's great ships, which in a hurricane off the mouth of the Hooghly was left with broken back, high and dry, half a mile beyond high water mark. He afterwards commanded the Bosphorus, carrying mails and passengers to the Cape and Cal- cutta. During the Crimean war he was conveying the first detachment of Sardinian troops to Balaclava, when, soon after leaving Genoa,the coals became ignited by spontaneous combustion. Examining the shore, he took the wheel and steered the vessel upon the nearest accessible spot. All on board were safely landed. Capt. Nall was the last to leave the ship, which at once burst into flames from stem to stern. He was then appointed to the Great Eastern on her first ocean voyage to New York. where his arrival was. the occasion of a great demonstration. One of his brothers was the Rev. New- man Hall.

div.head: TALE OF A GERMAN CLEBK-OR
div.p: A TALE OF A GERMAN CLEBK-OR
SPY?

The "City Press" says :—City merchants who have German clerks in their service will scarcely read with pleasure the following story that reaches us from a good source. A well-known city firm of the good old English school numbered among its clerks a young gentleman from Germany. Nothing could have been better than the conduct of this member of the staff, who soon proved himself a real acquisition in the effice. The manager was perfectly delighted with him, and within a year the zealous and hard-working Teuton was in a fair way to take up a responsible position in the counting-house. Then came the little rift in this German fiute—a rift which effected a serious change in the manager's opinion upon the subject of employing German clerks in English offices. On a certain Bank Holiday the manager had occasion to visit the city, and great was his surprise to find his Teutonic subordinate hard at work in the office. What was the meaning of this extraordinary zeal? Simply that the wily young German was making an elaborate list of the firm's clients, and carefully putting down all particulars concerning commissions and so forth for the benefit of some of his friends in Rhineland. Needless to say, he was promptly dismissed, and Ger- man clerks have not been much sought after since by the firm in question.

div.head: JAY GOULD'S TOMB.
div.p: JAY GOULD'S TOMB.

Jay Gould's tomb (says the " Scientific American ") is copied after the famous Nielson Carre, at Nimes, France, built some two thousand years ago, and it is perhaps the best preserved and most beautiful specimen .of Grecian architecture in existence. Reared as it is upon a grass- covered knoll, where it commands a striking view of the surrounding country, the full beauty of the handsome marble structure, with its graceful ionic columns, is ap- preciated by a beholder approaching it from any direc- tion. The design of the mausoleum was made by Mr. IF. r. FitzMahony, and it cost 80,000dols. It is built throughout of Westerly granite. It is 33ft. long, 22ft. wide, and 201 t. high to the apex of the roof. The technical name of the building would be a Greek hexastyle, peripteral temple. It has six columns in front and eleven columns on each oide in single sows (this counting the corner columns twice.) Three; rows of steps run up to the temple on all sides and form its base. Between the coluh.ns and the walls of the temple is a considerable space. Columns and walls are bare, without the faintest attempt at ornamentation. In the centre of the row of columns facing the south it looks as if a column had been removed to make a broad passage-way. Facing this opening is the double door of the tomb. Each section of this door is Bfl. high and .2ft. wide, and weighs a ton. The doors are of heavy bronze, and the lower part is panelled and 'ornamented on the outside with two dragons' heads, a big iron ring swinging in the mouth of each dragon. The upper part of the doors is a fret-work of cherubs and vines, through the opening of which the 'interior of the .crypt can be seen. The interior is Mt. long, 7ft. wide, and high. Its roof is a solid slab of granite which weighs six tons. The bprder of the ceiling is panelled egg and dart moulding. The Boor is one plain marble slab. Along the sides of the interior are the catacombs. Of these there are twenty, ten on each side, in double rows. The rows are separated from each other by granite slabs. Each catacomb is Wt. long and 2ift. wide. Between the lower end of the catacombs and the outside of the wall of the tomb' is a thickness of it inches. The out part of this thickness is, of course, granite, but facing the interior the walls are of light pink and cream-coloured Tennessee marble, highly polished. The light enters the crypt through a stained glass win- dowin the back. This window, which is 6ft. high and 3ft. wide, pictures a choir of angels. The roof of the mausoleum consists of granite slabs 32ft. long, each weighing 15 tons, and so placed together that they overlap, making the roof waterproof. The whole temple weighs about 300 tons, and rest on a, solid concrete foundation Bft. thick.
Jfl E EXAM INER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 31, 189". I THE DEATH AT LATCH VORD.-WANT I A TRIP TO A- FIXED STAR.

Dr. David Gill, lecturing recently on " Fixed Stars," hit upon the following adroit method to illustrate the distance to Centauri. The doctor said, as reported in the Boston " Globe": " We shall suppose that some wealthy directors, for want of outlet for their energy and capital, construct a railway to Centauri. We shall neglect, for the present, the engineering difficulties—a mere detail— and sappose them overcome and the railway open for traffic. We shall go further, and suppose that the directors have found the construction of such a railway to have been peculiarly easy, and that the proprietors of interstellar space had not been exor- bitant in their terms for right of way. Therefore, with a view to encourage traffic, the directors had made the fare exceedingly moderate —viz., first class at 2 cents per 100 miles. Desiring to take advantage of these facilities, a gentleman, by way of providing himself with small change for the journey, buys up the National Debt of England aid a few other countries, and, presenting himself at the office, demands a first-class single to Centauri. For this be tenders in payment the scrip of the National Debt of England, which just covers the cost of his ticket; but at this time the National Debt from little wars had been run up from 3,500,000,000 dols. to 5,500,000,000 dols. Having taken his seat, it occurred to him to ask: 'At what rate do you travel I'' 'Sixty miles an hour, sir, in- cluding stoppages,' is the answer. 'Then when shall we reach Centauri ?' 'ln 48,663,000 years, air I '

div.head: (W FOOD AND WARMTH.
div.p: (W FOOD AND WARMTH.

Mr. Jones, deputy-coroner tor the district, held an inquest at the Golden Lion Inn, Bnutsford-road, on Tuesday afternoon, on the body ot Thomas Lather- barrow, 59 years of age, a well-known character, who died suddenly at his sister's house, 11, New- road, Latchford, on Friday last.—The first witness called was Alice Wilcock, who said the deceased was her stepbrother. He was a general labourer, but had stone very little work for many years. He came to her house on Thursday last, and complained of a pain in his heart. She told him he had been drinking. She gave him a cup of tea, but he did not get any better,and died at half-past five o'clock on the following morning. —A juror expressed his surprise that the deceased had lived so long, as he had "slept out night after night."—Dr. T. Starkey Smith said he had made a post mortein examina- tion of the body of the deceased. Ha found the lungs in a very highly congested condition—almost approach- ing what was called pulmonary apoplexy. The heart was enlarged, and all the cavities contained mons or less blood. The spleen and liver were both enlarged, and one of tho kidneys was very highly congested, and the other was in a normal condition. The stomach and in- testinas were almost empty. The left leg and foot were almost in a state of gangrene, due, he suspected, to cold I—a kind of frost-bite—and privation. The cause of Ideath was exhaustion from want of food and warmth "predisposed to," the doctor added, "by his residence in India and intemperate habits."-Another juror said the deceased did not appear to care for anything to eat as ' long as he could get anything to drink.—The Coroner : Did you And any trages of excessive drinking P—Dr. Smith : Yes, the liver was very much enlarged.—A juror remarked that he had intended to ask Dr. Smith a question or two about one or two things, but he had anticipated him. (Laughter.)—The Coroner: Yes, Dr. ' Smith always clears everything up beautifully. He never leaves us any questions to ask. He seems to an- ticipate them.—The jury then returned a verdict in accordance with the doctor's evidence.

div.head: SHOCKING STORY OF DESTITUTION.
div.p: SHOCKING STORY OF DESTITUTION.

On Monday Mr. Wynne E. Baxter held an inquiry at the Poplar Town Hall into the circumstances attending the death of Hannah Osman, aged five hours, the daughter of a dock labourer residing at 122, Stehon- dale-street, Poplar.—George W. Osman the father deposed that he was out of employment. He had been a fitter's labourer, and was employed at Messrs. Samuda's for eighteen months, but left there on the 17th ult. owing to work being slack. He produced a testimonial from the firm giving him a reference as a steady, sober, and industrious man. Last Saturday his wife was taken ill, and he wedt to the Rev. J. B. Kite, of Christ Church, for assistance. That.gentleman sent a midwife, who attended witness's wife. Witness then went to the relieving officer, but did not see him. On returning home he found that the relieving officer had been to the house and also the Rev. Mr. Kite. Dr. Leslie arrived soon afterwards, and found that the child was dead. In answer to the Coroner, the witness said that he and his family had had sufficient to eat, although he had had to sell nearly everything he possessed to get the food. He had only had an occasional job at the ' docks lately, and being without means he applied to the relieving officer for assistance, as he thought he might be able to save his furniture, but the only assistance he got was the offer of the workhouse.—The Coroner : You evidently don't see that according to our poor-law a man must tumble in the gutter before he can be picked up. In Germany they do the other thing—they try to prevent a man tumbling into the gutter. It's a question whether that is not the cheapest in the end ; it is certainly more humane.—The witness added that he had found food for his wife up till the last moment, and said " I would rather have pawned my shirt than she should have gone without." He had now three little children at home. The Rev. Mr. Kite knew nothing about the case dntil witness went to him, but he (Mr. Kite) had acted very kindly since.—Sarah Chick, a mid- wife, deposed that she attended the mother in her confinement, and seeing how destitute the place was went and informed the Rev. Mr. Kite. He gave with ness clothes and food for the poor woman. Witness sent for brandy and a hundredweight of coals, and paid for them out of her own pocket. WiMess did not see any food in the house, and the room was in a terrible state of destitution. The poor woman was lying on a heap of straw, with nothing to cover her.—(Sensa- tion.) The only furniture in the room was a Ilttle table and chair. Witness asked the mother where the children slept, and she replied that that was the only place she had for them.—At the request of the Coroner, the Rev. Joseph Bertram Kite, curate-in-charge a Christ Church Isle of Dogs, gave evidence. He stated that the family had only been in his parish ten days, and he knew nothing to their prejudice. He found the case to be one of extreme destitution, though not what one would call actual starvation. The children said they had had break- fast on Friday, though they had had no dinner. They were wanting clothes, and were without shoes and stockings. The state of the room was just as Mrs Chick described it. He knew nothing of the case unti applied to on Saturday, and then,feeling that something ought to be done at once, acted accordingly.—Dr. Win. Murray Leslie, of 531, Manchester-road, stated that he was asked by the last witness to visit the case, and found the child dead. The mother was excessively weak, and looked as if she had not had enough food. The children looked well cared for, and he came to the con- clusion, from previous experience, that the mother had gone without herself to feed her children. Witness's opinion was that the man had arrived at the end of his tether, having nothing more to sell on Saturday. The cause of death wr,s congenital debility, due to a cer- tain extent, to the mother having been insufficiently fed. Witness testified to the good character borne by the man, and said that it was the horror of the work- house on account of the wife that had led him to undergo such privation.—The jury, in returning a verdict in accordance with the doctor's evidence, thanked the Rev. Mr. Kite for his kindness to the family as soon as he knew of their trouble, a remark which the Coroner en- dorsed.—The Rev. Mr. Kite thanked the jury for their kind expression of opinion, and said that he felt that he had only done his duty, that which anyone under the circumstances would have done.—The Coroner then gave Osman some tickets with which to buy food.

COAGULINE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 61. and is. ; postage, 2d. Sold everywhere, home and abroad.—Advt. The Cardiff Junior Liberals have adopted a resolution declaring their unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy, condemning Sir E. Reed's " injudicious and ill-timed letter, and characterising his refusal to pledge his support to the Home Rule Bill of the Government as an indication of wavering" on the Irish question.

The recount of the votes given at the Cirencester election was concluded and the result announced on Saturday. The sitting member, Colonel Chester-Master, was left with a majority of two votes, but Mr. Lawson as a majority of twenty upon the disputed papers. The value of the sixty-two disputed votes will be decided by the Election Petition Judges shortly before the meeting of Parliament.

div.head: "MISSING WORD" CRAZE.
div.p: THE "MISSING WORD" CRAZE.
£44,000 IMPOUNDED.

A representative of a Birmingham evening paper has been interviewing Mr. Pearson, who is staying at Bournemouth, with reference to the disposal of the impounded missing word money. Mr. Pearson states that the total sum at stake is much larger than is gene- rally supposed. There is first a sum of about £24,000, the proceeds of the "unaccountable" competition in " Pearson's Weekly"; there is a further sun/ of nearly £4,000, from No. 7 Competition in "Society News" ; and a third amount of about £l,OOO from the competi- tion in the first number of " Pearson's Companion." Since the competitions were stopped coupons with ac- companying postal orders have been pouring in, and there is from this source about £12,000, which has been impounded by the authorities in the same way. Finally a number of winners in the earlier competitions omitted to present their checks until after Sir John Bridge's ad- verse decision, and then the bank, in order to protect their own interests, declined to meet the cheques. In this way a further sum of about £3,000 is locked up. The total amount involved, it will be seen, is about £44,000, and five distinct actions are now pending in order to determine the ownership of the money. The first and most important of these is the action Barclay v. Pearson, which came before Mr. Justice Stirling in the Court of Chancery last week. The other actions are for the most part of a similar nature, dealing with other parts of the impounded fund ; but it may be assumed that the decision in the Barclay v. Pearson case will govern the disposal of the entire amount. Mr. Pearson spoke in very appreciative terms of the moderation dis- played by the bulk of the competitors during the period of suspense. There have, of course, been cases in which irate winners have threatened him with County Court summonses and similar terrors of the law, but, for the most part, the disappointed ones have recognised that his hands are hopelessly tied. Since the competitions commenced,Mr.Pearson says he has distributed £175,000 among the successful competitors, while some indication of the amount of work which this entailed may be gathered from the fact that the arrangements for con- ducting last week's competitions cost him £350.

div.head: _.150,000 FUR A LITTLE ACT OF KINDNESS.
div.p: _.150,000 FUR A LITTLE ACT OF KINDNESS.

A lady of small independent means, residing at Ash- ford, has just been informed through an old-established firm of solicitors, that the handsome sum of £150,000 has been bequeathed to her for a small act of kindness. It appears that in the spring of 1888, an old gentleman journeyed from one of the midland counties to London for the express purpose of witnessing the arrivals at one of the Drawing Rooms at Buckingham Palace, and at an early hour took up his position near the main entrance to the Palace. After several hours of deeply interested watching, he became giddy and faint. Seeing him stagger, the crowd shouted rudely that he was drunk. The lady, however, saw he was ill, and helped him through the crowd to a seat in the park close by, and sent for water for him. He soon recovered, and as she wished him goodbye, asked her name. She gave him her card, and heard no more until she received the com- munication that he had made her his heiress. THE CONDEMNED BLACKBURN MURDERER.

div.head: LETTER FROM THE HOME SECRETARY.
div.p: LETTER FROM THE HOME SECRETARY.
ANOTHER INTERVIEW WITH RELATIONS.

Mr. Riley, solicitor to the man Cross Duckworth, con- demned for the murder of the child Barnes at Black- burn, has received the following reply to a request for an interview with the Home Secretary :—" Re Cross Duckworth now under sentence of death. The Secretary of State regrets he must decline the interview requested as contrary to the practice of the Home Office in criminal cases. Any further representations you may wish to suhmit should be forwarded in writing, and will receive every consideration." Duckworth has had another interview with his brother I and other relatives at Walton Gaol. The condemned man inquired anxiously about his wife and family,who, it may be said, are being assisted by the relatives with the generosity which often characterises people in hum- ble circumstances. He was also concerned about the efforts to obtain a reprieve, of which, in consequence of his recommendation to mercy,he entertains strong hopes althoughup to the present no communication has been received at the prison from the Home Office. In zpite of his state of suspense Duckworth continues in his usual health, taking his meals and rest with regularity. His demeanour is quiet. He receives the administra- tions of the prison chaplain attentively, and occasion- ally he spends a little time in reading. Beyond this routine his prison life presents nothing to record. div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meet- ing held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present, the Rev. .7. W. N. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gaetaldi, Messrs. P. Speakman, QC., T. Baxter, C.C., J. Weir, J. Baguley, J. Stokes, T. Lewis, Pickering, W. M. Williams, j. Brandreth, J. Whitlow, A. E. Heywood, E. Bretherton, J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: COESTKIPTIOW OT woos.
div.p: THE COESTKIPTIOW OT woos.

The Local Government Board wrote drawing the attention of the Guardians to the great difference in expenditure in respect of spirits, wine and malt liquors for the indoor poor in different districts as shown in a statement appended. From this statement it appeared that in the county of Chester the daily average number of inmates was 3,039 and the expenditure on liquors £3ll, giving an average expenditure per head of inmates of 25. ld.—The Clerk stated that in Runcorn Union the average per head was ls. 11d. The highest on the list was Rutland, 12s. 10d. per head and the lowest, North- umberland, 4d. per heacl.—Mr. Brandreth : You would have it down at fourpence, would not you Mr. Lea.— Mr. Lea : I think so.—Mr. Brandreth : Our doctors pre- scribe it and we are obliged to supply it.

div.head: DECEASED INEBRIATES.
div.p: DECEASED INEBRIATES.

The British Medical Association forwarded the follow- ing petition for the approval of the Guardians :—" That your petitioners are gratified to observe the marked advance in public opinion in favour of legislation for compulsory reception and detention, in special home for curative purposes, of such deceased inebriates as have had their will power so broken down as to be unable of their own accord to apply for such admission and detention. Your petitioners therefore pray your honourable house to pass such measures as shall make suitable provision for poor inebriates, also for the removal of the present hindrances to the reception of voluntary applicants, and for compulsory detention.— Mr. Heywood expressed his approval of the petition and remarked that it was drink which filled our workhouses to a great extent.—Mr. Speakman proposed that the petition be forwsrded to Mr. Brunner, 11. r., for presen- tation to the House of Commons. From knowledge he possessed not only of the lunatic asylums in Cheshire, but of those in other counties, Mr. Speakman stated that they were filled with inebriates, and should Parlia- ment in its wisdom legislate on the lines of that petition, the asylums would be less overcrowded than they were. Mr. Lea seconded the motion. The Rev. Dr. Gastald. supported the motion which was carried unanimously

div.head: BEER MONEY.
div.p: BEER MONEY.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of the appointment of Miss Elizabeth Moran, as schoolmistress of the Workhouse, at a salary of £2O per annum. The Board also assented to the payment to the schoolmistress of £4 per anunm in lieu of beer.

div.head: PROTEST IGNORED.
div.p: A PROTEST IGNORED.

Mr. C. J. Spencer clerk to the Besford Union, for- warded a copy of a resolution passed by his Guardians protesting against the action of the Local Government Board in reducing the rating qualification required for the office of Guardian to £5, it being their opinion that there was no necessity for so great a change, the inevi- table result of which would be an increased distribution of the poor rate, by reason of the election on Boards of Guardians of persons having little responsibility and small interest in the funds they will have to administer. —Mr. Speakman : I propose the letter be loft on the table.—Mr. Williams : I second that.—Carried unani- mously.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL PIIVCEPT.
div.p: COUNTY COUNCIL PIIVCEPT.

The Clerk reported that he had received a precept from Mr. Potts, clerk to the County Council for the sum of £3,272 Bs. 2d., of which £2,308 18s. id. was for County rate; £ll5 7s. Bd. for constabulary general ex- penditure, and £84.8 3s. 11d. for constabulary local expenditure. The contribution of the township of Run- corn to this amount was set down at £BO4 15s. Od.— The Clerk said this precept was over £lOO less than the one issued in the previous half year.

div.head: ASYLUM QUESTION.
div.p: THE ASYLUM QUESTION.

Mr. Speakman said he should like to state how the matter stood with regard to the asylums at Upton and Macclesfield. The authorities had ruled that both asylums were one, but were managed by separate corn- mittes, and, therefore, when one was full, the patients must go to the other. Be had taken the matter up on behalf of the Runcorn Union and he thought fruit would be borne, when they came to make a fresh agreement with Chester, which must be done shortly. By the fresh agreement it would no doubt be decided that Chester patients must go to Macclesfield, until they had the anatexe which was about to be made to hold 400 patients; and all the Unions on the Chester side of the county would be enabled to send their patients to Upton. This was problematical; but the matter had been dis- missed.—The Chairman: That will meet our contention that we have a prior claim to Chester.—Mr. Speakman: Yes ;I have argued for my own Union. (Hear, hear.) —The Chairman: lam sure the Guardians are much obliged.
FINANCE.

div.head: On the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £460 7s. ed. were passed for payment.
div.p: On the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £460 7s. ed. were passed for pay- ment.
THE NORTHAMPTON MURDER.
A REMARKABLE SPEECH BY THE CONDEMNED MAN.

The last stage of the trial of Andrew George Macrae for the murder of Annie Pritchard was reached on Saturday night, at Northampton. At the sitting of the Court, the prisoner's counsel continued his address, re- lying mainly for the defence upon the theory that the woman had disappeared with one Guy Anderson, whose name had been mentioned in the case. Afterwards Mr. Justice Kennedy occupied over Ave hours in placing the case before the jury, and it was half-past seven o'clock when the jury retired to consider their verdict. At nine o'clock they returned with a verdict of guilty, and the prisoner was sentenced to death. Both inside and out- side the court there were some remarkable scenes to- wards the conclusion of the proceedings. The prisoner's brother, who had been ejected during the delivery of the judge's charge, created much disturbance by his efforts to re-enter the court, and a crowd of several thousand persons gathered round the doors, raised tre- mendous cheers when the result of the trial was com- municated to them. _ _

The prisoner, who stood in the dock with a warder on each side, received the verdict apparently unmoved. In reply to the usual question whether he had anything to say, he ccmmenced " Very little, my Lerd--"and was immediately interrupted by a scuffle at the back of the court, evidently caused by his brother, the ejected witness, trying to get in. Above all the noise could be heard his voice, " I shall come in." He seemed to be quieted, and the prisoner turning to the judge, added : " Any sentence you pass upon me has no terror." Again there was the scuffling at the back, and again rang out the brother's voice through the court : " He's my own brother. I shall come in." At this moment, too, the verdict was by someone communicated to the crowd of five or six thousand persons waiting in the street. They gave a tremendous shout, and then several prolonged cheers. The second ejectment of Macrae having been effected and the cheering having stopped, the prisoner in a firm voice said : I hope, my Lord, under the cir- cumstances, you will excuse my brother his excited state in making the interruptions in the Court some time ago and again just now. I beg to say no sentence I you pass upon me has any terror for me, because I am perfectly innocent of this charge. There are many things I could say in regard to the evidence brought for- ward against me, but it is needless, of course. All the evidence of the conversation supposed to have taken place between witnesses and myself is a mass of abomin- able lies. The Pritchards also know very well the exist- ence of circumstances connected with Guy Anderson which they have parposely kept back—Turning to the jury : Gentlemen, you have this day, each and every- one of you,become what you have made me—a murderer. You have this day widowed a good, devoted wife. You have this day, this night, this Christmas-eve, made fatherless loving children. Go home to your homes, can you, with a clear conscience. Have you, in giving your verdict, tempered your duty with mercy ? I say no ! , As long as you live your conscience will accuse you.— To his Lordship: My Lord, in as few words as you possibly can, if you please! His Lordship then passed sentence of death.
LETTER FROM THE CONVICT. PROTESTATION OF INNOCENCE.

Andrew Macrae. the condemned murderer, wrote on Thursday, from Northampton Gaol, the following letter to his brother Edward in Birmingham : " Let me beg you to make the best of the great trou- ble which has not only befallen me, but those I love so dearly. It is for dear ones I grieve. I am innocent of the charge brought against me, and do not trouble for myself. Again I say I have not had justice—not from the beginning. All were false witnesses. Every word seemed to have been put into their mouths by the police. Knowing, as I did, how untrue it was, I cannot but , think that they must have been the authors. [Nine lines her* have been obliterated by the authorities.] See darl- ing mother soon. What will my darling boys do, Ted ? I want them to grow up very good. See my darling leg boys, and I want you to remember I want the dear children never to know of this. God bless and keep you all. I am in God's hands. You are right about the judge. He is a most merciful judge. The jury took no notice of him. All thought oy the summing up that I was as good as free." .

A" Liberator" Relief Fund has A tall f.r been opened, the honorary secre- Help. tary of which is the Rev. J. STOCIC- WELL WATTS,. of Arnhurst Park, London, and the Committee includes, amongst others, three mem- bers of Parliament, namely, Mr. G. HOWELL, Mr..E. H. PICKERGILL,, and Mr. J. A. RENTOUL. As inay be inferred from its name, the fund is for the relief of those who have suffered most severely through the failure of the Liberator Building Society:and its allied companies. That there is a need for relief in numberless cases will not be gainsaid by anyone who knows the kind of investors that attracted by the Liberator Society, and the 113"7 letters which have been received by Mr. WA7ll° a sample of which he prints, give evidi3nce on this point which is as pathetic as it is convincing. Measured by the amount of human anguish and deprivation which result from it, a great financial " smash " is just as much a national calam- ity as is a disastrous colliery accident or a railway catastrophe. In the latter cases the loss of life and limb is, of course, Irr sur_ parable, and the suffering caused t 1 vivors and relatives may be more .1 during, but, on the other hand,tit ezbe y t and en_ not nearly so, i In° Xapt ese C the. widespread as when such 7etn'.ii of that Societv d t l collapse."LibertoTr h"ecoimnveessttoeda s.ucl " cap of some and its allied companies consisted lupartw for cla stshaen cml otshte er,oforthae savings of the working t 27,000,000, made up all events, of the poorer portion of the micliale clam. judging from the report of the provisional liquidator which has been made public, it seems ; only too clear that there is an extremely small !chance of the shareholders ever receiving a penny !back, and the depositors who have a prior claim will have to wait many months before they get any portion of their money. So general has the Idistress amongst the poor investors been found to be, that it is estimated "that at least some £lO,OOO will be required to relieve the worst cases, and tide them over Ithe beginning of the year, when the dividends fall ' duo; but fully £lOO,OOO will be needed to afforti anything like substantial relief." The letters from, investors which MT. WATTS publishes afford dis- tressful reading. A Broken-Hearted Widow writes " I and my children have lost all our money in the Liberator. You will think it not much when I tell you it was 412 ; but it was our all. I am a widow, left with five little to provide for. My eldest son is on
children entirely ly a poor clerk--
• k

His father died of con- ters are all more or less complaint. I have worked saved that little money, in th, a few shillings at a time, I have an aged father, 84 Mg on me. When we first Dme was more like a mad- , else." And well might , she add: "I do think •it a great shame that men should be allowed to rob the poor of their hard-earned savings." A " Broken-down Butler" says" I have had to leave my situation on account of ill-health, and have been laid up for six months, and am still confined to my room. My small stock of cash is nearly exhausted ; then I have only the workhouse before me. My age is 68. I had saved £240 in the 'Liberator 'for old age and sickness." Of two maiden ladies in Devon who had worked hard all their lives as servants, we are told that they, "being persuaded by trusted friends, put their hard-earned savings into the Liberator.' One of them, an invalid for the past ten years, has died since the failure—her end, doubtless, has- tened by the tronble. How hard if the other poor old lady must go to the workhouse, after being careful all her life to save a little, to make her comfortable in old age." The wife of the Rev. JAMES BLOOMFIELD, of, Lewisham, writes; "I know of a poor fellow who has worked hard all his 'life—how hard only those about him are aware—and placed all he could pinch out of his weekly wage in this society, and, with tears rolling down his worn cheeks, he has to tell that there is nothing but stone-breaking before him after all. I know of a poor old bed- ridden woman, depending for her comforts on this half-yearly dividend, who now lies in despair, and wishes only for the end to come upon her quickly." A CongregaVonal minister writes :—" I am a sufferer. I was so foolish as to believe that the directors were honourable, upright men, that their false trifiated balance sheets and annual reports were authentic, and that each society or company stood upon its own basis, and was quite independ- ent of the others. But I have been woefully de- ceived. I have a deposit of £5lO in the Libera- tor, 60 shares in the Lands A.llottment, and a very few shares also in the House and Land and Lon- don and General Bank. The savings of a lifetime and more, went in the direction of these institu- tions, as I never doubted their stability and excel- lence. Had I been a young man it would not have been so painful, but I am now in my 79th year, a retired Congregational minister, and am sadly perplexed about the future, having a wife and daughter dependent upon me. I fancied by joining these societies that I had made provision for old age, and was so thankful on that account. Now all has been suddenly swept from me." These letters, which are but the rseagrest selec- tion from the many that had been received by the Rev. J. STOCK WELL WATTS, speak eloquently of the need of help and in justification of the relief- fund. And they speak just as eloquently in con- demnation of those who, frors behind the mask of a pretentious piety, cheat the striving and thrifty poor of their hard-earned savings. "To me, as a Christian minister," says Mr. 'WATTS," The cruel- lest feature of the whale business is that these precious hard-earned saving were drawn into these rotten concerns by the professedly good names and Christian reputations associated with them."

THERE is a singular contrast be- tween two duels that have taken Duels. place within the last few days. One of these " affairs of honour" was between two French politicians, M. CLEMENCEAII and M. DERoULEDE. This duel took place amidst all the "pomp and circumstance " imaginable. The com- batants were accompanied to the "field' by a retinue of "seconds" and friends and—doctors, who were altogether needless personages. The whole affair ended in smoke, literally and figura- tively. Three shots were fired by each duellist, but none of them bad any effect, and it may be shrewdly surmised that they were never intended to have any effect. "Honour" was satisfied with this consumption of powder and ball, the two politicians shook hands, and they and the doctors left the sanguinary field. The other duel took place in Texas, and it was of a realistic character. A father and his two sons on one side met, by appointment, two other men, their opponents, at a railway station. Each man was well armed with Winchester repeating rifles and revolvers. In this case there was no ceremony, and no unbusinesslike " fuss " of any descrip- tion. Directly the two parties eyed each other the duel began, and almost instantly the father and one of his sons werc stricken down, mortally wounded, by bullets from the Winchesters of their opponents. The other son was, however, still to bereclroued with, and with two well-aimed shots from his revolver, he " winged " his two oppo-H nents. The father, by a last effort, raised him- ' self and emptied his revolver into the bodies of the two men already fatally wounded by his son's weapon. From this it will bo seen that there is a marked difference between a French and a Texan duel. In neither case is tho presence of doctors necessary. In France a doctor is not required be- cause nobody is wounded; in Texas because his services are unavailing. Were the wild, realistic Texan fa.shion of fighting introduced amongst Parisians, it is to be feared that the " honour" of the reckless rhetoricians of the Chamber of Deputies would lose a good deal of its sensitive- ness. As we have seen from the Panama scandals the honour of some French legislators is an un- reliable quantity.

WHILE upon the subject of duelling it may be remarked that French duels have not always been of the mild and harmless character which now distinguishes them. It was two Frenchmen who, in the earlier years of the century, settled their differences in a way which was as novel as it was disastrous to one of the parties. Each combatant, accompanied by a friend, whose daring was of the Quixotic order seeing that he had no "point of honour" to settle, armed himself with a blunder- buss and then ascended in a balloon. After the balloons had reached a considerable altitude, the blunderbusses were discharged, and one of the aerial vessels was so much damaged that it rapidly descended and the two occupants were dashed to pieces on the tops of the houses. It is needless to say that this method of duelling was far too effective to become fashionable amongst modern French politicans. In England it may now, fortunately, be said that there is no duelling, either real or pretended. It survived in the army even after it had been prohibited by the articles of war, and, it is said, that the death of many an officer was reported to the authorities as due to r, or cholera, when it was known Lis corps that be had fallen before of a duelling antagonist.

If published accounts be true the Master of Rugby Workhouse has given a very striking example of how the Poor Law should not be administered. A policeman in going his round the other night was moved to pity by the appear- ance of a poor homeless woman. He took her to , the workhouse gates, and rang the bell. The Workhouse Master looked out from a window over- head, and after hearing the policeman's tale declined to take the woman in and advised him 'to lock her up." This he could not do as there was nothing against her, but he went to the reliev- ing officer and obtained an ord( r for admission for his distressed companion. But even then the churlish Master would not, until after a good deal of delay, give shelter to the starving woman. At the same workhouse two men who had tramped from Northampton, a distance of twenty miles, applied for admission. They were quite destitute, and it was between eight and nine o'clock at night, but the same official refused to admit them and would give no reason for his refusal. When cited before the Rugby Board of Guardians, the Worxhouse Master had excuses, He thought the woman was drunk, and he was of opinion that the two men should "go to Coven- try," where there was another workhouse. The excuses were not considered adequate to the occa- sion, and the Guardians decided to ask this one of their officials to resign duties which seemed to be too onerous for him.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before the Mayor (Alderman F. H. The landlord, John Gerrard, heard the windows being smashed shortly before eleven o'clock, and Police Constable Wood met the prisoner coming from the direction of the public-house, and she admitted breaking the window. Oa Christmas Day special services were held. The Parish Church, St. Michaels, Holy Trinity, and St. Edward's Catholic Church, was decorated with ever- greens bre. div.head: THINGS HEA ItD AND SEEN AT . RUNCORN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: THINGS HEA ItD AND SEEN AT . RUNCORN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Merry Christmas has come and gone once more, and now the salutation for a day or two will be "A Happy New Year," and heartily it is wished to readers of this column. It is no use wishing it to those who don't, because they wont see it. Those who are always wishing for seasonable weather ought to be satisfied, for we have had a crispy cold atmosphere, the landscape made glorious with a glistening white mantle of beautiful ice crystals, and our ponds covered with a thick sheeting of ice on which skaters have enjoyed themselves to their hearts content. Confirmed grumbler as the farmer is, the present weather meets with his approval. But 1 am afraid the older members of our popula- tion would have preferred it a little less seasonable, and a more enial atmosphere would better have suited their constitutions. And to those who are not richly endowed with this worlds goods, hard , weather makes the pinch of poverty all the keener, and to many of our working class Population it ' means slackness of employment, a small draw at the week end, and, therefore, a reduced order to : the grocer and the butcher. Seasonable weather is always .very well in its way, but a mild open sea- son has many advantages, and the quarrymen, masons, bricklayers, and many other out door work- ers will feel inclined to shout hurrah when King Frost has bid adieu. But as there is no joy with- out its alloy, so there is no weather winter or sum- mer, springtime, or harvest but has its drawbacks.

The past year has been one of history making in our local affairs. We have seen Widnes transformed from a local board district. into a full blown muni- cipality, with Mayor, Aldermen and Corporation. A project has been commenced and so far carried on with considerable vigour, for constructing a bridge for vehicular traffic across the Mersey between Wid nes and Runcorn, at a cost of £lBO,OOO. That the local authorities of the two towns are in earnest in the matter is shown by the fact that they have each agreed to contribute £30,000, and hopes are entertained that the County Councils of Lancashire and Cheshire will provide the balance. Then the Runcorn Board of Commissioners have embarked upon a great undertaking, in the purchase of the works of the Rnncorn, Weston and Halton Water- works Co., involving an ultimate outlay of over £70,000. Widnes Town Council are proceeding with the erection of a Technical school, a.: an estimate cost of £6,000, and Runcorn con' template building a similar institution at an estimated cost of £4,000. Over half of the latter sum is practically previded, and Mr. F. Wiswall, the Chairman of the Board of Commissioners is endeavouring to form a Commit- tee to raise the remainder of the sum. Should the purchase of the Waterworks become an accomplished fact, the foundation of the Technical Institute be laid, and the scheme for the building of the vehicu- lar bridge become within measurable means of realisation within the next six months, Mr. Wis- wall's year of office will indeed have been a fruitful One and eclipse that of any of his predecessors.

In regard to the Vehicular Bridge, it is -unfortun- ate that the Local Government Board will not allow the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority to make a contribution towards the £30,000 promised by the Board of Couamissioners. According to the coummunication reaa from the London Board at the Rural Sanitary Authority's meeting on Tuesday, the Daresbury Highway Board • would be the proper body to approach for a contribution, and no doubt the Commissioners will act according. The development of the rural district, which would re- sult, is a building of the Bridge,vvhich would be im- mediate and far reaching, and the ratepayers in the district ought to be willing to bear a portion of the financial responsibility to be incutred.

The Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa Choir are to be com- plimented on their excellent readering of that, great oratorio' The Messiah" on Tuesday evening. Throughout, the concert was a most enjoyable one. The choir has fully established itself as one of our best musical institutions, and the standard of ex- cellence is being highered on each public appear- ance. A highly creditable past to look back upon. the choir may look forwatd to a still more success- ful and brilliant future. With two such institutions as the Tonic Sol-fa Chair, and the younger organi- sation of the Runcorn Musical Society flourishing in our midst, who will now level the accusation against us that we are an unmusical people?

The hard frost has covered all the ponds in the locality with a thick sheet of ice, and skaters have besieged them daily. Un- fortunately the weather has causetra cessation of work at the Quarries, and the workers at the telegraph manu- factory have had a week's holiday. Mr. Jas.
