ZION METHODIST FREE CHURCH.—On Monday after- noon, in connection with this place of worship a Christ- mas tree and sale of werk was opened by Mr. George Slater, of Woodford Hall, in an appropriate SDeeell, and brief addresses were delivered by the Rev. J. Trotter, and Mr. James Brandreth. The stalls were presided over by Mrs. Jno. Noden, Miss Miriam Brandreth„ Miss Maud Brandreth and Miss Carter, and they were well stocked with articles made and given by., the members of the sewing class. The affair was a financial success, and the money will be devoted towards the fund for building a new chapel, as the present one is not large enough to accommodate the congregation which weekly assemble there. Sr. Panes PARISH CHURCH.—The annual congrega- tional tea party was held on Monday afternoon, when a good number sat down to a substantial repast catered for by Mr. Joseph Jeffs. Afterwards an entertainment of songs, glees, and recitations was given. Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., who presided, delivered an address in which he mentioned the great interest he took in the day and Sunday schools, and said their present build- ings required enlarging to accomodate tke increasing population of the place. He believed in religious teach- mg in the day schools, and he should not like a School , Board to be established and religious teaching aban- doned. He paid a high compliment to the headmaster Mr. Hill, and went on to observe that it was 22 years since he took up his residence in the neighbourhood, and as he had always taken a deep interest in the village and its people in the past, so he would be prepared to help them in future, a henever it was necessary.—The Rev. ,W. T. Vale also spoke.—A very pleasant evening was spent.—On Tuesday afternoon the Sunday school scholars were entertained to a capital tea, and after- wards a Christmas tree was stripped of its contents which was distributed to the regular attenders. Oranges given by Mr. Reynolds were also distributed. The cost of this treat to the young people was borne by Mr. Priestncr as a thanksgiving offering for the restoration to health of his wife, who had had a severe attack of illness.
-11-___•_ CtiItISTMAS AND THE POS2 OFFICE
ARRANGEMENTS.

Christmas brought with it the customary amount of extra work to the post office officials of Warring- on as well as elsewhere. But thanks to the exceptionally smart arrangements made by the authorities this was carried out, even more satisfactorily than in previous years. The staff of postmen hisd been augmented to double its usual strength, and extra mail carts were brought into requisition. In town two extra deliveries were made on Sunday; but the rural postmen were not sent out, the ordinary Sunday custom being observed. To make up for this, however, two special deliveries were made in the country on Saturday after- noon and this would no doubt be very acceptable to the country people, especially the farm labourers, for we are lead to understand that the number of geese seat from " friends" in Ireland was prodigious. Both in the des- patches and the deliveries there was a decrease in the number of cards, whilst the number of parcels was in- creased correspondingly. Many of the large firms in town posted Christmas presents on Saturday to their customers, one lirw alouo eeudiug over 30Q parcels.

div.head: " MESSIAH " AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE " MESSIAH " AT RUNCORN.

The public of Runcorn were on Tuesday evening afforded an opportunity of hearing Hundel's im- mortal oratorio, the " Messiah," and it 14 gratifying to record that the enterprise of the Tonic Sol-fa Choir in producing the work for the second year in succession, was rewarded by a large and apprecia- tive audience. Nof matter how often heard the " Messiah " never palls upon the taste, and the familiar choruses and solos appeal with surprising fresh- ness, and an added beauty, at each repetition. Especi- ally appropriate at Christmastide, when the anniversary of the birth of Christ is commemorated, is the perform- MICA! of Handel'a master conception, and as Mr. Holford and his choir would seem to have made the giving of the oratorio at that season of the year their own prerogative. it is to be hop:al they will continue to delight crowded assemblages for years to come. Every part of the Public Hall was well filled on Tuesday evening and that the audience enjoyed the succession of brilliant orchestra- tion, soul stirring choruses, and dramatic and pathetic solos was evidenced as much by the rapt attention of '1 the listeners, as by the hearty applause which frequently I broke out on the completion of a number. The choir which was about eighty strong, were conducted by Mr. John Holford, 0.T.5.C., and their work throughout the entire performance was characterised by remarkable ac- curacy and power, and no good purpose would be served by giving one chorus prominence over another. the vocalists engaged as principals were Miss Mary I.:1710cm, Miss Annie Parry, Mr. Thomas Barlow, and Mr. Fred Owens. Miss Langdon is the possessor of a sweet expressive soprano voice, and the difficult music that fell to her share was interpreted in a highly satisfactory manner and she scored a marked success in " Rejoice greatly, 0 Daughters of Zion." Not a stranger to Runcornians, Miss Parry's capabilities are well known, and it will suffice to say that her performances on the present occasion were quite worthy of her reputation, and the beautiful music for the contralto lost none of its charm. Mr. Barlow was in good voice and lie made a capital commencement with the recitative " Comfort ye." and his singing throughout was highly appreciated. The possessor of a powerful bass voice of good quality, Mr. Owens was a decided success,his vocalisation being marked by appro. pi late expression and dramatic feeling. In the ever popu- lar " The trumpet shall sound," in which Mr. J. Murray played thetriumphobligato, heespecially pleased hisaudi- tore. In the " Messiah "the instrumental music is one of the charms of the work, and the opening overture and the pastoral symphony are twe compositions that concert-goers rarely miss of their own free will. The orchestra was a highly efficient one, and was composed as follows :---First violins, Mr. J. W. Collinson (leader), Mr. E. M. Bennett, Mr. J. Burgess. Mr. W. B. Kay ; second violins, Mr. H. Walker, Mr. T. Blamphin, Mr. C. Ditchfield, and Mr. 11. W. Handley; violas, Mr. J. Bate- man and Mr. J. Marlow ; violincello,Mr. G. F. Collinson and Mr. W. Simkin ; contrabasso,Mr. W. Morris ; flutes, Mr. .V. L. Needham and Mr. W. Craddock ; oboe, Mr. J. Richardson ; clarinette, Mr. W. E. Clark ; bassoon, Mr. J. Hewitt ; trumpet, Mr. J. Murray ; euphonium, Mr. T. Outhwaite ; and drums, Mr. W. B. Jackson, The organist was Mr. H. Walker, L.R.A.M.

div.head: PROPOSED TECHNICAL INSTITUTE FOR RUNCORN.
div.p: PROPOSED TECHNICAL INSTITUTE FOR RUNCORN.

Mr. Francis Wiswall, chairman of the Board of Improvement Commissioners, has addressed the following communication to a number of local gentlemen:— " I have been requested to form a large re presentative Committee to take in hand the raising of money for the establishment of a Technical Institnte. May I ask if you will be good enough to become a member of such Committee. I shall be glad of your co-operation in this important work. The estimated cost of the erection and furnishing of the Institution is about £4,000. Towards this, we are entitled to or have been proini::ed the followieg sums : Building grant by Science and Art Department, £924 ; Building grant by County Council, £444 ; accumulation of annual grants in aid from County Council, £3OO ; donation from F. T. Brunner, Esq., M.P., £530 ; dona- tion from P. Speakinan, Esq., C.C., £5O ; total £2,218. It is thought to be very desirable that the balance of £1,782 should be raised so that the Instltute may be, when erected, free from debt so that the grants in aid from the Clieshise County Council and the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners may be devoted entirely to the maintenance or the building and of the classes as there is rea,on to believe that the whole of these grants will be required for the efficient working of the Institute."

div.head: CHRISTMAS AT DUTTON WORKHOUSE.
div.p: CHRISTMAS AT DUTTON WORKHOUSE.

Christmas is looked upon as a red letter day, always to be remembered, and eagerly looked for- ward to by old and young alike, in every Work- house throughout the land ; but nowhere more so, than in the " House " at Dutton, belonging to the Runcorn Union, where, the ever considerate and worthy master and matron, Mr. end M rs. Joseph Gunnell, ably supported by the other officers of the institution, do all in their power to render everyone in the" House "as happy as they possibly can. Christ- mas Day falling on Sunday this year, the usual "Treat " 1 was given en Monday, that all might enjoy the festivi- i as, to the full extent. The dinner, which consisted of a bountiful supply of prime English beef, from Mr. William Gill, Warrington ; potatoes and plum pudding, was done ample justice to. Every praise is due to the matron, for the manner in which the dinner was served, as all the cooking is under her immediate supervision. Each adult inmate who chose, was allowed a half pint of beer for dinner, and the same for supper, granted by the Guardians. The children and other inmates Were given half a pint of new milk for dinner, and tea for supper, as well as bread and cheese. The dining halt had been most tastefully decorated by the same, vs);,11 zarlands of threaded holly, festoons, single and (70,ible triangles, pictures, venetian masts, nal mottoes appropriate for the season. At the last mastina of the Board the attardiana made a collection among themselves ; and thanks tO their generosity many of the adult inmates were supplied With tobacco, and the children with sweets, nuts and oranges. The children were permitted to take part in different games in the dining hall, under the direction of the school master and mistress, Mr. P. Naylor and Miss E. Moran. At five o'clock supper was served, and 6-30 p.m. an entertain- ment of a varied nature was given,the Master presiding. The programme being executed by the matron and her daughter Mrs. arid Miss Connell, who rendered severs! pianoforte solos and a duet with great credit ; the schoolmistress and children also fulfilling their part in , the entertainment, in the giving of songs, recitations I and Christmas carols. The day's proceedings were brought to a close about 5.30 p.m. When, after many expressions of pleasure and cheers for the Guardian., master, matron and other officers, on the part of their.- mates had been given, all retired to rest, evidently well satisfied with the enjoyment afforded. Thanks are due to H. Talbot, Esq., Dutton Lodge, for evergreens, Mrs. Marsden, Aston Vicarage, for bags of " mixed " fruit, Miss Best, Aston, for oranges, Mrs. Rodger, Darerbury, for hound volumee of "British Workman " and " Cot- tager and Artisan," alaia " Companion " and " Little Dots," Mr. Walter Collier, Buncorn, for oranges, and Mrs. Wright, Halton, for Christmas cards, also the Guardians for tobacco, massages. nuts, figs, and sweets.

On Wednesday evening the members of. the Runcorn Parish Church Choir, together with several members of the Band of Hope, journeyed to Dutton. to give an en- tertainment to the inmates of the Workhouse. The party, ueder the leadership of Mr. James Littler, the choir master of the Parish Church, gave an excellent render- ing of several Christmas carols and other musical items, which were much appreciated by the inmates, who showed their pleasure by frequent applause. The en- tertainment is the outcome of a plea made by the Chap- lain of the Workhouse, the Rev. J. D. Lyon-Bennett, at the recent Reri-decanal Conference, held at Runcorn, for help in the form of pleasant evenings during the winter months for the inmates ; and at the close of the proceed- ings, the rev, gentleman, in prcvosing a hearty vote of thanks to those who had so kindly presented such an excellent programme, expressed his pleasure that the suggestion which he had made had been attended with such sa,tisfatory results, and he trusted that they might again have the pleasure of welcoming the party.

div.head: HUSBAND AND WIVES AT WIDNES.
div.p: HUSBAND AND WIVES AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before the Mayor (Aid. F. 11. Gossage) and Mr. 11. Wade-Deacon, a respectably-dressed young man named John Kay was charged under a warreut with non-Compliance with an order made about three years ago to contribute 6s. per week towards his wife's maintenance. Mr. Knowles, who prosecuted, said prisoner was now owing to complainant £9 I6s. Pris- oner pleaded guilty to owing the money, but said he was unable to support his wife, who had, he alleged, misconducted herself of late. As pris- oner refused to make any offer, he was com- mitted to goal for six weeks with hard labour.— James Duxbury, a labourer, of Padiliam, was summoned by his wife, Fanny Jane, for deserting her. The com- plainant stated that she married the defendant on the 3rd of July last, and on the 26th of November he left her and went to his relatives in Padiham. He had since paid nothing towards her support, although he earned 223. a week. The defendant said he had a home for his I wife at Padiham, and offered to take her there. The case was adjourned for fourteen days.—Thomas Kandles, Victoria-road, was summoned by his wife, Clara Jane Handles, for not supporting her. The complainant, who said she was twenty-one years of age, had been married two years, and had two children. The defendant earned 223. 6d. one week, and 20s. another week, but he took more care of his pigeons and dogs than his family.—The bench made an order of 7s. 6d. a week. The defendant said he would not pay it, but would go to gaol fizst.

div.head: I? RODS HAM.
div.p: I? RODS HAM.

CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—At Frodsham Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Joseph Challoner, of Kingsley, was sum- moned for cruelty to a horse, by working it whilst in an unfit condition.—James Dowty, inspector for the Royal Society far the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, stated that he found one of the defendant's horses suffering from a sore shoulder and a contracted foot. It was totally unfit for work.—P.S. Doyle gave corroborative evidence.—Defendant said in his opinion the animal was fit for work.— A fine of 20s. and 10s. 6i ousts was ins—

posed. AN Ex-OYERSEEII AND MIS RATS.—In the case of the overseen; of Frodsham against James Edwards, of Main. at., for the payment of his lighting rate, amounting to 13s. 2d., Mr. Reynolds stated they had decided not to : iisue the warrant of distress for which application had been made.—Mr. Churton, who represented the over- seers, asked on what grounds they had arrived at such a resolution.—Mr. Reynolds said they had considered that point, and they thought it just as well not to go any further.—Mr.Churton expressed the opinion that the matter was so important that he would advise his clients , to apply for a mandamus. He referred to how serious it would be if the overseers were to meet every technical objection that might be raised.—Mr. Reynolds remarked that they had thoroughly considered the decision, and they knew how serious a matter it was.—Mr. Edwards said the rate would be paid. Those proceedings were not of his seeking. If the assistant overseer had accorded . to him the same civility he had to others, the rate would have been paid in due course.—Mr. Reynolds said he was pleased to hear that the rate was going to be paid, and thus end the matter. PEN KETH.

div.head: RETURN OF THE VICAR OF GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: RETURN OF THE VICAR OF GREAT SANKEY.

The return of the Rev. E. S. Jackson. vicar of St. Mary's Churcl,, Great Sankey, will be hailed with delight by all the parishioners of Penketh and Sankey. The rev. gentleman, who has been on a trip to Japan for the benefit of his health, arrived home on Wednesday night, and we are glad to state that his health is much improved by his journey, Socia.L. On Monday evening the "A" team of the Pen- keth Football Club e.ntertattecl the people of Pen- kerb to a concert in the Conservative Club. The proceedings were entirely under the direction of Mr. J. Woodward, the secretary of the club, who also acted as chairman. The members are hardly as large as their name might imply, being boys of from 9to 13 years. The cincert was a most enjoy- able one, and filled the audience with wonder and delight. The concert consisted of songs, pianoforte solos, violin and piccolo solos, Ste., all by the little footballers. The performers were Masters Manley Longshaw, Ernest Davies, Arthur Dwerryhouse, Arthur Molyneux, John Bingham, W. J. Pusill (captain), and Fred Foster, whose comic songs caused much amusement. Frank Dumbill accoto- paicd on the pianoforte. The concert was free.

div.head: UONVERSAZIONE AT PENKETII.
div.p: UONVERSAZIONE AT PENKETII.

In connection with the Mutual ImproTement Society, the annual conversazione was .seld in the esleyan school on Wednesday evening last. The room was tastefully decorated with evergreens and mottoes &c There were also tables in the room on which there were placed for inspection magazines, curiosities , and works of art. One of the finest things was the shield won by Fairfield Turner, which he had kindly lent for inspection. The assembly however, took such an interest in it that Mts. R. Garnett requested that it be explained from the platform. This was ably done by Mr. George Wilcox in whose care the shield was. The evening was admirably filled up with music, &c.,the artistes being Miss Langdon (of Liverpool) song, " The Maypole," and on receiving an encore " The Quaker," Miss Moses and Mr. R. E. Garnett, duet Where are you going to ray pretty maid,"Mrs. Garnett, Scotch reading, Mr. R. N. Foster, violin solos, Mr. Linney, recitation, " Hiawatha's Camera," which produced continued laughter. Mr. J. T. Guttersall reading on Tennyson. Mr. C. E. Parker was in the chair. Mr. David Garnett moved a vote of thanks to the refreshment committee and the friends who had contributed their aid to the con- cert. Mr. J. T. Gumersall seconded and included the decoration committee. Supper was also pro- vide.l. After the concert games were indulged in until 11 p.m. when the meeting clos2d.

div.head: ADDRESS TO MR. J. T. GUMERSALL.
div.p: ADDRESS TO MR. J. T. GUMERSALL.

Last evening week the Committee of Penketh Liberal Club journeyed to the friends School to present an illuminated address to Mr. J. T. G umer- sail, who is leaving the village. Mr. Fred Hughes, the secretary, read the address, which has been most artistically prepared by Mr. R. Routledge. The address read as follows : "To J. T. Gumersall, Esq. At a meeting of the Penketh Liberal Club held on the sth inst., it was resolved : That the Committee's thanks be tendered to J. T. Gumersall, Eq.. for his generous support to the club during his residencs in Peuketh, and more especially while actimz as vice-President, and for two years, 1888 and 1889, as President of the club; as well as for the valuable advice and assistance given to the club. they also wish to express their sincere regret, to hear of his intention to leave the district, where his services have been so much appreciated. The corn- mitt desire to record their heartiest hope and wish that the future, both of himself and his family, may be of the happiest ; and that, his valuable labours in the cause of Liberalism may be felt and appreciated wherever he may be located. (Signed) J. B. Aitkin, chairman ; Fred Hughes, secretary." Mr. and

Mrs. Gumersall entertained the committee to supper and a most enjoyable evening was spent'. In his reply Mr. Ciumersall said : Mr. kitken and Gentlema, I assuro you that I am deeply touched by the many kind expressions contained in the address that you have just present- ed to me. I thank you from the bottom of my heart, not only for the kindly thoughts which prompted these expressions, but also for the pains you have taken to have them so beautifully and tastefully prepared for my acceptance. At the same time I cannot fail to feel that you have placed a value on my simple services far beyond they merit, so that I find myself,through your generosity in a position that otherwise I could never have dreamed of occupying. Wherever my future lot may be cast I shall never forget the hearty manner in which I have always been received by the mem- bers of the Penketh Liberal Club. May it long con- tinue to occupy that sphere of usefulness which it has done hitherto, not only in imbuing the minds of the young men of this village with true Liberal principles, but also in binding them together in bonds of true friendship and social intercourse Mrs. Gnmersall joins me in wisldng you a very happy Christmas and a bright New Year.

div.head: ROWDY SCENES AT CHRISTMAS.
div.p: ROWDY SCENES AT CHRISTMAS.
DRINK, AND MISERY.

At the Borough Police' Court, on Tuesday, John Kelly, Ship-yard, was charged with being drunk and disoreerly, and assaulting Constabl-.8 Bell and Amson. Jane Kelly, his wife, was also charged with assaulting the offloers. P.C. Bell stated that he went to Ship-yard, and saw the male prisoner there. He was making use of had language and had his coat off, challenging everybody to fight him. He had just been ejected from the Vaults in the Ship-yard. He requested pri- soner several times to put his coat On and go on, but he refused, 'and when witness threatened to lock him up, he ran into his house and returned with a hatchet,with the back of which he struck witness on the chest. P.C. Arnson came up, and aftsr getting the hatchet out of the prisoner's hand they took him to the police s•Ation. As they were taking him out of the yard his wife threw a piece of a brick, which hit Amson on the head ;Lnd knocked his hemlet off. She then threw a heavier piece, which caught him on the right elbow. His arm was now swollen,and he had no use in it. After locking the man up, he got the assistance of a third con- stable to fetch the female prisoner to the police station. —lnspector Spinks said the female prisoner was brought to the Police Stition at 7-50 on the previous night, and she behaved disorderly until one o'clock in the morning. At eleven o'clock they went to the prisoner's house, and found a little child there, lying in a corner, with no one to take care of it, and no Ore. They brought it to the Police Station, and kept it by the fire. The two young children, who were now in court, were greatly neglected by their parents. The Inspector proceeded to state that if it had not been for the police on Christmas morning, the prisoner would I would not now have been alive. At ten past two that morning Constable Corbett reported that seeing smoke coming f rem the direction of a window at No, 6 Lower 'ship-yard, the residence of John Kelly, a labourer, he - entered the house and found Kelly on the floor ' drunk. A paraffin lamp was lying broken on the floor and a quantity of paper and clothing was burning close to. He got some water and extin- guished the flames. The flames had caught the fireplace and chimney. he went upstairs and found the wife and two children in bed. He aroused them and found that the woman was drunk. Inspector spinks added that he himself had put the woman into the house a short time before the fire broke out, and she was drunk then. The Chairman said the magistrates would discharge the female prisoner on her premising to sign the pledge and look better after the children. They, however, could not do the same with the husband. He had been disorderly, and had ccmmitted a dastardly assault on the police. He would be sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labc;:e.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

Christmas passed off • without any of the calam- ities which perhaps I may be permitted to describe as seasonable. No one met with a premature end by skating on thin ice and no deaths have been reported from excessive eating and drinking. But for all that, there have been deaths reported of a far more pathetic and tragical character ; not "sea- sonable " deaths, but such as occur every day throughout the year somewhere. The day before Christmas day a poor, homeless, destitute man made his way to the river bank near Wilderspool- road, and in the stillness and quietness of the morn- ing, threw himself into the cold black water, and ended his lot. He left no explanatory epistle ; no- thing but a patched and tattered coat,and a ragged vest-; which, if the truth were known, would pro- bably form an eloquent index to a story ill-fitted to harmonise with this season of "good will to all men," and luxurious feeding and feasting. Another man went into a room connected with the Bull's Head Inn, on Tuesday, and stood on a chair and fastened round his neck a rope, which was attached to a beam. He died. On Monday a man fell in a tan pit at Reynolds' Tannery. He died also. Considering these things, and reflecting also that the smallpox has not quite left us, I feel unable to say that we have had a very merry Christ- mas, and I can only hope with more cheerfulness for a "Prosperous New Year."

11 I hear that, in a short time, another young War- ringtonian will be added to the number of those 1 who have left the "good old town "for America. 1 allude to Mr. W. 11. Butler, who, together with Mrs. Butler, will sail from Liverpool in the steam- ship" Catalonia " on the 10th January. His de- stination is Boston,where he will enter the ministry of the Methodist Episcopal Church. Mr. Butler, I need hardly say, will be much missed in many circles of activity in Warrington. He has been for some years an able and acceptable local preacher in connection with the Wesleyans of this district. The Young Men's Christian Association will, upon his departure, lose an energetic and helpful mem- ber. Being a fluent and ready debater, and with a mind well furnished by reading and study, he has often figured prominently at local aebating societies, and in connection with these his pre- sence will also be much missed. Every one, lam sure, *ill wish that his career in America may be a successful one.

I have been asked to give publicity to the follow- ing statement of good work done in the town : "Mr. Joseph Wibberley, of 26, Battersby-lane, ,nia- sionery and evangelist, has made considerable effort during the winter in the way of relieving the poor as,whilst on his rounds of visita- tion he has met with a great number of persons who were in Vat di:siren. Mr. Wibberley has a good opportunity of obtaining information as to the real condition of the families he visits as he calls upon the same people frequently and usually reads the scriptures and offers prayer before leaving them. We may say that, for several winters past, Mr. Wibberley has made special efforts to secure contributions for the purpose of distributing amongst the poor some little food at Christmas time. Many kind friends have responded to his call and he has thus been enabled to distribute, bread, tea, sugar and meat to a:, least 160 poor people, Mr. Wibberley works under the directions of a few friends who have formed themselves into a committe,e, t he principal members of which are :—Mr. John Hamblet, of Winwick-st., and Mr. Robert Cook of Wilderspool-road. It may not be generally known that Mr. Wibberly has been working as a missionary in the town for over fotr years, and has administered spiritual and temporal relief to hundreds of poor persons, having visited them during sickness and also many on their death-beds."

A considerable amount of assistance has been needed by the poor people in Warrington this Christmas time, and, I believe, that many philan- thropic persons have quietly done their best to meet this demand upon their generosity. Probably no one has more claim for commendation, in this direction, than the Mayor and Mayoress. The chief magistrate fed soma thousands of poor people on Boxing Day, with hot-pot dinner, and to .a person who watched these indigents entering the Drill Hall, for their portion, there were sights both pathetic and humorous.

In one instance I noticed a particularly painful illustration of poverty. A widow, with worn face and sunken eyes, came with a tiCket for five din- ners, and the only utensil she could offer to carry the food away in was a half rusted bucket. In another case a little boy came along and tendering his ticket said, " The old 'un's sent me." " Whose the old 'un," queried a gentleman with the ladle. " Garn ! yer knew—lts mam." "Oh ! well, what have you got to put the hot-pot in ?" The boy looked dazed for a bit. Ile searched his pockets then said " Dunno, guv'nor." By-and-by his eyes suddenly sparkled with inspiration and he snatch- ed off his greasy pot hat and said, " I'll take it in my cady." But they wouldn't let him and hp went back for a more euitat,le vessel,

Speaking of Boxing t) ay fetnindS me of a fact which I was impressed with On that particular day. It was a very sympathetic, enthusiastic, and representative Warrington audience. I went to the Royal Court Theatre to see "The Crimes of Paris!' The " house " was packed, and the hearts of the managers must likewise have been filled with joy. The curtain had not been up many minutes before the audience—which was a real Warrington one,only to be seen on holidays—began to come out of its shell, so to speak. When the villain did anything nasty. they overpowered him with hoots ; when the hero came with his blond visage and blue eyes, and made a brave speech full of self-sacrifice, they cheered until the place shook. But it was finest when the heroine came along all sad and melancholy with dreamy eyes upturned to heaven, the image of a persecuted female, as she sank on to the floor, wishing that she might be placed under the green turf with nothing about her lonely grave but some lilies and a modest marble headstone. That was the time ; tears trickled down the women's cheeks, and the men under the gallery were silent and listened.

Once I came across an instance of the effect of pathos, well worth citing. Two women sat on the form in front or me. They were both in a constant state of feverish excitement at first; and to lull this one of them often resorted to a little bottle which had a label on it, and she began to get more sentimental. By and by, when the hero returned from exile, meets his wife who has become en- tangled with another man, the two women open their mouths in excited expectation. The wife pleads that he will think of the byegone balmy days of happiness, and take her on again. But he cries out in an anguished and husky voice. "Newer I Never You—have —broken your vow —you have broken my—heart." Then he glided forth in silent grandeur. The eyes of the woman with the bottle were only blurred with tears at first; now the crystal tokens of her sorrow ran copiously along her nose. she buried her face in her hands and wept. Iler companion pinched her on the arm,and said " Ilowd thee husht, Liza. It's not real, lass, it's not real." " Neaw, oi know that, but I carnt help it." And she went on crying so loudly that one of the attendants had to call her to order.

that a person can have There is an old saying "too much of a good thing." I have a slight idea that people at the County Court on Thursday had too much disinfectant powder, which is a good thing in its way. The floor of the court had been lavishly coated with the strong smelling powder. The desk in the defendant's box was also covered to the depth of almost half an in6h with it; but I noticed that the "book " did not appear to have been disinfected. Probably religious scruples had prevented the bailiffs from disinfecting this item of court property. On one occasion I saw a man in the box, with his fingers almost completely buried in the disinfectant, as though he was trying to keep them warm ; and I was told by an official of the court of a female defendant. Vl° entered the box with a basket, and coolly lifted the powder into her basket in handfuls. I believe in , disinfeetion; but I don't hold with the absurd waste of any useful thing.

I am told that the Mayor will make an important announcement at the Council meeting on Tuesday evening, to the effect that a gentleman of position in the town has offered a very large sum of mmev as a gift to the town for certain purposes which will be explained. I have no doubt it will give general satisfaction, but I am not in a position to give details and will leave my readers in suspense until Tuesday night. Di ERLLN.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. Burgess (in the chair). Alderman Chandley and Mr. J. Geddes and Mr. L. Voisey, CRUELTY TO A Hoasu.—James Edw,irds was charged with having on the 21st inst. worked a horse, which was in an unfit condition, and Thomas Kenrick was charged with having allowed it to be worked while in that con- dition.—P.C. Corbett stated that on the 21st inst. he was at Market-gate when he saw the horse going past, at- tached to a 'bus. He followed it to the stopping place in Corporatien-st., and there exansined it. • He found a piece of string tied round one of its feet near the heel, and there was a large wsund which was bleeding. He afterwards gave information to Inspector Dowty.—ln- spector Dowty stated that he examined the horse. On the near fore leg there was a large wound into which he could put his finger. The horse was not in a fit state to work.— A fine of 54. on each defendant was inflicted. WITIL THEIR JACKETS OFF FIGHTING.—Th(.InaS Glaven, 17, Bank-st., and Bernard Mcalanee, Dolman's-lane, were charged with having on the 19th inst. committed a breach of the peace by fighting in Bank-st.—P.C. Tur- ner said that he went to Bank-st.on the day in question, and there saw the defendants with their jackets off, fighting. They were both sober.—Both defendants were bound over to keep the peace for six months. OBSCENE LANciUAGE..—Mary Quin was charged with having made use of obscene language in the Old-road, Latchford; on the 20th Decensber.—The case was dismissed. 'PITCH AND Toss."—Johu Heaton andlohn Whittaker were eharged with having played " nitch and toss " in an opening off Museum-st., on the 18th of December. P.C. Lewis stated that he watched the defendants for a quarter of an hour playing " pitch and toss" with pen- nies behind Mr. Fletcher's works. There were other men there, but the defendants were the only ones play- ing, Heaton stated that he had not pbypd "pitch and toss "for the last 16 years, and he could not have played on the date named, for he had no money. The other defendant said he " didn't toss a halfpenny up." The defendants were fined ss. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment. Joseph Owen, Bernard Ilinnigan,Henry Marratt, James Binford, William Bradshaw, and Thomas Conroy, were charged with a similar offence on the 18th of December in Stout's-yard, off Winwick-road. P.C.'s Turner and Astmore proved the charge, Conroy, on account of his age, eleven years, was litwrated ; Blnford and Bradshaw were fined ss. and the rest 2s. 6d. each.-- Thomas Hardman, Gilbert Berry, Thomas Conroy, Joseph Owen and James Steward, were charged with a similar offence on the 19th inst., in Palmyra-square. The defendants pleaded guilty. Hardman was fined 55., and the other defendants 2s. 6d. each. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Monks (in the chair), Alderman

div.head: Wright, and Messrs. W. Pier Point and T.'f3irchall.
div.p: Wright, and Messrs. W. Pier Point and T.'f3irchall.

ASSAULTING a WOMA.N.--James Reed, a labourer, was charged with assaulting a woman whose name and address are unknown, at ten minutes to twelve o'clock on Saturday night.—The prisoner, it appeared from the evidence, was with a stranger in Mersey-street, with whom he quarrelled, and struck her several times. A crowd had assembled, and one of them struck the prisoner.—Fined ss. and cost:. DRUNKENNESS.—EIIen ; Connor, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butterrnarket-street on the pre- vious night, fined ss. including COSTS. TRUANT PAUPERS.—A woman named Mary Skullv, an inmate of the workhouse,was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the previous night.—lt appeared that the prisoner and two other women climbed the wall surrounding the house, and spent several hours in tawn. The prisoner returned in the evening in a state of in- toxication, broke several panes of glsss, and cut her arm very badly. She was very violent, and the police had to be sent for.—Prisoner said she had seven children, and she hoped the Bench would "look over it this time.' —She was sent back to the Workhouse in charge of a policeman, and admonished for her bad conduct. TUESDAY—Before Mr. R. Garnett (in the chair), Coun- cillor H. Roberts, Dr. Starkey Smith, and Mr. T. Birchall. SHE WENT FOR THE RENT—THEY " WENT" FOR HER. —Catherine Hannan, 35, Warburton-street, was charged with using threatening language towards Mary Barron, on the 21st inst.—Complainant stated that she was the owner of some property in Warburton-street, and on the day in question she went to defendant's house to collect the rent. There were four persons in the house, all drunk. Defendant shouted to her that she would get no rent, and if she didn't go out of the house quickly she (defendant) would do three months for her. She then rushed at complainant, but was prevented doing any- thing by her son. The Bench ordered defendant to be bound over to keep the peace. ON FOR "BLACK DlAMOND."—Patrick Farrington, 17 years of age, was charged with stealing a quantity of coal, value 6c1., from Messrs. Pearson and Knowles Iron Works.—P.S. Lawrence stated that having received complaints during the past fortnight of coal being stolen from Bewsey Works, he kept watch, and that morning at ten minutes to seven, he saw two persons cross the railway from Pierpoint-et., and one of them climbed over into the premises of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' works. In a short time he saw lumps of coal being dropped over the fence on to the railway. After four lumps had been dropped he and another constable, who was with him, made a rush to the spot.—The pri- soner ran awarlown the line, but was caught.—The Bench inflicted a fine of 103. and costs, or 14 days in default. A PREDATORY NAVVY.—William Wray, a Ship Canal labourer, was charged with stealing a horse rug, the property of Mr. Maginn, cab proprieter, Sankey-street. —Prosecutor stated that about half-past one on the prev- ious afternoon he was told that a rug had been stolen from a cab at the Arpley-street entrance to the yard. Ile immediately ran clown the street, and turned into White-street, where he caught up the prisoner, who had the rug under his coat.—P.C. Berry having corroborated, the Bench inflicted a fine of 20s. including costs. ASSAULT ON TEE Pormn.—John Mitchell, a labourer living in Lower Walton, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the Little Weint on Sunday night, at twenty minutes past ten, and assaulting Constable Clough. The officer stated that he was in Buttermarket- st. at the time named, when he saw the prisoner and another man fighting. He went up to the men for the purpose of separating them, when the pri:oner struck him in the mouth and tried to kick him. Witness bled freely from the mouth.—Fined ss. and costs. SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A MOTHER.—A young woman, Mary Ann Flansbury, Heaton's-yard, was charged with assaulting her mother' Ellen Reynolds, on the previous night.—Sergeant Taylor said that complainant visited the office at the police station on the previous evening. Her face was streaming with blood, and she informed him that " it had been done by her daughter Mary." He stopped the bleeding. dressed the old woman's wounds, and went in search of the defendant, who was locked up. Mrs. Reynolds said her daughter had as- saulted her with a clog and a hatchet (now produced). The complainant had a wound on her head about an inch and a half in length. Defendant was sent to jail for three months.
After

WEDNEKDAY.—Before Mr. J. Fairclough (in the chair), Alderman Wright, Councillor Fleming, Messrs. J. Geddes, and S. Wright. TICKET Or LAVE MAN IN TROUELE.—A ticket of leaf man named George Connolly, a hlwker, was charged with obtaining by false pretences from Miss L, Baker.

daughter of Mr. Joseph Baker, of Mill-lane, 7s. The evidence showed that the complainant was in the mar- ket on Monday last, and she saw the prisoner at a greengrocer's stall. She went to him as she had been in the habit of dealing with him, and told him she wanted one cwt. of potatoes. After further negotiations she consented to take two bags containine, each 112 lbs. Be offered to let her have these for 7s. each. Be brought two bags to the house and emptied them on the floor. After the prisoner had ' gone with the money, she and her brother weighed the potatoes and found that altogether there was a defici- ency of 100 lbs., in the weight of the potatoes. Two of the complainant's brothers who had witnessed the weigh- ing of the potat„es gave corroborative evidence.—Pri- soner was committed to take his trial at the next Quarter sessions. RESULT OH A FAMILY SQUABBLll.—Frederick Smith, a young man, was bound over to keep the peace for six months, for assaulting a woman named Alice Smith near the Old Ball, Winwick-road. The affair was the result of a family squabble.
- - FRlDAL—Before Mr. John White (in the chair), Alder- man .Wright, Councillor H. Roberts, and Mr. S.

Wright, A TALE OF TWO MILITARY BOOTS.—Ann Taylor (mar- ried woman), was charged under the Pawnbrokers' Act with pawning a pair of military boots, at Morton's pawn shop, on the 14th October, knowing them to be stolen by John Conroy, a soldier ; and Edwin Pie, manager to Mr. Morton, was summoned for receiving the same.—Mr. A. Browne appeared on behalf of Mr. Pie, and prose- cuted the first defendant on the charge set down against her. Mr. Browne stated that his client was in the 6habit of taking in a great many pair of boots from militia men, whose training had expired. The woman often came to the shop pledging her hnsband's boots, and when she tendered the boots in question, he thought there was nothing unusual about it ; she answered her questions satisfactorily and he lent her 3s. upon them.—P.S. Monaghan stated that from information he received he made investigations. He went to Morton's shop and Mr. Pie produced the boats. He identified them as boots having been stolen by Conroy. Conroy would have been brought up that morning, but he was now in custody at Widnes on a charge of shopbreaking. —The defendant who seemed much distressed said she was in Bodelia Knockton's mother's house, when she met Conroy. He represented himself to her as an honest man, who had every right to the boots and when he asked her to pawn the boots for him she did so, uncon- scious that she was doing wrong.—After hearing other evidence the Bench dismissed both cases. A DEFAULTING CORPORATION EMPLOYEE.—JOSeptI Had- land, a carter, in the employ of the Warrington Cor- poration, was charged with embezzelling from his employers the sum of 7s 6d., and two other sums of 2s 6d., each. Mr. Whittle, town clerk, appeared to pro- secute on behalf of the Corporation. The evidence showed that prisoner had been employed carting coke from the gas works to private purchasers. While so do- ing he had demanded the money for the coke, against instructions, and had confiscated the money. Be was arrested by Detective Monoghan, who stated that prisoner was the son of respectable parents, but he had succumbed to wild living.—Fined 20s. and costs.

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
TuESDAY.—Before Messrs.
J,p,Parr (in the chair), H.
la --and W. Long.

4LL THROUGH CHRISTMA3.—Dennis Dagnall, of Little Leigh, was charged with being drunk and disorthrly on the 7th December.—Defendant attributed his conduct to the influence of Christmas season, but he was told he had been somewhat precipitate in his festivities.—Fined 2s. 6d. AFTER A MELANCHOLY FATILITY.—Wm. Wright, of Budworth, was charged with being in possession of a gun without a license, on the 15th October. The evi- dence of the case showed that the defendant on the date in question had been at a farmer friend of his, and he and others were out shooting when the gun which the defendant had accidentally exploded, as he was mount- ing a fence, and the result was that another man who was with him was shot dead. It appeared that the defendant had been in the habit of taking out a license but had overlooked it on this occasion.—Fined 103. and costs. A CRUEL DRlTER.—Charles Herbert Birchall, a youth, was charged at the instance of the R.S.P.C.A. with ill- treating a horse on the 21st December, at Acton Grange. —lnspector Dowty comincted the prosecution.—The defendant was driving two horses attached to a canal boat, owned by the Ship Canal Company.—William Nein another fiatrnaia said he saw the defendant thrashing the horses and driving them so furiously that the animals were rushing along at almost ten miles an hour. By doing this the defendant was endangering the safety of other boats on the canal, and when remonstrated with, he abused witness in such a way as to prevent him being able to eat heavy food for a week. Witness brought a policeman to the scene.—The magistrates after considering the evidence ordered defendant to pay 7s. 6d. costs, telling him their leniency was in conse- quence of there being no traces of abuse on the animals. The cwistable who had been called out deposed that when he went in search of the defendant the latter upon observing ran away and left him the horses and boat.

- TIIII BREED LOST IN IRS BRIIISES.—Thomas Maines, a Ship Canal navvy, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the highroad at Walton Superior, on Sun- day, the 11th inst. Two constables stated that defend- ant had managed to get a couple of dogs fighting, and they saw him dancing and swearing round them. He threatened to "bosh" the policemen's heads with them when they interfered. Upon a policeman stating this, defendant said," Oh, you wicked,wicked, false man."— Defendant was fined ss. and costs on this charge, and he was further charged with cruelty to the dogs by setting them to fight. Defendant denied having set the dogs on to fight, and said that only one dog belonged to him,and the other dog met it and commenced to fight voluntarily A constable, on being asked to describe the breed of one dog couldn't, because it had been "to mauled. Its breed was lost in its bruises.—Defendant was ordered to pay costs for this offence. HAD NO GUN LICENSE.—Oratio Nelson, a Ship Canal navvy, wes also lined £1 and costs, for carrying a gun without a license at Grappenhall, on the 11th October.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. James Handley and Dr. Steele. DRUNKENNESS.—The following were fined for drunken- ness :—Thomas Stephen, Wm. Welsh, Thomas McHugh, John Sullivan, John Wilson, Edward Butcher, Isaac White and Charles Napston, all of" no settled abode."— In each case the penalty was 2s. 6d. and costs.

div.head: DYNAMITE OUTRAGE IN DUBLIN.
div.p: DYNAMITE OUTRAGE IN DUBLIN.
A DETECTIVE SHOCKINGLY MANGLED.

A desperate outrage, which unfortunately was at- tended with loss of life, was committed in Dublin, at eleven o'clock on Saturday night, when an attempt was made to blow up with dynamite or some such deadly explosive the detective office at Exchange Court,a build- ing which is close to the City Hall and adjoins the Chief Secretary's Department of Dublin Castle. A report like a burst of thunder was heard in the court, accompanied Iby a violent concussion. There was a general rush made from the office by the detectives, who were report- ing themselves at the time. It was then found that the pavement under the office window was torn up and the window and frame demolished, and that among the debris lay Detective Synnott almost dead. Synnott,who was shockingly mangled, was removed to Dr. Smith's house in Parliament-st., and afterwards to Jervis-st. Hospital, where he died. On examination it was found that the damage to property was not so extensive as might have been expected judging by the violence of explosion. All the glass in the detective office, a portion of the City Hall, and neighbouring structures was shattered, and the outer wall of the office wag cracked. It is supposed that the explosive was placed on the footway against the wall of the office, and that Synnott kicked it as he was passing down the court, thus pro- ducing the explosion.

The inquest on Patrick Synnott, a member of the Dublin detective force, who was killed by the explosion in Exchange Court, opposite the Detective Office, on Saturday night, was held on Monday in Jervis-st. Hospi- tal, by Dr. Kenny, Dublin city coroner. Several con- stables were examined, and stated the circumstanees under which Synnott was found lying in the court. 1 Constable Green, who passed through the court imme- diately before the explosion, said he observed a brown- looking parcel, in form like a book, lying on the foot- path opposite the detective office. Fle did not examine it, but passed on, and about five minutes later heard the explosion. After medical evidence had been given as to Synnott's hopeless condition when taken to Jervis- at. Hospital, the jury found that death was caused by I the explosion, but that there was no evidence to show by whom the explosive substance was placed in the court.

A public meeting of the citizens of Cork, convened by the Mayor, was held on Tuesday to express abhorrence at the explosion in Dublin. The Mayor presided. Mr. Maurice Healy, M.P., proposed a resolution strongly condemning the outrage. It was not, he said, the act of any friends of Ireland, and it could not have been in the interest of the political prisoners. The resolution was supported by the High Sheriff and carried unanimously.

In the second half Runcorn had much coining round to see the homes of the poor whom you best of the play. Pye added three goals and Hampson visit. Unfortunately 'the poor man's magistrate ' was two, the final being—Runcorn six goals ; Farnworth, never able to accompany the missionary on his mes- a, sages of mercy, because just after this his illness became more severe and complicated. Very soon, however, through the efforts of Mr. Williams, a clothing depot was fitted up in a house near the City-road, which was stocked with garments of every description, and many a poor wretched father and mother have blessed Mr. Montagu Williams for providing them with warm clothing, good food, fuel, and furniture. Beneath the keg.,, qnick, sometimes even abrupt manner of the raagistrate, there was one of the kindest and most sym- pathetic hearts that ever beat in man. One day in the coldest part of winter a poor mother told her sad tale of want and hardship to the ever-open ear of Mr. Williams. He immediately sent his faithful missionary to visit the woman's house and report forthwith. The scene which afterwards took place was most touching. The mis- sionary reported to tho magistrate that he had found in the home' to the woman a girl of 17, pale and emaciated, lying on an old bedstead chair, covered only with a few rags, and sick unto death' with con- sumption. On the table in the miserable room there lay some crusts of bread which the father had pilked from off the streets that day. Standing on some hot cinders in the grate was a little tin pan containing water, in which to soak some of this bread, in order that the sick girl might at it—the only food in the house. The father was out of employment and starvation was doing it deadly work. During the missionary's recital Mr. Williams was visibly affected, arid as the sad tale was brought to a close tears, which the humane magistrate could not keep back, rolled down his cheeks. Almost without speaking he handed the missionary some money to provide for the immediate ri,eds of the family ; the delicate girl was placed in Brompton Hospital, and work was found for the father. After being in hospital for a considerable length of time the girl returned to her home, and the missionary visited her regularly until her death. On her dying bed her last words to Mr. Massey were, as the tears stood in her eyes, and her breathing came in irregular gasps Please—Mr. Massey—tell— Mr.—Williams—how—gratef ul—l—am—for—his—kind- ness.' And in a little while she was dead. Had Mr. Wil- liams lived he intended, and there is no doubt that he would have been able, to extend his philanthropic work amongst the poor of the City and East End. His latest instructions to the missionary were to fit up rooms in his (Mr. Massey's) house for the storing of clothing to be given to the distressed, and his whole mind was filled with the question how best to meet the misery of the winter. At the beginning of last month he wrote : Dear Mr.--, as I told you, if I am alive and there is the same distress in my old neighbourhood, I shall re- open my depot . • . and with your help hope to do the same good as last a ear. . . . I have returned —'s cheque with thanks, saying I will avail myseif of it later on if the necessity arises. . . . I never can be really well again, but hope to return to my duties when my leave expires with a little more strength.— Yaurs always, Moarreou WILLIAMS.' It is suggested that the best memorial to such a man would be the perpetuation of his mission of kindly deeds."

CHRISTMAS-EVE IN THE TRAVELLING POST OFFICE. By general consent, it is a very quiet Christmas-eve in St. Martin's-le-Grand. Yet the stranger would hardly think so. The yards all round the " G.P.0." are thronged with vehicles in scarlet and gold ; the great beehive itself is filled with a great flood of light ; its doorways are all but blocked up with mail-bags and the hundreds of men who are heaving and hauling them about. The controller of the big machine (Mr. Bad- cock), the vice controller (Mr. Paniphilon), and the two assistant controllers (Mr. Smith and Mr. Cravrfurd), are preparing for an all-night sitting, and messengers are hurry-scurrying about, and reports are coming in and orders are going forth. During the day 700 sacks of letters have come in from Australia on the top of the season's flood at noon ; and to-morrow— Sunday, that is—a thousand sacks will come in from America, and all have to be instantly dealt with. And yet everybody agrees that not for some years have they had so easy a time if it on Christmas Eve. It is not that the Christmas postal traffic has fallen off this year. When the grand total comes to be made up the probability is that it will prove to have been heavier than ever. But the British public has taken to heart the behests of the Postmaster General to post early as well as often ; and so, after getting myself armed with a certain little document, I climb for a moment into a lofty gallery, and look down on the great sorting floor, with its dozen great blazing are lights and its 1,500 or 2,000 people all in full drive, and am assured that, busy though the scene is, the back of the season's job has been broken, and the worst of the work is over. And now with my slip of paper in my pocket I go out again under the frosty stars and betake myself to the hurrying hansom, and rattle away over the hard roads to Euston Square. Here is another crowd of vehicles in scarlet and gold, another crowded district of letter bags and parcel packages, and more blaae of light and lines of busy sorters. The other was "G. P. o."—the General Post-office. This is the " T. P. o."—the Travelling Post-office.—and the paper in my pocket authorises me to step in and go rumbling out into the darkness as far as Crewe-158 miles nearer the North Pole—and back again by another "'r. P. 0.," which will bring me home with the milk in the morning. The mechanism by which letters are given out to stations or taken in from them while the train is rushing at full speed has been often described, but I could always stand and watch the uncanny business with a sort of fascination. A bag of something under 50Ib of letters is enclosed in a tough leather " envelope " and laid by in readiness. Then a sliding panel in the side of the carriage is pushed out of the way, and the lights flash down on the bare earth scudding away through the night at the rate perhaps of a mile an minute, and presenting to the baffled eye only an indefinite streak flashing out of the dark into the dark, with a deafening roar. The leather package has to be hung out over that murderous torrent —dangled at the end of an iron, supported by means of , a stout leather strap and a massive piece of wrought iron known as a"T piece." A young man last night in endeavouring thus to suspend a heavy burden of letters all but overbalanced himself. Perhaps his danger was more apparent than real, but it was at all events suffici- ent to make one of his mates clutch him from behind, and to all appearances he was thus saved from falling headlong out, and perhaps carrying the parcel with him. Another inch, apparently, and the young fellow would have been all but dashed to pieces, and very likely scores of correspondents would have had reason to complain of the ridiculous delays of the Post-office. " It is very dangerous work," said Mr. Mac Donnell, a chief superintendent of the Travelling Post, who was looking on. " Many men haven't the nerve for it." And not only have they to be men of nerve, but they require experience and acuteness of perception to enable them to judge of the exact position of the train as it goes ' tearing along through darkness, and perhaps rain or blinding snow, sr even a dense fog. An exceedingly keen lookout is necessary for all sorts of landmarks— trees or houses, or streams or bridges, and sometimes when they can see nothing they have to be guided largely by sound. " You hear that peculiar roar ? " observes Mr. Mac Donnell, at one point. "We are running over the water trough, laid between the lines to enable the driver to take up water without stopping." At some stations we have to hang out two parcels, they go for a time gliding over the special track flashing along beneath them, and then come two tremeadous thuds, and they have vanished into the night. .A strong net hung out near the station they are intended for has scoped them up and they are left far behind. At the same instant, by another aperture, one or two similar burdens of letters have been hurled in upon us like thunderbolts, that seem to shake the train from end to end, and might be a certain death to anyone in their way, as though they were cannon balls. We know, of course, that they are coming, and by means of a huge lever we have hung out our net to receive them, the movement of the lever setting to ring an electric bell to warn all and sundry to keep out of the way of the bombshells of love-letters and Christmas-cards, of cheques and bills, and packets of good advice and tid- ings of deaths and births and marriages, that the mis- cellaneous world outside is about to hurl in upon us,and which will come booming out of the net with terrific thuds. All night long we go on sending out or taking in these budgets, with their tough bull-hides, something like 200 to 300 of them being despatched and as ntany received as the train rushes on from London to Carlisle. There our staff of about forty men will be exchanged for others, who will take on the train to Aberdeen, where it should arrive at nine o'clock in the morning. Meanwhile, however, we have to stop at some inter- mediate stations, and wherever we do so huge. barri- cades of baskets and boxes and bags are awaiting us. A t Tamworth the North-Western is crossed overhead by the Midland, and we have to exchange mails by means of an enormous hydraulic lift, which in severe weather is apt to be frozen hard. To-night, however, the freez- ing has not yet taken place, and we haven't much to exchange. The rather awkward platform with its numerous posts that always seem to stand just where they are not wanted, is for a few minutes a scene of great bustle. The ground sparkles with frost, and the stars glitter down, and one or two panting engines are throwing up fantattic columns of golden vapour and glaring out into the night with the fiery eyes of mythical monsters, and soon we are all on board and ploughing again through the gloom. And all the while our sorters are patiently plodding on with prebably not far short of a quarter of a million of letters, which they .are deftly sticking into pigeon holes, almost with the readiness and facility that, a compositor will " dis." his type— those of them, tit any rate, who are old hands. But there are a good many here who are temporarily en- gaged, and who for the two or three days of high pres- sure have'had to undergo some weeks of preliminary training. It is not a cheerful thought as one stands and looks along the line of these men, working with such diligence and conscientious care, that a large proportion of them will in a day or two have to turn out more or less "unemployed." One of these novices a night or two back, came within ail ace of a frightful death. These mail trains have a gangway from end to end of them, and with the regular vehicle there are perfectly safe passages between them. Owing, however, to some irregularity, an ordinary guard's van had 1 to take the place of one ot them, and a gap was left between them. One of the supernumer- aries fell into this gap, and was carried some distance dangling down between the buffers, while the train was travelling at five-and-forty miles an hour. Fortunately he just managed to hold on until his com- rades got a grip of him and hauled him up practically unhurt. That is not an ordinary risk, but such are some of the risks encountered by those who through the livelong night are plodding industriously through irksome duties in Order that we. may get our posts with promptitude and precision. During the past few nights nearly 500 men have been engaged in these postal trains rushing all over the country, or at least on the main lines, and the amount of work involved in the. planning and arranging may be estimated in some faint degree when it is stated that it has been in hand ever since the beginning, of October, and that the whole arrangements are set forth in a folio baok of 180 printed pages. All this travelling postal bueiness devolves on the London ' controller and his colleagues.—Daily News.

RUGBY. RUNCORN A Y. ST. EIHLRNS RECRHATION A.—Those

teams met each other on the Irwell ground, Runcorn,on Saturday afternoon. The ground was exceedingly hard in consequence of the severe frost. There was a fair number of spectators. The visitors kicked off, and a speedy reply was made by the homeaters, who exhibited a nice piece of passing which ended in a minor. They continued to keep the upper hand, and on several occa- sions experienced hard lines in not scoring. This was the condition of matters until the last minute, when Wardle succeeded in dropping a goal. The game thus ended in favour of Runcorn by one dropped goal and three minors to St. Helens Recs. A nil.

WIDNES v. LEIGH. Played at Leigh before 1,000 spectators. Widnes were without Barber, Fraser, Wynne, Gordon, and Whelan. 'rho visitors kicked off, and a weak return by Leigh enabled Clark to make headway along the touch- line, and later on Hughes made a grand rush, but it came to nothing, and Widnes were hard pressed. Ewan cent across to Bouth, who dropped a goal five minutes from the start. From the centre kick Leigh again at- tacked, and Brennan saved and reached the centre line,. where Widnes were penalised. The free kick gave an anxious time, but Wright cleared the danger, and Coop was called upon for the first time,that player responding with a huge punt, which Brennan attended to, with difficulty. Hughes had a splendid opening, but unfor- tunately he fell on the hard turf, and the chance was lost. Widnes then worked their way to the Leigh lines, but the home defence were equal to all emergen- cies. Try as they would, however, the homesters could not make headway until Coop got in a flying kick. Half-time : Leigh 1 dropped goal; Widnes nil. Final result : Leigh 2 goals 4 minors, Widnes 2 minors.
WARRINGTON A Y. MANCHESTER. A.—Although Man:

clicster had the assistance of ['lain, late of Stockport, and Jackson, a clever three-quarter from Salford A it was unfortunate for their chance of success that they could only muster 14 men. Warrington started against the bitterly cold wind, and after Massey and Jones had ex- changed kicks, Fitzgerald made a strong dodgy run into the home quarters. Lally and Antrobus regained the lost ground, and Barnes receiving a pass made a fine run, the ball being subsequently dribbled over the line by Bailey and Newey, a minor resulting. The drop-out was charged, and then Manchester experienced an anxi- ous time of it, Potts on one occasion making a fine effort to get in, but slipped when he had apparently a clear course. About this time the passing of the Warring- tonians was extremely wild and ill-judged, and Man- chester, taking advantage of their opponents' mistakes, got into dangerous quarters. Here Barnes received the ball, and was instrumental in forcing the visitors into their 25, Eden, Monks, Bailey, and Edwards dribbling over the line into touch-in-goal. Again Manchester had to bring their defensive powers into operation until Dain came away into Warrington territory, where a most foolish pass almost ended disastrously for the home team. Some neat play by Lally, Antrobus, Barnes, and Potts then transferred the warfare to the other end of the ground, but a couple of splendid runs by Pagden and Fitzgerald nullified the advantage. Then Lally made a brilliant run, and :after getting clear away, was overtaken by Vichoff, and half- time arrived. The brief rest seemed to have an inspir-

ing effect on the home team, for they at once: attacked, a strong run by Potts enabling Monks to score. Dain, flampsoc, and McManis then dashed away, but a re- taliatory movement by Bailey, Newev, Glover, and Buckley, forced the Mancunians to kick dead. Some tall kicking WAS then indulged in, and Vichoff fol- lowing up his kick, again got possession, and succeeded in getting a splendid try amidst loud cheors, the same player kicking a goal. Then Manchester showed up splendidly, effecting several splendid bouts of passing, from one of which Jackson made a beautiful run. Here Eden and Buckley showed up prominently, but another exhibition of ground passing by the visitors took the leather to the line. The cheers had barely died away when Warrington followed suit, Massey running to mid- field, whence Barnes ran to the line, and again the visi- tors were obliged to kick dead. The excitement caused by this fast and open play, was maintained when Fitz- gerald made a strong dodgy run, and Antrobus scored from the ensuing scrimmage. Directly after Lally got a try from a line-out, and Barnes placed a goal, leaving Warrington winners of an extremely fast and open game by 1-2-5 to 1-0-2.

div.head: WARRINGTON T. MANCHESTER.
div.p: WARRINGTON T. MANCHESTER.

Thanks to the exertions of the Manchester executive, the Whalley Range ground was rendered capital turf on Saturday, when these teams met for the first time this seasan. Warrington played the original team selected, but it was to be regretted that Woods, the county three-quarter, was away from the home side, this vacancy letting in Wincey, a capital three-quarter. There was only a moderate attendance when Cameron kicked off towards the city goal, Nevins' reply landing Warrington aggressors. Lawless improved the visitor's position, and then a neat display of passing between Bate and Evans forced Crews to save. Webster beat the Mancunians back on the drop out, and had Teare fielded the oval at all Warrington must certainly have scored from the mulling of W. B. Steel. As it was Bannerman and Dobson rushed the oval to neutral quarters, but a dashing run by Webster found the tall Warringtonian falling a yard from the line. After this brilliant effort came a brief relief for Manchester, Little and Jones doing the needful, but the visitors would not be denied, and ' Jolley, Ashton, and Turner leading the way into Man- chester quarters, Bate ran through a host of opponents, I but finally finding the opposition a trifle too severe, he passed splendidly, across to Fair Turner, and the stalwart forward taking the chance his speed was suffi- ciently strong to allow of the score, the try being heralded with cheers by the small muster of Warrington enthusiasts. Webster failed at the difficult place. Webster again demonstrated what a flue turn of speed I will do by running from half way, being held near the line, and had he parted to Turner a second try would have been notched. However, the run led up to an in- cessant attack, for despite the exertions of Crews to clear, Nevins got over only to find the point overruled. From a scrimmage ordered near the line' Ashton, Thcrni- ley, and Davies took the oval over, and the home cap- tain sent up the secoad try. This time Fair Turner was entrusted with the place, and a grand kick augmented the score by three points. With the substantial lead of seven points Warrington did not relax their exertions, and a dribble by Holmes was followed by Teare again missing an excellent opportunity, Crews leaving his goal at the mercy of the Warringtoniani. Luckily Steel was at hand, and in conjunction with Dodson and Coghlan changed the venue. Mullineux made his mark and sent to Boscow. who was the usual safe custodian. Holmes, Berry, and Jolley dribbled well, and the former immedi- ately met with an injury to his knee, which practically incapacitated him from doing service. Another dis- play of passing by Bate and Evans was followed by Webster being pulled down under the posts. Wincey cleared his lines beautifully, but Ashton led the visitors back. Nevins being finely held on one occasion by Jones. Exchange kicking on the popular side by Lawless, Turner, and Jones, ending in favour of the visitors, Crews again had all his work cut out to save his chaoge. The Warrington half backs and three-quarters now possed excellently, and relief came to Manchester when half-tinse was reached, with the score as Warrington 1-1, Manchester nil. So far the West Lancashire combination had had all the best of the game, and with ordinary luck their score during the first half would hove been considerably aug- mented. Early on in the second half s everal of the visiting forwards got damaged, and, as a consequence, the Warringtonians were so severely handicapped that they failed to sustain that brilliant reputation which they had established in the first half. Turner's kick-off saw Warrington early invading, but after a while Bos- cow's defence was tested, the Manchester forwards over- coming all opposition with the exception of the visiting custodian. Needless to say he met them in his sown cool manner, and neutrt I ground was the scene of operation. Manchester persisted in the attack, Little putting in a good run from a line out, and thrice Wincey was within an ace of scoring. However, Warrington were pena- lized a minute later, though for what reason no one could make out. and Mullineux had little difficulty in placing a goal. The homesters still maintained the attack, and Steel dribbled well, and when in the act of grounding under the posts Lawless raced up and kicked dead—a very narrow shave. From this point Warrington had a turn—of attacking, and Heesom taking a pass well got clear of everyone with the exception of Crews, who safely hauled him down. Wincey transferred the game to the Stretford goal, and Boscow tacked finely, savinz a certain try. Both Bate and Lawless experienced the hardest of luck after tricky play, and then Turner and Berry failed in their finishing essays. Bannerman and Dobson got clear from a line out, and the Warrington goal was again assailed, Boscow saving repeatedly in brilliant fashion. Another passing movement, initiated by Evans, saw Coghlan retaliating, and Evans again ' responded with a dribble, which realized half way. The last quarter of an hour saw Manchester attacking vigor- ously, but the defence of Boscow, Evans, and fleesom was very fine, and a grand game ended in a victory for , Warrington by a goal and a try to a penalty goal—seven points to three. Teams :—Manchester :C. E. Crews, back ; G. P. Win- cey, W. R. Steel, and C. L. Jones, three-quarter backs ; W. Mullineux, and T. Little, half backs ; J. H. Smith, D. C. Hampson, K. P. Birley, G. N. Cameron, F. Dod- son' H. G. Coghlan, E. H. Milnes, W. G. Hogg, and H. P. Bannerman, forwards. Warrington : J. Boscow, back ; P. R. Lawless, F. Fleesom, and H. Webster, three- quarter backs ; John Bate and J. Evans, half backs ; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins, T. Davies, J. T. Thornlley, J. Berry, J. Holmes, and. H. Teare, forwards. Referee : Mr. J. H. Turnbull, Blackley.

div.head: SUICIDE ON THE EVE OF MARRIAGE.
div.p: SUICIDE ON THE EVE OF MARRIAGE.

An inquest was held on Monday at Harlow, near Bishop Stortford, on George Pratt, a jeweller. Deceased was a widower, and was about to marry again. The banns were to have been published on Christmas Day, but two days previously he was found dead in bed with a bullet wound in his head, and a revolver in his right hand. A fortnight ag,,, he wrote a letter, which he placed under his sweetheart's portrait, every time he went out. In it he said he might be taken any time, and wished her to have £2OO of his money. The jury returned a verdict of temporary insanity.

div.head: li&N TORN TO PIECES AT HARRINGTON.
div.p: li&N TORN TO PIECES AT HARRINGTON.

On Tuesday afternoon, an inquest was held on the body of Thomas Blair, thirty-eight, of Whitehaven, who ware killed under shocking circutnstances on Monday. Blair was employed at Sir James Bains' Harrington Ironworks, and his duty was to attend to a crusher used for breaking limestone for the furnaces. When in the act of oiling the machinery his foot slipped, and he fell on his back with his head against the flywheel, , which caught him up, and he was jammed between the wheel and crushed, causing instant death. A chain and blocks had to be used to move the wheel so as to release the body, which was torn and mangled so dreadfully that the pieces had to be gathered up and placed in a bag.—A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned,

div.head: SENSIBLE CLERGYMAN.
div.p: A SENSIBLE CLERGYMAN.

Speaking at the opening of a recreation hall in his parish on Tuesday, the Rev. A. C. Talbot, rector of Church Eaton (Staffordshire), said they wanted livening up in country places, and to be taught to use their hands an. heads a great deal more than they did at present. He wanted, among other things, to see bciys taught to box and use singlesticks, as he believed that such exer- cises would help them to take care of themselves, to keep their tempers, and to take a licking without showing spite. He also hoped to see the ladies and girls of the parish taught to provide better dinners, for he was con- vinced that life would be much pleasanter in many homes if the food were better prepared for the wage- earner.

div.head: PAN AMA SCANDALS.
div.p: THE PAN AMA SCANDALS.

Dr. Brouardel's report on the post-marten examina- tion on the body of Baron de Rein- will, according to the " Figaro," be to the effect that the deceased was poisoned, and it is added that counsel for the defence in the coming trial will endeavour to show that the Baron had no adequate motive for committing suicide.

An important discovery has (according to the Figaro) been made in connection with the Panama Canal scandals. It is stated that the authorities in the course of their search at the officers of the Panama Company : found a copy letter-book belonging to M. Fontanes, which compromises a large number of senators and deputies. The book is said to reveal the whole of the Company's correspondence with Dr. Cornelious Herz and Arton with regard to the steps which it was proposed to take in Parliament, and to contain records of the pay- ment of various sums. the " authorities" give a denial to this report. At a meeting of Paris Socialists on Tuesday night a resolution was passed in favour of the appointment of a committee to summon people to the Palais Bourbon on the day of the reassembling of the Chambers and to issue an appeal to the army. It is now reported that an analysis has convinced Dr. Brouardel that Baron de Reinach's death was due to natural causes.

div.head: PENNY-IN-THESLOT IfICHINES.
div.p: PENNY-IN-THESLOT IfICHINES.

INGENIOUS DEVELOPMENT. The latest application of the penny-in-the-slot princi- ples is characterised by common sense, ingenuity, and utility.. Hitherto the public has fed the automatic machine with coppers in return for value. In the latest plan the process has been reversed. The public will re- ceive pennies instead of giving them. The idea is this. To the person who turns a crank a hundred times the machine yields up one penny. The crank is connected inside with a dynamo, and the hundred revolutions of the handle manufacture and store a quantity of electri- cal energy, which is to be eventually retailed by the owner of the machine for the purposes of producing illumination. The plan appears to be feasible enough, and it would certainly, in districts where unemployed labour abounded, be productive of considerable good. No man need go in want of a meal who can apply him- self to the electrical automatic machine. And the in- vention might be capable of wide application. Why should not every household be provided with one ? Every membar of the family might, in the name of exer- cise, give the handle so many hundred turns a day— sufficient, if that were possible, to provide electricity enough for the purposes of lighting. The turning of the crank might supersede dumb-bell practice in the mornings and during the summer months it might be possible to store enough electrical energy to tide over the winter. From the point of view of the man in the street, it would be interesting to know what income he could make in a week by a reasonable expenditure of effort. Even if only a hundred resolutions could be per- formed in five minutes, the operator would be working at the rate of a shilling an hour—a scale of renumeration much in excess of that paid in some industries involv- ng quite as much physical exertion.—Electricity.

div.p: At Banbridge, in county Down, William Henry Black, a boy, has died from eating poisonous berries. The lad's father got from a nurseryman sonse branches of a shrub, which bore pink-coloured berries, for the purpose of decorating his home at Christmas. Both his son and daughter ate a few of the berries. The boy sank into a state of coma, and never recovered consciousness.
