DONKEYS WITH DISTINGUISHED NAMES.

Writing from Cairo, Mr. Clement Scott says, in the " Daily Telegraph :" It is the fashion of the Arab don- key boys to name their beasts after the celebrities of the day. In Cairo and the deserts generally the re are Mrs. Langtrys and Mary Andersons by the score, and the nomenclature extends to " Two Lovely Black Eyes," " Ta-ra-ra-boom-de-ay," and" The Old Lent Road."

div.head: ITBALL.
div.p: ITBALL.
THE OVERDUE UMBRIA.

some intelligence was received on Thursday regarding the overdue Cunard steamer Umbria. The Wilson liner Galileo, which has arrived at New York, reports that on Christmas Day, in latitude 42.52 N., longitude 58.05 W., she passed the Umbria, which signalled that she was unmanageable, but did not require assistance. Although a heavy sea was running she was lying comfortably in the water, and it is supposed that the engineers were repairing the machinery. The Moravia si zhted the Um- bria on the 21st, steaming westward apparently in good condition, but of course the report of the Galileo is four days later. A number of other steamers are overdue, and the Cunard Company's agents on both sides of the Atlantic confidently anticipate the Umbria's safe arrival.

div.head: PRIESTS AND POLITICS.
div.p: PRIESTS AND POLITICS.

In an article which he contributes to the " Nineteenth Cen\tury " on Priest and Politics " Mr. Davitt says it is sought to be shown that to clerical agency and corrupt spiritual influence was due the majority which Ireland gave to the Nationalist party, and that the present Gov- ernment is in power by the favour of the instruments of Archbishops Walsh and Croke. " Must we say," asks Mr. Davitt, "by way of similar reasoning, that the corrupt agencies which voided the elections at Walsall, Flexham, and Rochester were but a repetition of those practices to which the Anti-Home Rule party in Parlia- ment;owe the strength of Her Majesty's Opposition ?" The priests in the Meath elections honestly believed, rightly or wrongly, that the follow ors of Mr. Parnell, by their public conduct, speeches, and associations, were assailing a great moral principle, and the mistake made was in treating men ,who said they hold by Mr. Parnell's political principles as if they had committed Mr. Parnell's sin. Mr. Davitt adds that in the whole of Ireland there is not a voter so obtuse • as to believe that he places his soul in peril by acting contrary to the advice of bishop or priest, and he points out that fifty thousand Catholics voted in opposition to the side taken by their clergy last July only.

div.head: liR. LAJ3OUCHERE'S DILEMMA.
div.p: liR. LAJ3OUCHERE'S DILEMMA.
AN AWKWARD STRIKE.

" Truth," Mr. Labouchere's organ, this week con- tains the following note :—I explained the other day, in a warning to correspondents, that it is my custom to turn over all letters exceeding a certain length to a clerk, and that I am consequently dependent on his ability and conscientiousness far a knowledge of their contents. lam sorry to say that this clerk has now struck. The occasion of his striking is a letter from an officer in India on the Royal Engineer Civil Staff, con- sisting in itself of nine foolscap pages, closely written in a peculiar fine writing, and accompanied by two en- closures, one of which is a printed pamphlet of forty pages. Much as I should like to know more of the grievances of the Royal Engineer Civil Staff, it is now impossible tor me to do so until the strike of my clerk is settled. At present neither side shows any signs of yielding. It is a question, therefore, whether my Engineer friend can state his case with sufficient brevity , for me to be able to read it myself. That, of course, I I must leave to him.

div.head: INCREASE OF RAILWAY AND POSTAL BUbINESS AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: INCREASE OF RAILWAY AND POSTAL BUbINESS AT ST. HELENS.

The returns from the St. Helen Railway Station show for three days an increase in passenger traffic of 1,257 over Christmas last year, and also a slight increase in the parcel traffic. At the Post Office there was a very large increase in postal work, both in the outgoing and incoming correspondence and par- cels. This great increase is apparent when it is stated that Messrs. Beecham alone posted upwards a 10,000 Christmas parcels to their customers in all parts of the country. Monday was observed as a general holi- day in the town, and business was entirely suspended. The principal event was the" Cinderella" promoted by Mr. H. L. Riley, for which about 1,250 tickets had been issued to the poorest children in the town. So great was the crush of this class of children, however, that the arrangements were upset, and there wore three " sitting- downs." The tickets were distributed by clergy, minis- ters, newspaper proprietors, and others. This was followed by an entertainment, at which a number of boys from the Cowley British Schools gave-gymnastic exercises, and Miss Maggie Williamson sang " The Robin ;" but the principal part was a magic lantern entertainment given by Mr. Gabriel Moon, and the scenes, which were of a comical character, brought forth vociferous applause. As the children left the hall they were given an apple, an orange, and a Christmas card, 1,200 of the latter being distributed by Mr. W. N. Leckie, stationer. The principal subscribers to the fund included Lord Gerard, Sir A. B. Walker Bart., Colonel Gamble, C.B , the Mayor (Mr. A. Sinclair), the Vicar (the Rev. J. W. Willink, M.A.), the County Coroner (Mr. S. Brighouse), his Honour Judge Collier, Mr. J. Davies (Warrington), Dr. Wigglesworth, Mr. Walmesley- Cotham, J.P., Mr. W. Tyrer, and Mr. Castle-Spenceley. At the Cottage Hospital the annual tea party and concert took place, the proceedings being of a most enjoyable character. There was skating on some of the shallowest sheets of water, but such deep places as Eccleston Mere were not used. Football was abandoned on account of the hard state of the ground.

div.head: VOLUNTEER P RIZE DISTRIBUTIONS.
div.p: VOLUNTEER P RIZE DISTRIBUTIONS.
ST. HELENS.
A se] several

The annual distributions of Christmas prizes to the 2nd Lancashire Engineers and to the 2nd Vol- unteer Battalion S.L.R., took place on Friday night at St. Helens. The prize-winners in the Engineers assembled at their hetrdquarters, Coppers'-hill Colonel Rothwell, the commanding officer, distri- buted the prizes. , About £BO was given in the sergeants' attendance prizes, attendance prizes for men at engineering drill, third-class shooting prizes and recruits' prizes. The Calcutta Cup, presented by Captain M. Hughes, Sherdley Hall, of the 2nd Life Guards, had been won by Captain John Rothwell, who had also won the County of Lancaster Grand Aggregate Challenge Cup, in addition to £96 in money, after pay- ing all his travelling expenses, &c. The Christmas prizes consisted of the usual fare and a few useful articles presented by tradesmen. The corps will next I year camp at Douglas. At the Volunteer Hall the prizes were distributed by Colon White in the absence of Colcnel W. W. Pilking- ton, immanding officer. Colonel White said the prizes were numerous and of a good quality, and they must thank their friends of St. Helens and neighbourhood for presenting them. Last year 326 men fired and this year ' 321 fired, There were 176 prizes last year, and the same number this year. Last year they were only able to give prizes to those who had made 24 points and up- wards, while this year they were able to give prizes to those who made 21 points and upwards. That was accounted for by the difference in the value of shots on the targets and not because the shooting had deterior- ated. Three hearty cheers were given for the donors of the prizes, which were of the value of about £6O, and for Colonel Pilkington and Colonel White.

div.head: FEARFUL WEATHER IN THE ATLANTIC.
div.p: FEARFUL WEATHER IN THE ATLANTIC.

NEW YORK, DEC. 27.—The Inman steamer City of Berlin, which arrived here at 10 o'clock yesterday morn- ing, experienced heavy weather throughout the voyage. On the 19th inst. the sea ran so high that the vessel made only 232 miles. In the meantime one of her boats was smashed and several ventilators were also carried away. The gale blew with still greater fury on the fol- lowing day, when only 113 miles were made. Ice covered the decks to a depth of several inches, and the steamer's sides were similarly coated from stem to stern. Happily there was no mishap to any of the passengers notwithstanding unusually rough seas. All other vessels arriving here from Europe appear to have encountered fierce storms, accompanied with in- tense cold. The deckwork of several steamers was smashed by the heavy seas, and some of the crews were frost-bitten. The captain of the Lauresmina, front Bremen, reports that his deck was covered ;with ice, which in some places was two feet thick. Huge icicles hung from the yards. The vessel's three compasses all froze in their alcohol baths, and the captain was then obliged to steer by the stars. The French Transatlantic Company's s.s. La Norman - die arrived in harbour looking like a vessel from the Arctic regions, being covered with ice from stem to stern. She reports having struck the tail of a cyclone on the 22nd inst. The hurricane lasted for eight hours, during which the sea ran mountains high, and the posi- tion of the vessel caused great anxiety to the officers. Severe cold prevailed throughout the voyage, which was of the roughest, the heavylsea causing the vessel to pitch terribly, while the water which came on board froze in sheets across the deck, rendering them almost impas- sible. The passengers had to be kept below for nearly the whole of the voyage. The National Line steamer Denmark and other vessels arriving report similar ex- perience of storm and cold, and all bear evidences of the terrible weather which they have experienced. Many vessels are overdue.

div.head: SUPPOSED SUICIDE OF A ROCIIDILE
div.p: SUPPOSED SUICIDE OF A ROCIIDILE
MERCHANT

On Thursday morning William Lord,flannel merchant, of Rochdale, but who lived at 166, Portland-et., South-- port, was discovered hanging to his bedpost by a thin piece of string. All alarm was at once raised, but life was extinct before any assistance could be obtained. The deceased was a widower and 55 years of age. For some time past he has been in low spirits, and subject to nervousness and fits of depression.
THE BAMFITRLONG COLLIERY ACCIDENT.

The Coroner's inquiry into the circumstances attend- ing the flamfurlong colliery accident, in which several lives were lost, was concluded on Wednesday. The jury found a verdict of accidental death. They expressed the opinion, however, that the boy who was left in charge of the engine and open torch light lamp was not com— petent for such work, and that it was not safe to use such a lamp where the engine was bedded on wood and where there was a wooden floor.

div.head: CURIOUS LICENSING COMPLICATION.
div.p: CURIOUS LICENSING COMPLICATION.

The magistrates at Bangor on Wednesday decided by a majority to grant the transfer of the license of the Manchester Arms Hotel, Upper Bangor, from Miss Ottley, to Mr. Williams. The case was one which involved a curious point arising out of the renewal of the licence at the licensing sessions in the name of Miss Ottley's mother, who was then dead. Miss Ottley was afterwards proceeded against for selling drink without a licence, but she then produced an Excise certificate signed by two magistrates which had been obtained after the mistake as to the licence was discovered, and the case was dismissed. The contention of the temper- ance party on Wednesday was that the licence had lapsed, and on this point it is intended to take the mall— ter to a higher court.

div.head: GLASGOW MITI-OER.
div.p: THE GLASGOW MITI-OER.
SENTENCE OF DEATH.

At Glasgow, on Wednesday, before Lord Adam, sitting in the High Court, William McEwan, gardener, and Thomas M'Neilly, ship fireman, were indicted for the murder of Elizabeth O'Connor, in West Lodge, at Pol— lockshields. The trial began en the previous day. *On Wednesday M'Neilly's declaration was read. He stated that when he left the house, after the night's caroute, the other prisoner and the woman were apparently friendly, and he knew nothing of the crime. there was no evidenze, in fact, against the man, and he was line- rated. The evidence against McEwan showed that he had murdered the woman, dismembered her, and buried her body in the garden. An attempt was made to prove that he was insane,but in vain. The jury found MrEwan guilty of murder, arid he was sentenced to death, his execution being fixed for January 18.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE'S, BIRTHDAY.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S, BIRTHDAY.

Thursday was Mr. Gladstone's birthday. The veteran statesman was born in 1809, and has completed his eighty-third year. Mr. Gladstone's eighty-third birthday was ushered in at Hawarden on Thursday morning by merry peals froni the parish church bells. The flag was also hoisted at the church. Early in the morning the members of the family now at Hawarden, namely, Mr. Herbert Glad- stone, the Rev. Stephen Gladstone, the Rev. Harry end Mrs. Drew sent a telegram to Biarritz congratulating the aged statesman on his anniversary. The morning post brought to Hawarden as usual quite a budget of letters of congratulation from political associations and private, friends, and these will be forwarded to Downing-street, unopened. Many telegrams received from Liberal Asso- ciations all over the country are being dealt with at the Castle. On Wednesday, Mr. Gladstone received from an admirer in Guernsey a valuable antique silver Guernsey milking jug, which is winch admired. The Executive Council of the Midlothian Liberal Association, on Thursday, despatched to Mr. Gladstone a telegram conveying an expression of good wishes and offering congratulations at the close of the year which has witnessed both the return of the Liberal party to power, under his leadership and the cornpleti.m of his 60 years' service in the House of Commons. The Coun- cil assured the Premier of the fullest confidence ant most hearty support of his policy.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE'S UNIQUE POSITION.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S UNIQUE POSITION.

It is said that no man who has reached the age of Mr. Gladstone has ever before taken an active part in the Government of this country. Lord Palmerston died in - harness, but he died on the eve of his 82nd birthday. Chatham died at 70, Fox at 57, Pitt at 47, Canning at 58, and when Sir Robert Peel met with his fatal accident he was 62. Earl Russell obtained the good old age of 86, but he did not hold office after he was 74. Lord Beaconsfield at 7T.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOSEPH P. BRUNNER,
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOSEPH P. BRUNNER,

Very widespread regret will be felt at the annotnce- ment on Monday morning of the death of Mr. Joseph P. Brunner. This sad and unexpected event took place on the evening of Christmas Day, at "The Knoll," the deceased gentleman's residence in Sefton Park, after an illness of only five days. On Tuesday evening, after having spent the day in town at business, as usual, and appearing at the Liverpool Reform Club in his usual health, Mr. Brunner attended the performance of " Elijah "at the Philharmonic Hall. On the way home, however, he was seized with a fit of shivering, and retired to rest, after everything had been done to relieve him. The following morning he was confined to hie room, and was attended by Dr. Steer 3. His indisposi- tion being somewhat severe, Dr. Gly. i was also sum- moned ; but the illness did not reach an alarming stage until Friday, when pleuro-pneumonia supervened. Dr. Carter was then called in, but, in spite of the attentions of the medical men, the malady made rapid progress, and at six o'clock on Christmas evening Mr. Bruniaer passed away, at the early age of forty-eight years. His family, his brother, Mr. John T. Brunner, M.P., and other relatives were present at the eud. The late Mr. Brunner, who was born in Liverpool, in 1844, who the son of the Rev. John Brunner, a native of Zurich. After having for some time held a chaplaincy in the Swiss Army, the latter came to England, and whilst still in early life settled in Liverpool. He estab- lished a school at Mere Bank, Everton, at that date a fashionable subrub, and at this school his eons received their education. On leaving, Mr. J. P. Brunner entered business. He became associated with the chemical trade, and whilst still under thirty years of age began upon his own account, founding the firm of Joseph P. Brunner and Co., chemical brokers, of which he was the head. This was previous to the esta.blishment of the works of Brunner, Mond, and Co., at Northwich. When, after the discovery of important economies in alkali manufacture, Brunner, Mond, and Co., rose rapidly into prominence in the trade, Mr. J. P. Brunner, as their commercial agelit in Liverpool, experienced a considerable expansion of his business. His commercial career was one of success, whilst his integrity and credit were far beyond question. He was a director of Fowler Brothers, Limited, general merchants, Liverpool. It was in association with politics, however, that Mr. Brunner became in fact a public man, kdown as one of the most energetic among the leaders of the movement for municipal reform. In this subject be was deeply in- terested, and it is but truth to say that his labours on behalf of a better government for the city of Liverpool were, apart from considerations of party, untiring. An ardent Liberal in general politics, Mr. Brunner was one of the first members of the Liverpool Liberalat Federal Council, taking an active part in .11 1s tmheeansuerfoesrm. eu Club, soof swe rhvi ecdh oinn stthi teu tPi oo lni i dc aul nogm mi ,t t f ie? he was chairman. His pleasant and unassuming manners made him extremely liked, and he was a charming host. Not many men who have fought so hard in politics have made so very .few personal enemietsd, or hreavelsfohue wnitends the suavitor to nbodo with the forer • disappointed in his desire of serving the public and furthering his views in the City Council, he strove in his prematurely closed career as much as any man to bring about that reform in municipal government which it is hoped will make more enduring the prosperity of Liver- pool. Mr. Brunner was one of the magistrates added to the city bench in November last. He leaves a widow, two sons, and four daughters.

div.p: letttrs to tin attor.

RUNCORN AND SMALLPDX. Sir,—lt has been reported in the press, and the im- pression commonly obtains, that there is an epidemic of Smallpox in Runcorn. There have only been five eases here during the past five months. One case notified as smallccx has died at his residence and the other four have been successfully treated in the hospital, and are now convalescent. It is also reported that smallpox is pre- valent in Weston, an adjoining township. The three cases alleged to be suffering from smallpox there are de- clared by the medical practioner attending them not to be cases of smallpox at all.—Yours faithfully, E. MARSHALL. Secretary to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. NATIONAL AGRICULTURAL UNION.
Sir,—! think it will interest your readers if you will

allow me to make known to them through your columns the progress that has already been made towards realis- ing my proposal for a National Agricultural Union, com- posed of all classes interested in the soil, whether owners, occupiers, or labourers, in order to meet the present grave crisis in our affairs by united action in detence of our common interests. This proposal, as your readers are doubtless aware, received the unanimous approval cf the conference, and a draft scheme in which I embodied it was immediately sent down for the consid- eration of all the agricultural bodies which were repre- sented there. On the whole the proposal has been received, both in the press and in the country, in a manner which justifies the highest expectations from it when it is realised. One or two mistakes have been made as to its aim and objects, but in general these have been both clearly understood and warmly approved. Several existing associations have already passed resolu- tions, forming themselves into branches of the National Agricultural Union. This is an example which cannot be too soon f dlowed in every part of the country, in order that the Central Organisation, which we hope to form before the meeting of Parliament, may find the work in country districts ready to its hand. I have been invited to address large meetings at York (on the sth of January) for the North of England, at fp.swich for the Eastern Counties, and in other parts of the country. I have promised to do so. But although I should be glad to have an opportunity of explaining the scheme fully in every county in England did time permit, I feel that not a moment must be lost, when once the country is thoroughly in possession of the scheme, in taking practical steps to carry it into effect. Nothing, I am convinced, can be done to remove the dire distress under which we are labouring until we are organised. Every hour that we delay in taking tins first and most necesAary step in the right direction may mean the ruin of many poor fellows whom otherwise we might be in time to save. If we are true to onrselves the country is in sympathy with us, and will heed what we say.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, WINCHILSEA. Haverholme Priory, Sleaford, Lincolnshire. Dec. 28th, 1892. RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE PUR- CHASE OF THE WATERWORKS. Sir,—l notice that the Commissioners accompanied by their law-clerk are at present running up and down to London in express trains, conferring with some legal uminaries there anent the purchase of the waterworks. This is strange, seeing that outside the Board and the company's shareholders they have not yet got the sane- ticn or authority of a single ratepayer to spend one penny even in preliminary expenses, far less the pur- chase of a concern which, in my opinion, will prove ruinous to the rates of the town. It is all very well for the Chairman of the Board to playfully suggest the tapping of the Liverpool water main so that every old woman and silly old man in the town can brew a better cup of tea and do with less soap. I am, however, rather inclined to the belief that the tapping business may indeed have something to do with " soft soap ;" to cover, it may be, the intention of the Board of running a continuous pressure of water into the sewers at the ratepayers expense to force the sewage matter which now lies festering in the sewers through the syph:n in No Man's Land, which they in their blindness allowed the canal company to construct. I am told that three deaths have already resulted from inhaling the" Aroma " emitted during the cleaning out process of this factory of disease, which has spread desolation, sorrow and death in many a humble home in the town, through the unsatiable ravages of typhoid fever. Every person of even ordinary intelligence knows that the very essence of all decomposing organic matter whether on the surface or not is being continually car- ried into the sewers by a process of nature where it meets with kindred matter from all parts of the town; it cannot now rapidly pass into the river as formerly, but is held in .combination in the sewers in the lower lying part of the town where a chemical process is con- tinually carried on, the gas from which—the very germs of typhoid and smallpox—is oozing out at every grid in the town. Is it to be wondered at then that the ',kap- missioners are in such a terrible hurry to utilise the water. In the hands of the Board within twelve months the present staff would be greatly increased and their wages doubled. Fellow ratepayers, and particularly property owners, unless you want the value of your property seriously exhausted and jeopordised by an enormous increase of the district rate rally together as one man, and oppose to the death, not only the purchase of the waterworks but the other wild goose schemes which seem at this moment to haunt the brains of the Commis- sioners—Yours, &c., Runcorn, December 27,1892.

div.head: TUE NEW YEAR.
div.p: TUE NEW YEAR.

Sir,—Next Sunday is New Year's Day. It is only at intervals that the New Year begins on Sunday; but, whenever it so happens, the combination is striking and suggestive. I ask your kind permission to call attention to, at least, one practical suggestion in regard to it. We have always been accustomed to look upon New Year's Day, not only as an occasion appropriate to mutual expressions of gcod-will, but also as an occasion for personal forming of good resolutions, and, wien neces- sary, of "turning over a new leaf" and making a better beginning. Doubtless New Year has often been to most of us a useful season in such respects. But, sir, this combination of New Year's Day and Sunday conveys a strong suggestion in favour of renewed and increased observance of Sunday as a day of religious worship and work. I venture respectfully to present this to your readers as greatly desirable, and as a very worthy beginning of t6e new period of time.

I am afraid that if a census of the attendance at public worship were now to betaken in Warrington, we should End that the numbers are considerably lower than when such a census was taken eight or ten years ago. But however that may be, it is only too certain that large numbers even of such as used to attend wor- ship, have either become verry irregular in attendance,or have ceased altogether. And there are also, besides, larger numbers still who have never attended the public worship of God. Would it not he a good and helpful beginning of the new year,if the irregular worshippers resolved to become regular ; and if the abstainer from attendance resolved to turn over a new leaf altogether, and to begin taking himself, and his family, if he have one, to a place of worship on Sunday next? This is hardly the place for me to enter upon any argument upon this subject. And hence I refrain. But many who have of recent years abandoned their krmer custom of attendance are not in need of argument. Various circumstances, many of them trivial, have brought about their non-attendance. Suppose they, with their New Year, forgive and forget any offences which may have alienated them from their old religious associations. Let byegones be byegones ; and let the New Year see a return to the older and, surely, wiser habit. To say nothing else, attendance at a House of Worship is a sound, healthy, elevating habit, and helps to give a truer tone to life. Without, I hope, appearing pietistic, may I remind your readers that Warrington has, during the last two years,passed through some severe ordeals in the epidem- ics of influenza, scarlet fever, and smallpox. •Surely these are experiences that should make their own appeal to the religious side of our nature, and suggest ear-

nest and serious reflections. Whatever our opinions may be as to the human causes of such invasions of disease, and whatever we may regard as the obvious teachings of such invasions concerning the sanitation of the town in future, let us not be unmindful that all seasons of trial and sorrow are Providential admonitions to guide men into truer and better ways. 1 do, therefore, most respectfully and earnestly invite such of my fellow townsmen as you may enable me te> address in your columns, to enter upon 1893 in a reli- gious spirit,and to find their way on Sunday next to such places of worship as may seem best to them, that they may seek that Divine Blessing which alone maketh rich and addeth no sorrow."

I trust that these words, should you see fit to insert them, will be regarded in the earnest spirit in which I seek to indite them, and that the New Year may witness a largely improved attendance in all our churches upon "the means of grace."—Yours faithfully, JOHN YONGE. Wycliffe Church, December 29th, 1892.

div.head: RATEPAYER.
div.p: RATEPAYER.
SHIP CANAL.

SHIPS FOR THE CANAL. Five vessels were reported on Thursday as being off Holyhead and Point Lvnas bound for the river Mersey. Of the five, three are for the Manchester Ship Canal—the Linwood, 1,233 tons register, from West Bay Nova Sootia, with deals, for Messrs. Pierce, Watts, and Co. ; Argentina, 1,034 tons register, from Pensacola, with pitchpine, for Messrs. Bass and Smith, and the Toivo, 944 tons register, from Nova Scotia, with deals, for Messrs. James Smith and Co. The Lindwood has more than 1,0000,000 superficial feet of timber on board. SHEBEENING ON THE CANAL.

On Thursday, at Frodsham Petty Sessions, before Mr. A. Thomas and other magistrates, James Foster, Wm. Andrews, Wm. Bellows r occupiers of huts on the Man- chester Ship Canal Works, Frodsham Marsh, were sum- moned for selling drink without a license on two differ- ent dates. The defendants pleaded guilty. Mr. Churton, solicitor, Chester, appeared for the police. He stated that the defendants had rendered themselves liable to penalities for a first offence of £5O, and for a second offence £lOO. He briefly stated the facts—namely, that drink having been sold to a man, search warrants were granted. These were executed by Superintendent Meredith, Police Sergeant Doyle, and Police Sergeant Burgess, and so successful was the raid made on Decem- ber 23 that they found in Foster's hut, situate next to a mission-room, two nine-gallon casks', one full and the other partly so. One was concealed under a bed. A similar discovery was made on the premises occupied by Andrews. In Bellow's hut were two eighteen-gallon casks, one nearly empty and the other untapped. Small penalties were useless in cases of that kind. The de- fendants were under no expenses, and thus were able to unfairly compete with publicans, who had to pay a large sum annually to the Government, and in many cases were tied to brewers. The defendants could get large profits. A fine of £5 and £2 Is. cost was imposed npon each defendant ;in default, a month's imprison- ment.

div.head: RUNCORN SECTION.
div.p: THE RUNCORN SECTION.

During the year just about to close vast progress has been made with the Runcorn and Weston Point sections of the Ship Canal works, and especially has this been the case since the beginning of July, when the Runcorn docks were closed. Operations were carried on continuously, night and day, by an army of nearly 4,000 men until the end of October, but since then the working hours have been confined to the day. The manual labour has been supplemented by a large number of locomotives, steam cranes, steam navvies, horses and pumping engines. Some delay was exprrienced in carrying out the work under notice until it was possible to arrange for the shipping to be done at Salport. When that had been accomplished the course of the canal was enclosed, and since then tl:e excavations along the whole length from Weston Point to the Old Quay, Runcorn, have been pushed forward with all expedition. The largest side locks on the canal—the Weston Mersey locks, which are 600 ft. long by 45ft. wide, with concrete walls 500 ft. long—are well advanced. The walls of the Bridgewater Lock, so seriously damaged by a gale in February, has been reconstructed, and is very nearly completed ; and the other walls are so well advanced as to allow the gates to be placed in position. Work in I connection with a deep water lock, nearly 500 ft. long and 261 t. deep, and a lay-by has just been commenced, and it is thoueht that the excavations for these will be completed in the course of six months. The canal from Duke's Dock to Runcorn Bridge has been practically completed, and the operation has just been commenced of underpinning the large Cheshire abutment of the bridge. The concrete wall from No Man's Land to the Old Quay is finished, and the locks specially for the ac- commodation of the Widnes traffic are completed, with the gates hung, so that there only remains the removal of the outer dam dividing the lock from the river. There is every promise that in three or four months this por- tion of the cannl will be sufficiently advanced to admit the water. rrogress is also being made with the Run- corn graving deck. Some idea of the extent of the work accomplished may be formed when it is stated that on this section over one and a quarter million cubic yards of material have been excavated.

div.head: _,•,_ WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: _,•,_ WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
THURSDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes.

- A SOLICITOR AND His CLIENT.—An action was heard in which Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw, solicitors, Warrington' sued Thomas Dutton, Burtonwood, for £lO Is. 6d., the balance of a hill of costs.—Mr. Dobson ap- peared on behalf of plaintiffs, and stated that they acted as solicitors for the defence in a case Regina v. Dutton, in which Dobson was charged witn unlawful wounding. Counsel was engaged in the person of Mr. Mulnolland,at a cost of £lO Is. 6J., and Mr. Davies charged £.lO far his own services. Mr. Kilshaw, a friend of Dutton's, paid £lO on account. When the case had been tiled and Dutton acquitted, he came to Mr. Davies's office and al- leged that an agreement had been entered into between Mr. Davies and himself "to do the job" for £lO. This Mr. Davies denied.—Defendant now stated that Mr. Forshaw told him when he first called that it would only cost a guinea. He alleged that when he visited the office after the case had been dismissed,plaintiff spoke warmly about his ingratitude.—A considerable amount of evi- dence was heard, after which the defendant said he ob- jected to pay £lO, because he thought it an exorbitant charge. He believed that neither counsel nor Mr. Davies had done their best for him.—Mr. Arthur Browne, soli citor, was called, and stated that he considered the charge made by Mr. Davies had been a most reasonable one ; and he considered that the case had been handled properly. The defendant was acquitted, whereas a charge of "attempted murder" might have been sus- tained with more prima facie evidence.—Judgment was given against defendant. A CHanwoateit AND HER DRESSMAKING BILL.—Mrs. Frances Brocklehurst sued Miss Annie Smith, for the sum of 9s.,made up in the following manner :-Bs.for making a ball dress and Is. for cab hire. The plaintiff said that there was no price named at the time of taking the order. On the completion of the work defendant borrowed Is. in order that she might take a cab for the ball.—The defendant denied that plaintiff was entitled to more than 55., and that amount would have been paid but for some trouble that ensued over a ring that had been missed. When the article in question was restored she offered to pay thE amount of the account, but then the plaintiff demanded twice the amount of the sum prev- iously arranged, viz., 43. for the make of the skirt and Is. borrowed in order that a cab might be engaged.—ln reply to several questions from the judge, the defendant said that the plaintiff was a charwoman at the house where she formerly resided, and the only work she did in respect of the dress was to stitch the skirt, and even that she did not make entirely, as she (witness) had to fix a number of flowers.—The brother of the defendant gave evidence to the effect that 48. was the sum arranged.—Plaintiff (excitedly) : You spat in my face three times when I asked your sister for the money, now didn't you.—Judgment was given for 55., to be paid at the rate of 2s. a month. CLAIM AGAINST A WARRINGTON BUTCIIER.—Thomas Vi'ooley, 13, Mill-lane, Warrington, sued T. Carlisle, butcher, Warrington, for the sum of £22 10s. in respect of a pony which was alleged to have been driven tø death by the defendant, who had seized it without the permission of plaintiff.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defendant and Mr. P_ Davies for the plaintiff. The evidence showed that en the 31st October the plaintiff sent his son in company with his brother to Liverpool to purchase cattle. Returning home the younger brother was told to drive to Rainhill where he would meet him. On the way the younger brother was overtaken by the defendant and a man called "The BasPfer." They ordered him to leave the trap and drive their 14 cattle to Bold. He was frightened and aid so. Upon reaching Bold with the cattle he met the defendant, who counted the cattle, exclaimed " there is one missing," and drove madly in the direction of Rainhill again alter the miss- ing beast. When he returned with it the pony was in a very distressed condition. The defendant and " The Basher," then left the boy with the pony and trap, and shortly afterwards the boy's brother arrived. He noticed the distressed condition of the animal, and when he got it home he endeavoured to feed it ; but it would not eat, and shortly afterwards died from the effects of the ex- haustion —The case was adjourned until the next court day for the bearing of the defence.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE'S BIRTHDAY.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S BIRTHDAY.

ICE CARNIVAL AT HAWARDEN. The celebration at Hawarden was concluded late on Thursday night by a brilliant ice carvival on the pond in Hawarden Park, where, by invitation of Mr. Herbert Gladstone, about fifty ladies and gentlemen from the surrounding district were entertained. The scene was illuminated by Chinese lanterns and bonfires, near which refreshments were served. Besides Mr. Herbert Gladstone there were present Mrs. Stephen Gladstone and the Rev. H. and Mrs. Drew. The festivities con- tinued till a late hour.
Miiillll

THE MAYOR'S HOT POT. But there were others who enjoyed themselves more modestly ; others who were poor and destitute, and ragged, and who found the one gleam of pleasure on the day following that one day of all days of rejoicing, a dinner of hot pot which they received as" needy poor." This was-the provision which the Mayor had kindly made for the poor, a part of the community who un- doubtedly enjoy his ana his wife's earnest compassion. The frost seemed healthy and invigorating to cue well fed and comfortable ;it made the blood tingle -Ind the spirits rise to a pitch of hilarity. But it simply meant the very opposite to those who were not that way cir- cumstanced. Many a picture of slow starvation was intensified at the Drill Hall that day. The various ministers in the town had between them tickets for 1,300 dinners, all of which they distributed and were then short. The holders of those tickets began to assemble in expectant groops whilst the hundreds of other people tripped away with their skates, or accepted the assistance of the cheap trains to visit the Liverpool and Manchester Pantomimes. Right on to dinner time several gentlemen from the Town Hall offices including Mr. Wilson, assistant town clerk, Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, kindly lent their assistance in distributing the steaming compound, which had been cooked by Mr. Powis, Town Hall attendant,and his wife. Some of the applicants for this food brought tickets for twelve dinners; tor a family of twelve father- less children. The average number of dinners per family was three.

DOWN AT THE WORKHOUSE. According to the old custom the inmates of the War- rington Workhouse were entertained with a substantial dinner at the Workhouse on Monday. There was plum pudding and roast beef each adult also being allowed a pint of beer. As usual, the dinner was served at twelve o'clock in the large dining hall, there being present about 100 men,so women, and 20 or 30 children. Other inmates were in different parts of the establish- ment or in hospital. The Guardians present were ' Messrs. Robert Fleaton (chairman), Ratcliffe (chairman of the House Committee), James Hill, Thomas Smith, W. J Shaw, Alfred Jclley, Samuel Davies, as well as several visitors, including Mr. Steel (Seacombe), Mr. Henry Smith (Liverpool), Mr. Ralson (Earlestown), Mr. Thomas Mason (Warrington), and the chaplain the(Rev. H. V. Pigot). Assistance was rendered not only by Mr. and Mrs. Ward (the respected master and matron), Miss Ward, Mr. Hfflidge (assistant master), Miss Daniels and Miss Curry, but by the Guardians and visitors, and no inmate had long to wait before he or she was supplied with the good things which had been provided, and which were thoroughly enjoyed. After dinner Mr. Ward wished all present "The Compliments of the Season," and said lie had to announce to the inmates the gifts which had been received for Christmas. They.had had the usual dinner consisting of rounds of roast beef (3001b5.), plum pudding, and beer, to be followed by a distribution of tobacco, snuff, oranges, sweets and apples. Mr. George Ratcliffe had sent a box of oranges; the Mayor and Mayoress tea and sugar for the women, toys for the children, tobacco and pipes for the men, with Christmas cards and other papers. The Mayoress had also written the following note :—" Town Hall. Warrington, December 24th, 1892. Dear Sir,—We hope you have received from the Mayor and myself some small gifts for the use of the inmates of the Workhouse— tobacco and pipes for the men, tea and sugar for the women, and some toys for the children. Please wish all for us a happy Christmas. We regret this year we are prevented from being present at your Christmas einner.—l remain, sincerely yours, A. M. Greenall." (Applause.) Miss Lythgoe, Sankey-st., had forwarded , sweets ; Miss Dakin and Miss Robinson, (Penketh), Christmas cards; Father Craven, a box of books and papers : Mrs. Brundrett,half a barrel of porter. Several ladies and gentlemen had subscribed money for toys and sweets, Ike., for the children,which were distributed by the House Committee on Friday last. He would like ter say a word or two to the inmates about the ex- ceptional circumstances relating to them. They had, he regretted to say, been afflicted by an outbreak of smallpox, and the result was that they had had to put as much restraint as possible upon the inmates, who had not been allowed to go out to see their friends, nor had their friends been allowed to visit them. He must say that he had been exceed- ingly pleased by the manner in which the inmates had conducted themselves during the whole of the time they had thus been confined to the house. He hoped they would bear with that restraint a little longer until it was safe for them to leave the institution, as they were anxious to do all they could to prevent the spreading of the disease.—Mr. Heat on expressed the pleasure it afforded him to be present to see the inmates, both young and old enjoy their dinner. Owing to the outbreak of smallpox in the town and in the Workhouse, they had not been able to ' enjoy the privileges, which had been usually extended I to them, but he hoped they would spend as pleasant a I time as possible in the grounds of the building. He could ' promise them that when the outbreak had subsided they would be allowed to enjoy the liberty which had been recently taken from them. They would be permitted to visit their friends again, and their friends would occa- sionally be allowed to visit them. (Applause.) He hoped the master and matron would have no cause to complain of their conduct during the remainder of the day. It was owing to the conduct:of the Inmates that the Guardians felt called upon every year to give them a substantial dinner. He thanked them all for the kind manner in which they had received the names of the Boards of Guardians. (Applause.)—Mr.Rat- ' cliffe remarked that he had been Chairman of the House Committee for two or three years, and he could assure the inmates that he had never met with a body of men who were more anxious and determined to do their duty, not only to the inmates themselves,but to the master and matron,and the other officers. The greatest attention was paid to all complaints made to them. If he spoke for an hour he would not be able to add anything new to the two speeches which bad already been delivered. He concluded by proposing a rote of thanks to Mr.and Mrs. Ward and the officers for their services in connection with the treat.—The motion was heartily agreed to.— Mr. Davies also spoke. As vice-chairman of the House Committee he could not help expressing the pleasure it afforded him to be present that day, and seeing the able manner in which the master and matron and other officers had got up the annual treat. The committee had only one object in view, and that was to make Christmas time as happy as it was possible to make it for the inmates. Many present would not, probably, see another Christmas, and be could only beg of the aged and infirm to make the best of the time that God might be pleased to give them. He wished them all the compliments of the season. (Applause.) The Rev. H. V. Pigot seconded the remarks which had been made by Mr. Davies, and hoped they would remem- ber the advice he had given them. (Applause.)—Mr. Heaton announced that one of the inmates (George Gee) wished to read some verses he bad composed for the occasion. He called upon him to do 80. Old Mr. Gee stepped forward, and read about a dozen verses, headed " Lines written on the occasion of the Guardians' Christ- mas treat to the inmates of the Warrington Uni0n,1892." We give four verses of Gees' inspiration The poor amongst us ever were, And will be to the end ; And they who help them and can spare, Unto the Lord do lend." May He His mercy grant to all, „ And let us watchful be; The best of men are apt to fall, ` There's none from error free. • , To Master and to Matron Ward, Great praise and thanks are due ; In catering they have laboured hard, And to perfection, too. Then 'ere we part, to Guardians give Three cheers and thank, profound ; Clod prosper them, long may they live Honoured by all around.

TI-1E EXAMINER, SAI URDA.Y. DECEMBER 31 1892 • . 110 W CHRISTMAS WAS SPENT AT WARRINGTON. Christmas is gone ; and with it has disappeared for another year the festivities and feastings which come and go with it. From the climatic eccentricities of the early part of last week we were promised naught of an "old fashioned " Christmas. But we got one. The genial mildness of the few preceding days passed suddenly away. and on Saturday King Frost with his nipping breath was on us. All Saturday he worked hard ; and Christmas day dawned with the whole of the neigh- bourhood clasped tightly in the embrace of the silvery king. The roads were hard, the pits were frozen ; and the country wore one vast white cloak of hoar, which sparkled with dazzling brilliance in the golden rays of the wintry sun. People were astir early on the morning of the eventful day ; and by the time the church bells bad buret forth into their mad, merry peals, Warrington streets were alive with pedestrians. Some wended their way to church and chapel; others chose rambles in the bracing air and frozen lanes, whilst the majority went to enjoy that anticipated pleasure of a good old winter—a skate. A large number of juvenile skaters repaired to the various pits in Arpley meadows, though they were not by any means in a safe condition. During the morning a young man whose name is not known to us had a narrow escape from drowning while skating on what is locally known as "The three-cornered pit." He had been en the ice some time when, without the slightest warning, it gave way underneath him, but luckily he succeeded in scrambling out of danger, and afterwards appeared apparently none the worse for his cold bath, it is remarkable that he was not drowned, as the pit is well known to be very deep in places. The pit was deserted for some time after the accident, but towards noon there were about 50 persons on the ice, who continued skating throughout the day, but no further accidents occurred. A few people paid a visit to the canal at Walton Arches, but soen found that the cracks were much too prominent to be pleasant, and this favourite skating place was entirely deserted during the greater part of the day.

At the conclusion of tho proceedinizs, the Guardians Ind visitors present were entertained to an excellent dinner provided by Mr. and Mrs. Ward, at the entire cost of the Chairman, who was very heartily thanked for his hospitality. A number of toasts were proposed and responded to. In the evening a smoking concert was given for the pleasure of the inmates. PADGATE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS.

On Monday, the children of the Padgate Industrial Schools had their annual Christmas dinner, which was served up in the schoolroom. The building with its beautiful decorations, presented a bright and cheerful appearance, and the effect was enhanced by the long rows of tables, with their spotless white coverings, adorned with plants, and surrounded by about 400 children, whose merry countenances spoke volumes as to the gusto with which they partotok of the splendid repast that had been provided for them. The work en- tailed in preparing such a feast must have been very great, and Mr. Mines, the indefatigable superintendent and his worthy partner, who evidently spared no pains to secure the well-being aad comfort of their young charges, must feel a sense of relief now that everything has passed off so successfully. The proceedings were rendered more enjoyable by a few selections given in excellent style by the band, which is made up of a few of the elder boys, who do credit to the training they have received at the hands of Mr. Mines. Among those present were the Rev. J. I. Lmigham, chaplain, and Mr. Aukland,representing the Board of Guardians.Mr.William Houghton, Springfield, had written expressing his ina- bility to be present. After dinner the children were wished the compliments of the season, both by Mr. Mines and the Rev. J. J. Langham, who afterwards tendered some kind advice to the children. In the evening an entertainment VMS provided.

div.head: BLUE 00A'T SCHOOL.
div.p: THE BLUE 00A'T SCHOOL.

As Christmas Day fell on Sunday this year, the child- ren had their usual Christmas dinner of roast pork and plum pudding, with oranges and apples for dessert, on Sunday, and then the rest of the day was spent in the usual manner. Sunday school in the afternoon, and service in chapel in the evening. On Monday the children had their tea party, and after enjoying them- selves to their hearts' content on the good things pro- vide I for them, the rest of the day WAS spent in games of various kinds. Oranges, nuts, crackers, &c., were distributed at intervals during the evening, and before retiring to rest cheers were given for the Mayor and Mayoress, who had kindly forwarded a supply of oranges and crackers, and who wished the master to convey to the children their wishes for a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. THE RAGGED SUNDaY SCHOOL. The officials of the Ragged Stffiday School, had to dis- pense with the usual tea party, and arranged instead the distribution to the children of bags each containing 211,. of provisions, including buns, scones, currant bread and jam and bread. The distribution took place at the school at four o'clock on Monday. There were about 900 recipients, and Mr. Skelland, the persevering superintendent, who has worked so faithfully and ener- getically in this philanthropic movement, had a busy time of it. He was assisted by Mr. Owen, the assistant superintendent, Mr. Sparkes, the secretary, and the teachers, about 20 in number. We have been asked to announce that the school will re-open on Sunday next. Mr. Skelland wishes to return his heartiest thanks to the tradespeople and others who have so kindly and gener- ously assisted him in his good work. COUNCILLOR ROBERTS AND THE NEWSBOYS. On Tuesday evening the newsboys of Warrington were generously entertained to an excellent tea at the British Workman Coffee-louse, Florsemarket-st., at the expense of Councillor and Mrs. Henry Roberts. About 70 lads put in an appearance, and they thoroughly enjoyed the good things which had been provided. After tea they assembled in another room, where several speeches wero delivered, and where also a performance was given for their pleasure by the Warrington Amateur Christy Min- strels, some of whom had given up private engagements to be present. Mr. Galloway was at the piano, and Mr. Frank Aukland acted as chairman of the troupe. Oranges having been distributed by Councillor Roberts, Mr. W. Roberts, and Mr. C. Lyons (" Echo" Office), Councillor H. ROBERTS called upon the youngsters to give three cheers for the manager and manageress (Mr. and Mrs. Evans), for providing the tea, and the request was heartily complied with. Shortly aftcrwares the ' " donor of the feast" gave some very suitable advice to the newsboys. He said that they were neither editors nor reporters, but there was no telling what they might become in the future. They were connected with one , of the finest a gencies,one of the most important agencies ' in the country, as they sold newspapers in the streets. He would give them a " tip"—not a gambling tip. In- stead of crowding together, three, four, five or six of them, and rushing at a customer, they should spread themselves out in the streets, and he believed that if they did so they would do more business as well as make themselves not quite such nuisances. (Laughter.) He urged them also to be teetotallers, not to gamble, but to save what little they could and to endeavour to make their way in life. (Applause.) The Rev. Father CRAVEN addressed a few suitables words to the boys, who, at his request,gave three cheer for Mr. Roberts for his hospitality. The Rev. JOHN YoNon, whose speech was also full of instruction, called upon the boys to recognise Mrs. Roberts's services in connection with the treat, and they did so by several hearty cheers. Other speeches were delivered during the evening, which was spent in an enjoyable manner, the minstrels providing an entertainment which not only amused the audience, but which reflected considerable credit upon themselves.

ROUND THE CHURCHES. At the Roman Catholic Church of St. Alban's, Bewsey- st., masses were held every half-hour on Sunday from half-past six until eleven o'clock. The church was not decorated to such an extent as in previous years, and there was nothing special in the musical portion of the services owing to the alterations that are being carried out in the chancel. Benediction was held in the evening when the choir under the conductorship of Mr. White- head, gave an excellent rendering of Gounod's " Nazer- eth."

At St. Mary's Buttermarket-st. Catholic Church, mass was celebrated every half hour from half-past six until eleven o'clock, when there was Solemn High Mass, the celebrant being Rev. Father Wray: deacon, Father Dug. an; sub-deacon, Father Turner. Father Sumner ad- dressed a few remarks to the cengregation and wished them all a happy Christmas. The musical part of the service consisted of Haydn's No. 2 Mass. In the even- ing. at Benediction. the choirmaster, Mr. Eccles, sang "Nazareth" in a very pleasing manner. The " crib " a representation of the stable at Bethlehem—was, as usual, erected, near the entrance, and looked very beau- tiful. The architectural beauties of the building are becoming apparent more and more as additions and improvements are effected. Several new "stations of the cross "of white stone, beautifully sculptured, have been erectea to replace the old ones. There are also two new holy water fonts, of very substantial design, in Cork marble.

A special Christmas service was held at the Wycliffe Congregational Church, on Sunday evening, when selec- tions from the " Messiah" were given by members of the choir, assisted by a string band. lhe soloists rere Miss M. Payton, Miss Rathbone, Mrs. R. H. Pearson, Miss Roberts and Messrs. W. fl. Wallington and A. Griffiths. The instrumentalists consisted of lffessrs.R.H. Pearson, J. Roberts, Johnson, H. Bond, R. Whitfield. Mr. G. Wallington conducted, and Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ. The Rev. J. Yonge delivered a short but excellent address, taking as his subject "Peace on earth." There was a large congregation and the service was much enjoyed, the music rendered being of a very high order. A collection, amounting to £5 95., was made for the choir fund. At the other places of worship in town the usual special services were held.

div.head: mr. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL.
div.p: mr. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL.

-- At a meeting of the Channel Tunnel Committee, Limited, held in London, on Thursday, Sir Edward Watkin. Bart., M.P., said they had got a new Parliament and a nevr Government. So far as they knew, the Government was favourably inclined to the enterprise which the company had taken in hand. He had always conceived that this question of a tunnel for connecting England with the Continent was one for the Govern- ment rather than for individuals. He then spoke of the importance of securing, an independent line of communi- cation with the Continent, and of developing the coal field they had discovered.

DISGRACEFUL ASSAULT ON A SCHOOL- MISTRESS. EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT. At the Pontefract West Riding) Court, on Wednesday John Ellis, miner, Nestell-row, Wakefield, was charged with an aggravated assault upon Miss Louisa Fawbert, a mistress under the Halifax School Board. The prisoner nleaded guilty to the charge.—The complainant a young lady of comely appearance and smart address, said : "lam a teacher under the Halifax Board. On Satur- day evening I came to Featherstone station to proceed to my home. I left Featherstone station at about 6.20 About five or ten minutes walk from Ack worth Old Hall I met the prisoner, who asked me. 'What village shall I come to next?' I said Featherstone.' He asked me how long it would take him to walk, and I said A quarter of an hour.. He asked me to shake hands with him, and I said No.' I then got off the flags on to the road to get out of his way. He came across to me and asked me to shake hands with him, but I said I can- not ; you see I have my handa full.' He then said, 'Give me a kiss.' I said, ' Indeed I won't,' and pushed him from me. I ran along the road, but he caught me and demanded a kiss. I pushed him from me, and again got away, but he caught me, and in the struggle knocked me down. He kissed me and I then saw his face. I got away, but he caught me, and we had a severe struggle. in which he knocked me down. I screamed, and he told me if I did that he would take my life. I screamed harder than ever, and he said, 'I will murder you if you scream.' "—Prisoner now pleaded guilty, but said he was in liquor at the time, and way very sorry.—The Chairman (Mr. W. F. Tempest) said prisoner would be committed for six months' hard labour—the ful- penalty the bench could inflict.

OTIIS ON GAMES AD

The Warringtonians were not up to the " scratch " in the match against Manchester on Saturday. Want of practice was a striking feature, and for once in a way, we are told, Warrington were a beaten team long before hostilities ceased. It was indeed lucky for our local club that they established the substantial lead which gave them the victory in the early portion, and had they ! showed like proper combination even in the early stages ' of anything the game the score must have been consi- derably augmented. As it was that old eagerness on the part of a few players spoiled the chances of the whole combination, hence the laxity in scoring.

Manchester had a lot the best of the second half, and I after their penalty goal had been obtained, the game I was rarely out of the visitors' 25. To this fact may be attributed the loss of at least four Warrington forwards, who, although they continued to struggle on, were little or no use, owing to injuries received' It may safely be said that thirty minutes out of the last half were con- tested with five Warrington forwards only doing duty, and praise is due to Ashton, Jolley, and Turner for their untiring energies.

Of the backs none did better than Bate, Webster, and Boscow. The last-named had all his work cut out for him in the last quarter of an hour, but he played his usual cool game, as the Manchester men can testify. Webster's fine turn of speed was of immense service, whilst the well-timed passing of Bate in the first half led up to an almost incessant attack.

The Lancashire Rugby Cup Competition has not yet reached its half-time stage, though the season may be said to be entering on the second portion of its career. But a glance at the statistical table gives the impression that Swinton will run out the champion club. The lead they possess now is so marked that unless something unforeseen happens that lead will be maintained.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

_ __----. King Hoar and the festivities of the season have played the everlasting mischief with local football. The hard white frost has held the ground in such hard grip as to prevent at least the senior teams from conducting their gymnastic performances. And some of the junior teams whilst not suffering in this way, have suffered by keeping up the festivities of the season.

Real genuine football has been so decidedly "or! "this week end that I am afraid I must trouble the readers with a little correspondence, which I would otherwise have omitted. And the first letter is thus:—

" Respected sir, as a constant reader of this column I have received a considerable amount of entertainment, and information from the utterances of yourself and the P.D. I wish to show my gratitude. So please find en- closed a toy trumpet to amuse yourself with, and a classical dictionary and some undiluted laudunum for the P.D. That will make him as snug and peaceful as the best of them in the cemetery."

I thank this correspondent,whose name I will not dis- close ; I have given the P.D. his present, but my own I have left with the fighting editor, a nice, kind, man,and he says he will return it to the benevolent correspon- dent with another present.

Respecting the observations which I made last week anent Hampson's play with the A team against Fallow- field, another correspondent writes :—"Sir,—As a con- stant and regular reader of the Examiner, and especi- ally the Athletic Notes, I think I may freely confess that I have not for a long time come across anything which I think is more uncharitable than the remarks you made last week about F. Hampson's play. He certainly did not distinguish himself particularly, as you said. But no one expected that he would, because had he been in the habit of playing a much better game than he did, I think he would have been in the first team by now. He is a young player, and ought to receive a little more consideration. I think you were somewhat unjust with him."

Pablo Lamerre, a Spanish General,had under him some of the smartest young officers Spain possessed. When asked how he trained them to such perfection, he said, 'By honest criticism." I hope my corresponent, who signs himself the " Bumble Bee " will think about this ; and when he has grasped its meaning I hope he will claw it to his bosom, and then if he doesn't mind, try and recover sufficient presence of mind to take from the nib of his pen the little hairs which have caused so many blotches on his epistle. Goodbye Mr. Busy " Bumble Bee?

Now before getting to the more solid portion of this official bulletin, I will reiterate a little story once told by a contemporary. A certain footballer not living a hundred miles away, who had a very fine nose, played on a frozen field. His name was if and when he fell upon his probuscous upon the ground, he shouted " Oh !" for the prominent feature hung limp and lanky on his face. He was sorely afraid he would spoil his beauty for over, and so he hurried away to a doctor, who, soon put the splints, and made John as happy as a man with chronic catarrh who has lost his handker- chief. He was very anxious to know whether it would grow again as pretty as it was before, and felt greatly relieved and delighted when the doctor told him when the nose was broken it could be re-modelled to any shape desired.

This was glorious news to the plastered player and his jog was even more radiant when the man of medicine said if It —would choose his style, he would fix him up like a mythological hero. Would you like a Duke of Wellington, a Grecian nose or a Roman knocker said the surgeon. John decided for the Greek god style, but when the doctor told his man to go into the study and fetch the fashion book of noses, it dawned upon the brain of handsome John that he was being" spoofed." He left before the messenger returned.

div.head: TRICKED.
div.p: TRICKED.

All's fair in love and war—and in modern Association football. I once refereed in a match between two well- known teams which, to separate them from professional combinations dub themselves " gentlemanly." Bogus claims were made by one side until I became wearied, so I said to one of the players during a lull in the game, " You know very well that that last shot was not a goal." "Of course I do," he replied; " but I didn't know that you did, and nothing is lost by appealing." That is exactly the standing motto of the average pro- fessional footballer—" Nothing is lost by appealing." When a goal is hotly attacked it is a regular dodge for the keeper or one of the backs to shout" Off-side !" and many a time have I seen a free kick result and the goal thereby cleared. Another trick that often pays is prac- tised during a" bully "or crush in goal. One of the defending side will deliberately handle the ball and then claim a foul for hands—a claim which is allowed sadly too often. Or, if a goal is scored, some custodians will occasionally bring back the ball with all the coolness ' imaginable, and declare that the attackers claimed, and must take a free kick. More than once to my know- ledge this dodge has meant all the difference between the winning and losing of a match. Touching this mat- ter of hands 'and of the difficulty which a referee sometimes has in deciding between conflicting claims, I remember a very funny experience. From a corner kick the ball was dropped right in front of goal, and was shot through. At the same moment a" smack " was heard, and immediately the cry of " Hands !" was raised. The referee was inclined to allow the claim, but the centre forward of the side which had scored drew attention to his ear, which was red and evidently pain- ful. The centre, it seemed, went to head the ball just as the goalkeeper tried to fist out, and so received a blow in the ear that nearly stunned 'him. Some q tick passing and across-shot into goal frequently result in the ball going just inside the posts. The referee is un- able to keep up with ball, and, consequently, is uncer- tain whether it went between the pasts or not. , " Smart " goalkeepers, in these circumstances, quickly pick up the ball and kick off from goal, as if it had gone ontside. The attacking team appeal, as a matter of course, for a goal ; but the referee, not being certain, gives the defenders, as magistrates give prisoners, "the benefit of the doubt." I remember an instance of this kind of thing which occurred in a cup tie. One of the full backs deliberately stepped forward in order to obstruct the view of the referee, and a legitimate goal was disallowed. On the other hind, I have heard it said, though I have never seen this myself, that weak- willed referees have been deceived by confident appeals when the bail has just gone outside the posts. All this, however, is done away with by using the nets which have recently been adopted. About foul play—tripping and "settling' players—no referee can say all be thinks. Enough that a good deal of what is ascribed to accident is really malicious injury. The referees are deceived, and so is nearly verybody else.—Casselt's; Saturday Journal. •

div.head: LIBERATOR BUILDING SOCIETY
div.p: THE LIBERATOR BUILDING SOCIETY
AID FOR THE SUFFERERS.

A meeting of the committee formed for raising a pre- liminary fund of £lO,OOO in aid of the sufferers by the failure of the Liberator Building Society and kindred institutions was held at the Memorial Hall, Farringdon- st., London, on Thursday afternoon. It was reported that a large number of applications 'or relief had been received from persons who had been entirely ruined by the disaster, and that a considerable portion were from people exceeding sixty and seventy years of age. The Rev. Herber Evans, chairman of the Congregational Union, had written that no part of the kingdom had been more heavily stricken than Wales by the failure, and there was a general opinion expressed that the downfall of the Liberator was the worst crash which the country had experienced since the Glasgow Bank disas- ter. It is anticipated that relief for the most distress- ing cases will be voted at the next meeting of the com- mittee, on Thursday next.

div.head: "YOU CANNOT BE TOO CAREFUL."
div.p: "YOU CANNOT BE TOO CAREFUL."

A young man of good family was before the police authorities in Vienna a few days ago, on a summons which caused consternation to his parents and friends. He was informed that he had been denounced as a for- ger. It was not until he had received some hints as to I the circumstances of the denunciation that he found it possible to explain his innocence. Some time ago he brought home a small press for printing, and showed his astonished family how by putting pieces of white paper the exact size cf florins into the press and turning the handle twice real florins, the genuineness of which no one could doubt, could be obtained. A servant had been in the room at the time. She was discharged by her mistress some days afterwards, and eut of spite she sent the information to the police. The young man was allowed to send for the apparatus, and when it came the officials amused themselves by playing with it. The secret was that real florins were put in a hidden drawer of the press, and the turning of the handle placed these where the blank paper had been before,thus creating the delusion that the florins were forged ones coined on the spot.

div.head: HALLELUJAH LASS AND THE CHURCHWARDEN.
div.p: THE HALLELUJAH LASS AND THE CHURCHWARDEN.
A CURIOUS COMPLAINT.

At the South-Western Police Court, London, a curious application was made to Mr. Plowden, by a middle-aged woman, dressed in the Salvation Army uniform, who complained of the conduct of the churchwardens of St. Peter's, Battersea. She stated that they refused to per- mit her to attend the service. Mr. Plowden: Why did they prevent you P—Applicant : I don't know. I shall never leave the church as long as Christ sends me there. I mean to be in the front rank. (Laughter.)—Mr. Plow- den : What did they do P—Applicant : One of the church- wardens stood at the door, but by the strength of God he went on one side and I entered. (Laughter.)—Mr. Plowden : That is all right.—Applicant : But a grey- headed old sinner—(loud laughter)—prevented me from entering a pew, stating that it was appropriated.—Mr. Plowden : I will have inquiries made.—Applicant : Do you think that will do ?—Mr. Plowden : I think so.— Applicant: You will find what I say is'correct. I will win my victory yet. (Laughter.) She left the court wish- , ing "God's blessings" on all.

div.head: DANGERS OF SKATING.
div.p: THE DANGERS OF SKATING.
DROWNING FATALATIES.

A sad accident occurred at the deep lodge connected with the Mareland Dyeworks at Rochdale on Monday. While skating there a couple fell, and, breaking through the ice, almost disappeared beneath the water. During the efforts made to rescue them no fewer than twelve skaters were immersed, and five persons were drowned, Skating on Monday, owing to the brittleness of the newly formed ice, was perilous. Not only at Rochdale but in several other parts of the country there were fatal ic accidents. A boy was drowned in a pond at Folkestonee a lac' was drowned at Macclesfield, a youth was drowned in the Waterloo Lake at Roundbay Park, Leeds, and three men were drowned in the lake in Wanstead Park, Essex.

The water was drawn off at Marland lodge, Rochdale, on Tuesday. No additional bodies were found, and the number of lives lost owing to the ice accident on Mon- day is four. On Tuesday a boy was skating on the pond near the Barrow Printworks at Clitheroe, he broke through the ice and was drowned. Several other fatal ice accidents are reported.

A sad accident occurred on Wednesday, at Jack Kay lodge, Spring Vale, near Darwen. Mr. Frank Moore, aged 19, a student at Oweus College, and eldest son of the Rev. H. H. Moore, vicar of St. John's, Darwen, was skatingfon the pond with his sisters and a college friend, when the ice broke. Mr. Moore fell into the water, managed to get one knee on the ice again, and shouted to his companions to keep away from the treacherms place. Suddenly the ice broke a second time, and though desperate efforts were made to rescue him he sank ex- hausted and was drowned. At Oulton Broad, near Lowestoft, on Wednesday, the ice gave way,and a youth was drowned.

COUNTY OF CHESTER, TO WIT. TcOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER, will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 2nd day of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hun- dreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all pris- oners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 2nd day of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clack in the Forenoon. - THE Court will be Adjourned to the Court House, Nether Knutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the 4th day of Janu- ary next, at Eleven o'clock in the forenoon. The hear- ing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attend- ance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 4th day of January next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS. Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 12th December, 1892.
