RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present, the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Baxter, C. C. Weir, J. Baguley, J. Stokes, Pickering, Lewis, Williams, Knowles, 11. E. Hey- wood, J. Whitlow, Wilkinson, J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (nuisance Inspector). SEWERAGE SCHEME FOR APPLETON. The Appleton Parochial Committee recommended that Mr. Silcock's scheme and plans fcr the extension of the sewerage works at Stockton Heath be approved, and that application be made to the Local Government Board tor sanction to a loan of £1,500 for carrying out the scheme. the Clerk was instructed to arrange for such wayleaves as might be necessary. The recom- mendation was adopted on the motion of Mr. Whitlow, seconded by Mr. Knowles. AN APPLETON NUISANCE. The Inspector reported that in accordance with the instructions of the Appleton Parochial Committee, he had served notice uprin Mrs. Margaret Percival, the owner of three cottages situate in Walton-road, at Stockton Heath, to provide drainage and closet or privy accommodation to the cottages. The Inspector added that he considered that it would be a hardship upon the owner to insist upon the notices being com- plied with in their entirety, and he (the inspector) had received a censure for making such a statement, and was directed to see that the notices were complied with. As an officer under the Sanitary Authority it was his bounden duty to caution them to be very careful in accepting and sanctioning the action proposed to be taken by the Committee in reference to the notices, or they might find themselves in a very awkward position. In answer to questions, the Inspector said there was no land whatever to the cottages, and it was proposed to pull down one house to supply the other two with sanitary accommodation. He pointed out that all the expense would devolve upon the Sanitary Authority. The Clerk said it would be time enough to deal with the matter when the notices had expired. THE PROPOSED VEHICULAR BRIDGE OVER THE MERSEY. The Local Government Board wrote adverting to an in- quiry with respect to the vehicular bridge and in reply stated that the Rural Sanitary Authority of the Runcorn Union,not being in the present case the Highway Autho- rity, are net empowered to make a contribution to- wards the cost of the erection of the proposed new bridge across the Mersey.—Mr. Heywood said under these circumstances he proposed that a communication be forwarded to Cheshire County Council, urging them to help forward the scheme by all means in their power. —Mr. J. Baguley seconded the motion, which was car- ried unanimously. THE IMPORTATION OF CHOLERA. Dr. Williams gave an account of the proceedings at the conference held in Liverpool during the previous week, with respect to the formation of a great Sanitary Authority for the Mersey, to prevent the importation of cholera. It was stated that if the intentions of the Government were persevered in, the sum of £7,000 a year would be required, instead of £7OO, as at present ; and a resolution was passed approvinz of the present arrangements, and stating that they were quite suffi- cient.—lt was probable that the question would be made a national one, but in the meantime, Mr. Williams considered it would be advisable' that the Authority should make arrangements with reference to the ships arriving in Saltport.—A committee was appointed to make the necessary arrangements. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The medical officer (Dr. Adams) reported a case of typhoid fever at Helsby. He had made an exhaustive examination of the premises, and could find no explana- tion of the disease unless it be in connection with the sewage from houses situated above the railway station, which for a short length is not piped, but afterwards joins the station sewage, in properly laid and trapped drains. Two cases of scarlet fever had occurred at Wildorapool-read, and one in Wilderspool entry. The usual precautions had been adopted. No fresh case of smallpox had yet been reported. SMALLPDX AT WESTON. Mr. Stokes said he underst sod there was an outbreak of smallpox at Weston.—lnspector Farrington said lie had heard nothing of it until he arrived at the work- house.—He was instructed to at once make inquiries and to take immediate steps to prevent the disease spreading. -Os JUVENILE GEMS. The following quotations from examination papers of Some of the ingenious youths of England have been selected and published in the" University Correspond- ent." From them we learn : " Esau was a man who wrote fables, and sold his copyright fora bottle of potash.- " Titus was a Roman Emperor, supposed to have written the epistle to the Hebrews—his other name was Oates" " Henry 111, was a zealous supporter of the Church, and died a dissentry." " Perkin Warbeck raised a rebellion in the reign of Henry VIII. He said he was the son of a prince ; but he was really the son of respectable people.' "Fossils are those remains of plants and animals which keep best when left to themselves. In some rocks we find the fossil footprints of fishes." " The two chief volcanoes in Europe are Sodom and Gomorrah !" THE BISHOP OF CHESTER EXPLAINS HIS SCHEBIE. A correspendent states that the Bishop of Chester, wishing to correct some misapprehensions with regard to his licensing scheme, denies that the rate of 5 per cent interest mentioned was definitely part of the scheme. The amount was mentioned simply by way of illustration. In this country a lower rate of interest would undoubtedly suffice. His Lordship also explains that he has from the first and very distinctly guarded against the employment of the surplus profits to aid the rates, and he also is anxious to put himself right with the public as regards the expression " attractive public- houses." He explains that the public-house he would establish would be one in which alcoholic beverages would he deposed frem their aggressive supremacy, and different and more beneficial attractions provided. A DEADLY FEUD. THE WAY THEY DO IN TEXAS. A telegram from Arlington, Texas, reports an extra- ordinary tragedy, entailing the loss of four lives. J. Hargrove, with his sons, Walker and George, arrived by train at that place heavily armed. As they left the train two men named Harry Spears and William Smith, sud- denly emerged from behind the railway station, and shot Mr. Hargrove, senior, who fell fatally wounded, after which they ran to the other side of the train and shot and killed George. Walker's Winchester rifle refus- ing to work, he ran and got a revolver from his father; and killed both Spears and Smith, who fired about a dozen shots at Walker without hitting him. When the train moved so that the father could see the bodies of Spears and Smith, he raised laimself on his elbow and fired several bullets into them. He then fell back and expired. It appears that the tragedy was the result of ass old feud, and that the parties had met by mutual ar- rangement for the purpose of fighting it out.

A CHAPTER OF FATALITIES. _- A batch of fatalities engaged the attention of Mr. Flint the Burton coroner, yesterday afternoon. Walter Daw- son, labourer, hanged himself in the racking-room of Messrs. Bass and Co.'s old brewery; John Henry Bennett, a hale and hearty young fellow in appearance, fell dewn and died immediately while at wor. in Messrs. Worthington's cqoperage ; the body of a barber named George Smith was found in the Trent; and Thos. Jones was fatally injured by a fall at Newhall Colliery, Swad- lincote. SHOCKING GAS EXPLOSION THE OLD STORY. A gas explosion took place on Thursday, at Gates- head, by which a house was wrecked. One man was injured, and the other inmates had a marvellous escape. Mr. Kowe, an insurance agent, smelt gas in several of , the rooms, and turned it off at the meter. He opened the door, and than lit a match in a front room, but remembered nothing more till he found himself lying outside the door with his shirt and trousers on fire, and beard, moustache, and hair almost singed off. When he became conscious he found his wife, three children, and his wife's mother had all escaped unhurt. The windows of the house were blown out, the ceiling was destroyed and large stones had come down. All the furniture, pictures, glass, and crockery were smashed to pieces, in fact, the house was wrecked in a most complete man- ner. Part of the furniture which was inside the house is now lying in the gardens broken. THE ROYAL COMMISSION ON THE AGED POOR. THE PRINCE OF WALES A MEMBER. It is stated that the Prince of Wales has consented to act as a member of the Royal Commission upon the Aged Poor, under the chairmanship of Lord Aberdare. The terms of reference are whether any alterations in the system of poor law relief are desirable in the case of persons whose destitution is occasioned by incapacity far work resulting from old age or whether assistance could otherwise be afforded in those cases. The other members of the Commission number 17 making 19 in all—viz., Lord Lingen, Lord Brassey, Lord Playfair, the Right Hon. J. Chamberlain,the Right Hon. C. J. Ritchie, Sir Herbert E. Maxwell, Bart, M.P., Mr. C. P. Roundell, ALP., Mr. James Stuart, M.P., Dr. W. A. Hunter, M.P., Mr. Joseph Arch, M.P., Mr. Albert Pell, Mr. Henry Broadhurst, Mr. J. J. Henley, C. 8., Mr. Charles Booth, Mr. C. S. Loch, Mr. A. C. Humphreys Owen, and Mr. J. J. Stocked. The secretary to the Com- mission will be Mr. E. Austin Browne, ot the Local Government Board. It is stated that Mr. Stansfield, ALP., and Mr. John Burns, M.P., were asked to serve upon the Commission, but declined on the ground that other engagements would interfere with the due discharge of their duties.

ST. HELENS CORPORATE OFFICIALS' SALARIES. The salary of Ur. Jeeves, town-clerk, St. Helens, is to be increased by £2OO per annum, making it £7OO, and that of Mr. Broom, surveyor, £lOO, making it £5OO. It is understood that an implied condition cf Mr. Jeeves' increase is that he will hold the town-clerkship without further increase for five years.

1 STRIKE OF MANCHESTER PANTOMIME HANDS. SINGULAR MOVEMENT. The scene shifters and supernumeraries engaged in the Manchester pantomimes struck work on Thursday morn- ing and left the theatres. The movement was evidently ) a premeditated and combined one, but the reason is not , yet known. Some inconvenience and perhaps a little i anxiety were caused to the various managers, but new i hands were speedily forthcoming, and the difficulty . , overcome. Mr. G. H. Brooks, of the Comedy Theatre, ... who was seen on the subject, stated that lie had no i previous intimation of the movement, nor is he able to suggest any ground for it. A similar step was taken some time time ago in Lonlon, the grievance of the men in that instance being that they were underpaid. It is supposed that the local hands feel themselves similarly aggrieved, and that they acted in unison with their , -I brethren in London.
